https://claude.ai/code/artifact/344c5a6c-2da1-44ef-87c7-2b4e978f154f 

**Benchmark numbers are promising but don't paint this as a slam dunk:**



Custom Metrics

Three numbers for "did the extraction keep the page's content, and nothing else."
Everything is computed on **normalized** text, so markdown, emphasis, quotes,
dashes, whitespace and rendered-vs-LaTeX math (`κ` = `\kappa`) never count as a
difference.

Let $G$ be the gold text and $P$ the prediction.

- $S(x)$ = the **set of 5-grams** of $\text{normalize}(x)$
- $U(G)$ = the **sentences of $G$** with at least 8 words

## KEPT — recall

Fraction of gold's sentences that survive. A sentence counts as kept if at least
half of its 5-grams appear anywhere in the prediction:

$$\text{KEPT} = \frac{1}{|U(G)|}\sum_{u \in U(G)} \mathbb{1}\!\left[\frac{|S(u) \cap S(P)|}{|S(u)|} \ge 0.5\right]$$

Sentences shorter than 5 words can't form a 5-gram, so they're matched by direct
substring containment instead.

## CLEAN — precision

Fraction of what we emitted that actually exists in gold:

$$\text{CLEAN} = \frac{|S(P) \cap S(G)|}{|S(P)|}$$

## FIDELITY — the headline

F-score of the two, with **recall weighted twice as heavily** as precision
($\beta^2 = 2$), because dropping content is worse than keeping extra:

$$\text{FIDELITY} = \frac{(1+\beta^2)\cdot \text{CLEAN} \cdot \text{KEPT}}{\beta^2 \cdot \text{CLEAN} + \text{KEPT}} = \frac{3\cdot \text{CLEAN}\cdot \text{KEPT}}{2\cdot \text{CLEAN} + \text{KEPT}}$$

The same construction gives **CODE**, **MATH**, **TABLE** and **WHO** — identical
to KEPT, but with $U(G)$ replaced by gold's code lines, math expressions, table
cells, or speaker names.




Overall I think our new spec is better but it wasn't as easy to hill climb this as I had hoped.

Details Spec-Driven Mix: Surprisingly it doesn't move DCLM that much, although it makes HQ competitive with DCLM: Fully inverts the OLMO scores though when you mix for DCLM instead:
--- --- **BLEnD Cultural QA:** From here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.09948
Details Spec-Driven Mix: Interestingly the DCLM data is better for cultural QA than our old spec, but I suspect our new spec will be better: I also suspect this might have more to do with models being good at in-context MCQ than cultural understanding
---
---
The Problem with DCLM Core DCLM Disaggregated: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/dc5f1cf5-eb62-4c99-9e2f-70472b28797e OLMO Disaggregated: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/ce4e61f6-f3e9-433b-ae76-805a12015ee5 DCLM Core is super noisy. Some are higher signal (basically hellaswag), and with mixing we can improve over Hellaswag: But many **many** are just noise, and no sense of trying to win on them at this scale: In contrast OLMO bpb seems to be pretty high signal: Although there are some that are still noisy here too: My thought: **maybe we forget about DCLM Core and showcase wins on OLMO Base Easy instead at least for spec-driven project at smaller scale** This is where we already win, no new specs, no mixing needed!
---
Distillation Progress Distilling back into our FastText -> ModernBERT -> Resiliparse/JustText pipeline for LLM_Curated_v1.1. **FastText**: **ModernBERT**: Still training - ModernBERT 1M: 40.3% (step 1,575 / 3,906) — on pace to finish tonight, F1 lands right after in its end-of-run eval. - ModernBERT 10M: 11.1% (step 4,317 / 39,062) — the multi-day flagship, pace steady at ~5s/step, ETA roughly 2 days out. **Resiliparse (instead of JustText since it is faster)**:
---
Plan **Experiment Idea**: Scale everything down by 20x. So instead of a 100B model we are training a 5B, and instead of nemotron producing 7T tokes we sample 350B tokens. And instead of a 2T token target or similar we have a 200B token target. Once I extract 5% of the internet I will have about 3-4T tokens or so. We would be comparing 350B tokens of nemotron to 2T tokens of my data, on a 200B token target for a 5B model. We can do whatever data mixing we choose but at the end of the day we need to find the best 200B tokens to train that 5B model. This seems like the most fair way to compare the data at smaller scale and should be achievable within a week or so of launching my big run.
---

# Weekly Sync 8/31-9/4 ---
"Hero" Data Curation Run Progress We currently have about 10T tokens of pre-dedupe data processed! This will be significantly lower after dedupe, but dedupe alone now takes many hours (days?) to run, so I don't have timely feedback about how much data we have post-dedupe. **Updated this morning:**
> [!TIP] > The run is about 15% of the way through and will finish in the next 2 weeks if I don't steal my compute for other experiments. ---
More principled FLOP estimation ## Inference FLOPs of the fast curation cascade **Estimate: 1.3e10 to 1.7e10 FLOPs per extracted document, 5.1e14 to 6.7e14 per WARC, and 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 for the 8M-WARC run (7,925,398 WARCs).** The low end charges each document its real token count; the high end charges the padded length the chip actually runs. ettin68 accounts for 98% of the total. | | Actual lengths | Padded lengths | |---|---|---| | Per extracted doc | 1.3e10 | 1.7e10 | | Per kept doc | 6.9e10 | 9.0e10 | | Per WARC | 5.1e14 | 6.7e14 | | Per kept token (ModernBERT tokens) | 5.1e7 | 6.7e7 | | 8M run total | 4.0e21 | 5.3e21 | The rest of this note explains how the numbers are produced. The deployed pipeline (`lpv11_fastpipe_v2_1_fused`) scores every extracted document with three classifiers in sequence: fastText, a pooled super-token transformer, and ettin68. Each stage only sees the documents the previous stage passed on, so the cost per document is an expectation over the stages a document reaches. ### Stages and reach rates | Stage | Model | Context | Condition to run | Share of extracted docs | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | fastText w640 | full doc | always | 100% | | 2 | pooled transformer (90M-doc ckpt) | 8192 | fastText prob ≥ 0.0048 | 58.2% | | 3 | ettin68 | 2048 | pooled prob in [0.079, 0.8883) | 20.1% | Of the documents the pooled model scores, 18.3% are accepted outright, 47.2% are dropped, and 34.6% go to ettin68. Overall, 19.2% of extracted documents are kept. Rates are measured from production catalogs (52 shards, 12,824 WARCs). Per WARC: 39,464 records, 38,560 extracted docs, 22,423 fastText survivors, 7,749 band docs, 7,413 kept docs. ## Expected cost per document ``` E[FLOPs per extracted doc] = c_ft + p_ft * E[ c_pool(min(L, 8192)) | passed fastText ] + p_ft * p_band * E[ c_ettin(min(L, 2048)) | in band ] p_ft = 0.5815 p_band = 0.3456 ``` Each stage's cost is averaged over the token-length distribution of the documents that actually reach it. Those distributions come from the 100k comparison sample, which stores every stage's score per document: we tokenize its deployment text with the ModernBERT tokenizer and apply the production thresholds. The sample's reach rates match production within two points. **How padding works.** Within a WARC, the scorer sorts a stage's documents by length, takes batches of 32, and pads each batch to the smallest bucket in (128, 256, ..., context) that fits the longest document in that batch. The last batch is filled to 32 rows with empty rows. Because batches are length-sorted, all 32 documents in a batch are close in length, so the padded cost is well approximated by charging each document its own bucket; simulating the real per-batch procedure on the sample gives the same mean within 1%. Padding raises the mean charged length by 1.37x for the pooled stage and 1.30x for ettin68, which is the gap between the two columns below and in the headline table. | Stage | Reach rate | Mean tokens, actual (capped at context) | Mean tokens, padded | Cost per doc, actual | Cost per doc, padded | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | fastText | 100% | 1,318 (no cap) | n/a | 2.0e5 | 2.0e5 | | pooled | 58.2% | 1,010 | 1,380 | 4.1e8 | 5.7e8 | | ettin68 | 20.1% | 608 | 792 | 6.5e10 | 8.5e10 | ## 8M run document counts (7,925,398 WARCs) | | Count | |---|---| | Docs scored by fastText | 3.1e11 | | Docs scored by pooled | 1.8e11 | | Docs scored by ettin68 | 6.1e10 | | Kept docs | 5.9e10 | For reference, 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 FLOPs is the 6ND training cost of a 1B model on 700B to 900B tokens. ## Caveats - FLOPs and chip time diverge. Measured chip time from the catalogs implies MFU of 0.1 to 0.4% for the pooled stage and 1.4 to 5.7% for ettin68. All-in, the run is 26.2 v6e-8 slice-seconds per WARC (about 58k slice-hours for 8M WARCs), which is 0.35% MFU against the FLOP total. - fastText FLOPs count arithmetic only. Its measured cost is 0.55 CPU-ms per document, mostly hashing and table lookups. - Token counts use the ModernBERT tokenizer, not the training tokenizer. - Reach rates are from the current ladder's crawl mix.
Conventions - Forward pass only; a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs. - Embedding lookups, layer norms, softmax, activations, and the pooling reduction count as zero. - Length `L` includes the two special tokens and is capped at the stage context. The padded variant rounds `L` up to the next bucket in (128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192). - Empty tail rows in a WARC's last batch are included in the per-batch simulation and add under 1%.
fastText formula dim 100, word bigrams, no character n-grams (read from the model header). Features are words plus bigrams, about twice the word count; words are taken as 0.75 of ModernBERT tokens. One add per dimension per feature, then a 100 x 2 output layer. ``` F = 2 * 0.75 * T c_ft = 100 * F + 2 * 100 * 2 ≈ 150 T + 400 ``` At T = 1,318 this is 2.0e5.
Pooled transformer formula Levanter's `PooledTransformerConfig.flops_per_token`, called directly. `L` padded tokens, `S = L / 64` super-tokens, hidden `D = 512`, pooled input width 768 (mean, max, min of 256-dim embeddings), feed-forward 2048, 4 layers, 2 labels. ``` proj = 2 * 768 * D * S layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 * S # q, k, v, o projections + 2 * 2 * S^2 * D # QK^T and AV + 2 * 2 * D * 2048 * S # MLP head = 2 * D * 2 c_pool(L) = proj + 4 * layer + head ``` About 4.1e5 FLOPs per input token, nearly flat in `L`.
ettin68 formula Hand-derived (Levanter's generic helper adds a vocabulary-head term a classifier does not have). Hidden `D = 512`, GeGLU feed-forward 768, 19 layers, 8 heads, global attention on every third layer starting at layer 0 (7 layers), sliding window 128 on the other 12. ``` linear_per_token_per_layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 # q, k, v, o + 2 * D * 2 * 768 # GeGLU up and gate + 2 * 768 * D # down attn_per_token_per_layer = 4 * span * D # span = L (global), min(L, 128) (local) c_ettin(L) = L * sum over 19 layers of (linear + attn) ``` Linear term 8.5e7 per token (two times the 42M non-embedding parameters); attention 3.2e7 at L = 2048; total 1.17e8 per token.
Data sources - Reach rates and per-WARC counts: fused catalogs, 52 random shards of the 404 to 8079 ladder. - Per-stage length distributions: 100k comparison sample (`extractor_compare/high_quality_200warc`), deployment text tokenized with `answerdotai/ModernBERT-base`, production thresholds applied to stored scores. - Model shapes: checkpoint `config.json` for pooled 90M and ettin68; fastText hyperparameters from the model binary header. - Chip time: catalog columns `pooled_s` and `score_s` times device count, per device type.
> [!TIP] > The distilled pipeline is projected to take about 5e21 flops to run on the full 8M WARC files. > The previous 8B model running on all of the internet was projected to take between 3e25 and 1.8e26 flops depending on if I used the pipeline version or the single call spec. > The fact that it is taking a month is likely somewhat due to poor MFU ---
Updated Main Results from Mixing
> [!TIP] > Finally showing signs of how the "more data" really helps at scale (100B+ tokens) ---
Beta Paper Outline Old Paper: https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4 New Paper (extremely preliminary for now, will auto-update here): https://www.overleaf.com/read/tzzfngmmyqsp#daf616 **Introduction:** Something about how we should spend way more compute on data curation but it doesn't need to be more complicated. **Background**: Current data curation pipelines including data mixing **Method**: Spec-Driven Curation, as well as the distillation into FastText, Pooled Transformer, and Ettin68 (modernBERT) **Swapping the spec enables control of the data distribution**: We show different specs lead to expected changes in data downstream
Plots
We then argue that because of the mixing and the growing demand for tokens we opt to use the coverage spec. **Spec-Driven Curation Yields Bigger and Better Data**: We show that by using our high coverage spec distilled pipeline we get more data and can mix it to be better at many domains.
Plots **Bigger**: Everything else bends upwards, but we can train on 100B+ tokens from just 10k WARCs. If we 800x (which is a bad way to do this bc no accounting for dedup), then we should be able to train on 80T tokens without issue. **Better Coverage**: We can mix for several downstream target capabilities.
**Ablations**: When we remove parts of the system how much does it impact performance. All ablations will be done on the olmo base easy eval set.
Plots **THESE ARE JUST STAND IN PLOTS, I HAVE TO RUN THESE EXPERIMENTS:** **Original Resiliparse vs Our "AutoResearch" Resiliparse**: **Spec for Quality ("High Quality") vs Spec for Coverage ("High Coverage")**: **Distilled Pipeline into Classifiers vs Original**: **Mixing vs No Mixing**:
**Discussion**: Scaling this up to the full internet **Conclusion**: Invest more flops into the pretraining data curation.

## TL;DR

MI350X best: 14.31% MFU (`ring_dedup` + gather combine + ROCm top-k + flash attention + new `ragged_dot`, bf16, batch 64, `save_moe` remat, 1.580 s per step). Before the MoE changes: 12.70% (batch 96, `save_moe`, 2.670 s). All from clean compiles.
MI300X best: 10.3% MFU at batch 32 (unconfirmed: hung at step 10); confirmed 8.66% at batch 16.

## Description

#9462 got the full 67B-A2B Snowball (June) model training on one 8-GPU AMD node. This issue tracks raising its MFU, mainly on MI350X, with MI300X as the reference. Each experiment gets one comment with the commit, the exact command and the result; the tables below index those comments and are edited as results land.

Shared setup, unless a row says otherwise: full June model, one 8-GPU node, EP8 (`--expert-axis 8`), reference attention, `ring` MoE backend, 4096 context, synthetic tokens, XLA command buffers off. Benchmark script: `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py` (#9693, not yet merged). Slurm wrapper: [`run_gpu.sh`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6018393879) (to be committed).

MFU is against AMD's dense bf16 peak (MI300X 1,307 TFLOP/s, MI350X 2,307 TFLOP/s).

### Slurm wrapper used by every command in this issue

All commands submit `run_gpu.sh` from `$WORK/marin` on the AMD HPC Fund cluster. It turns XLA command buffers off; a later `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=...` in `XLA_FLAGS` overrides that. It will be committed to the repo; this comment is the reference until then.

<details><summary>run_gpu.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -o pipefail
cd "$WORK/marin"
export RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=${RAGGED_DOT_IMPL:-xla} PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Command buffers (HIP graphs) corrupt memory on this ROCm stack: nan gradients and segfaults after a few steps.
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer= $XLA_FLAGS"
uv run --no-sync python "$@" 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered -v -E "rocm_pcie_bandwidth|rocm_executor"
```

</details>

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

MI350X reaches 3.86% MFU with bf16 Triton `ragged_dot`; its fp16 XLA runs reach 2.59–2.83%. The reported ~10 ms Triton expert matmul is a bottleneck hypothesis; the current MI350X results do not include a pinned-revision profile that attributes the full step. MI300X batch 32 reached 10.3% MFU over steps 2–9 but hung at step 10, which coincides with the trainer's watch interval; the cause and sustained throughput remain unconfirmed.

**Relevant code**
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108) — benchmark flags; no watch control
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166) — trainer uses default watch configuration
- [`train.py#L641-L649`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/train.py#L641-L649) — interval selects watch computation
- [`ragged_dot.py#L341-L367`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L341-L367) — XLA/Triton selection

# Proposed Fix

1. Extend the existing benchmark PR #9693 with a benchmark-only watch interval flag (0 disables watch) and the Slurm wrapper used in the issue. Pin one post-rebase benchmark commit and the ROCm/JAX versions for every comparison. Keep the production watch default unchanged.
2. On 8× MI300X, rerun the full EP8 batch-32 configuration for 20 steps with watch intervals 10 and 0, `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla`, memory fraction 0.90, no profiler, and command buffers off. Record the step-10 outcome, median time over non-watch steps 2–9 and 11–19, tokens/s, MFU, and peak memory. Treat 10.3% as preliminary until a 20-step run completes; if both variants hang, capture the failing step's trace before changing the model.
3. At the same pinned commit, rerun MI350X bf16/Triton batch 8 and fp16/XLA batches 8, 16, and 32 with the same 20-step setup. Profile a separate run of the fastest completed configuration and report time in expert GEMMs, collectives, other kernels, and host gaps. Compare against the MI300X reference only after these reruns.
4. Use that profile to choose one next change: test `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` if communication dominates, or tune the Triton expert GEMM if it dominates. Test command-buffer types separately on a smaller shape with finite-loss checks before a full-model run; the [current ROCm setup](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/559) has produced non-finite gradients and crashes with command buffers enabled. Post each run's commit, exact command, job ID, step time, MFU, peak memory, and negative results here.

Completion criterion: a full 20-step MI350X run with finite loss and a measured improvement over the rerun bf16/Triton batch-8 baseline (previously 3.86%). #9777 already covers ROCm architecture parsing; RCCL ragged all-to-all remains unsupported in its reported test, so it is not a parallel implementation target for this issue.

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
🤖 ### MI350X bf16 matmul ceiling: 1,192 TFLOP/s in JAX (52% of datasheet peak), 1,261 sustained in PyTorch with TunableOp

Commits: 265ea0f (MAMF jobs 453328, 453329), d733a95 (453334), 52cf1ee (JAX 453412), 08516a7 (JAX 453420, 453421) · GPU: one MI350X or MI300X, whole node reserved · Scripts: [`experiments/amd_matmul_ceiling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/08516a7dd961b26fa87f5d9fe955493564175c7c/experiments/amd_matmul_ceiling) (PR #9840)

This measures how fast one GPU runs a plain dense matmul, to give the MFU numbers above a measured ceiling. Two tools ran on the same node for each GPU type: k007-002 for MI350X, k002-003 for MI300X. Both venvs install AMD's `rocm-sdk-libraries==10.0.0` wheel, which provides hipBLASLt; the nodes' system ROCm (`/opt/rocm-7.2.0`) is not used for compute.

- Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py) (PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_ENABLED=1`, which benchmarks every hipBLASLt kernel per shape) searches about 2,100 shapes. It reports MAMF (maximum achievable matmul FLOPS): the median of the 5 fastest of 200 iterations, run in bursts of 20 after 250 ms idle. It also reports MSMF (maximum sustainable matmul FLOPS): the best rate held for 2 s under continuous load.
- `jax_matmul.py` (JAX 0.11.0) times `jax.jit(jnp.matmul)` with XLA autotuning on: 1 s of warmup, then the median of ten 0.2 s windows of back-to-back calls. This is a sustained rate, so MSMF is the PyTorch number to compare it with.

Hardware and theoretical peaks:

| | MI350X | MI300X |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture, compute units | gfx950, 256 CUs | gfx942, 304 CUs |
| Memory per GPU (as torch reports it) | 288 GB HBM3E (294,896 MB) | 192 GB HBM3 (196,592 MB) |
| Dense bf16 and fp16 peak | 2,307 TFLOP/s, as in this issue (brochure: 2,309.6) | 1,307 TFLOP/s (datasheet: 1,307.4) |
| Node, Slurm partition | k007-002, `mi3508x` | k002-003, `mi3008x` |

The peaks are AMD's dense figures without structured sparsity. `lib/fray/src/fray/device_flops.py` stores the brochure values; the percentages below use 2,307 and 1,307 to match the tables above.

Software, identical on both GPUs:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| ROCm user-space libraries | `rocm==10.0.0` wheels (`rocm-sdk-core`, `rocm-sdk-libraries`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx942`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx950`) from `https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/` |
| hipBLASLt, rocBLAS | 100401-8d1ae90e, 5.6.0.8d1ae90e (from TunableOp's results file) |
| PyTorch | 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, with `amd-torch-device-gfx942` and `-gfx950` 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0. `torch.version.hip` is 7.15.26333 and `torch.version.cuda` is None: a ROCm build, no CUDA |
| JAX | jax and jaxlib 0.11.0, `jax_rocm10_plugin` and `jax_rocm10_pjrt` 0.11.0+rocm10.0.0 |
| MAMF-finder | commit [0359db8](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py), benchmark version 4, auto search, default tuning |
| Python, OS | 3.12.12, Linux 5.14.0-611.54.1.el9_7 |
| JAX flags | `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`, `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` |

Each run used GPU 0 while the other 7 GPUs on the node were idle.

```bash
sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 120 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd_matmul_ceiling/mamf.sbatch --dtype bfloat16"
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 45 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd_matmul_ceiling/jax_matmul.sbatch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --ranges --m 4096 20480 4096 --n 4096 20480 4096 --k 4096 20480 4096 \
  --shapes-file experiments/amd_matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt"
```

Results in TFLOP/s per GPU, with the share of the dense peak. Shapes are MxNxK.

| GPU | dtype | MAMF (PyTorch) | MSMF (PyTorch) | JAX best | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI350X | bf16 | 1,445 (62.6%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 (54.7%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,192 (51.7%) @ 4096x4096x16384 | 453328, 453420, 453412 |
| MI350X | fp16 | 1,377 (59.7%) @ 4096x4096x20480 | 1,177 (51.0%) @ 8192x4096x14336 | 1,031 (44.7%) @ 4096x8192x8192 | 453329, 453421 |
| MI300X | bf16 | 698 (53.4%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | 645 (49.3%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | not run | 453334 |

The JAX column covers a 125-shape grid (M, N and K each 4096, 8192, ..., 20480), the June model's dense shapes, and, for bf16, the 28 shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted.

Measured against these ceilings instead of the datasheet, the MI350X baseline above (3.88% MFU, 90 TFLOP/s per GPU) runs at 7.5% of the JAX bf16 ceiling. The confirmed MI300X batch-16 row (8.66%, 113 TFLOP/s) runs at 17.5% of PyTorch's MSMF; JAX was not measured on MI300X.

The MI300X run reproduces the MI300X bf16 row in [Stas Bekman's table](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/README.md#maximum-achievable-and-sustainable-matmul-flops-comparison-table) (MAMF 676, MSMF 659, PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0): MAMF is 3.3% higher and MSMF 2.1% lower. His table has no MI350X row. His MI355X row reads 62.6% of peak, the same share as our MI350X MAMF.

The next table times the same matmul shapes in both frameworks, in bf16 on MI350X, using the shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted. MSMF is PyTorch's sustained rate after TunableOp has benchmarked every hipBLASLt kernel for that shape and kept the fastest. JAX is the sustained rate with the kernel XLA's autotuner chose. JAX / MSMF is the ratio of the two, so 80% means JAX gets 80% of PyTorch's throughput on that shape.

JAX is 2-23% slower on these shapes. Both frameworks call the same hipBLASLt library, so the likely cause is that XLA selects a slower kernel than TunableOp for some shapes. We have not confirmed this yet; the last note describes how to check it.

| Shape | MSMF | JAX | JAX / MSMF |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 | 1,008 | 80% |
| 4096x4096x8192 | 1,246 | 1,150 | 92% |
| 3584x4608x8192 | 1,237 | 1,137 | 92% |
| 4096x4096x20480 | 1,224 | 1,153 | 94% |
| 4096x2048x20480 | 1,089 | 1,065 | 98% |
| 2048x4096x4096 | 1,080 | 828 | 77% |

On MI350X in bf16, the June model's dense GEMMs at 4096 tokens per GPU run at 519 (k and v projections) to 1,046 (lm head weight gradient) TFLOP/s through JAX; the q projection reaches 820 and the lm head forward 1,020. Full list in [`snowball_shapes.txt`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/08516a7dd961b26fa87f5d9fe955493564175c7c/experiments/amd_matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt). The routed-expert `ragged_dot` is not covered.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- fp16 is slower than bf16 for dense matmuls on MI350X: MAMF is 5% lower, JAX 14% lower.
- The best 10 JAX grid shapes in bf16 fall between 1,157 and 1,192 TFLOP/s.
- The node matters. JAX on MAMF-finder's 28 shapes ran a median of 3% faster on k007-002 than on k007-004, from 8% slower to 5% faster per shape (jobs 453412 and 453338). The bf16 grid's best was 1,156 on k007-004 (job 453314) against 1,192 on k007-002.
- With `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, JAX ran bf16 matmuls at 15-17 TFLOP/s, 1% of the autotuned rate (job 453316, stopped by its 45-minute limit after 99 shapes). Any hipBLASLt kernel is far faster than that, so level 0 appears to switch to a different GEMM path on ROCm, and it cannot measure hipBLASLt's untuned default choice.
- MAMF-finder's telemetry on MI350X read the wrong GPU. It samples `amdsmi` GPU 0, but HIP device 0 on k007-002 is PCI 0000:77:00, which is `amd-smi` GPU 3; `amd-smi` GPU 0 is an idle GPU at about 308 W. The 38 MHz and 308 W in the MI350X MAMF-finder logs, and its "not a boost burst" warning, come from that idle GPU. MAMF-finder's TFLOP/s do not depend on telemetry. On MI300X it reads 750 W and 1,315 MHz sustained and 2,096 MHz at boost, matching the 750 W cap in note 9 of Stas Bekman's table.
- Power cap on MI350X (`amd-smi static --limit`, job 453520): the socket power limit is 1,000 W, equal to the maximum limit and to the brochure's maximum TBP. During a sustained bf16 4096x4096x16384 matmul in JAX (job 453523), the GPU held 1,000 W at a 70-73 °C hotspot, below the 100 °C slowdown temperature, and its 8 compute dies ran at 1,332-1,513 MHz, about 1,400 MHz on average. At 1,400 MHz the peak formula (256 CUs x 4,096 bf16 FLOPs per clock) gives about 1,470 TFLOP/s, 64% of the 2.2 GHz figure. Against that power-limited peak, MSMF is about 86% and JAX in that run (1,145 TFLOP/s) 78%. MAMF's short bursts may run above the sustained clock before the GPU reaches its power limit, so the 1,400 MHz figure does not bound MAMF.
- With torch imported, the `amdsmi` Python binding from `/opt/rocm-7.2.0` reports no GPUs, because torch has already loaded the ROCm SDK's own `libamd_smi.so.27`. `setup_envs.sh` uses the SDK's binding instead.

### MI350X Triton `ragged_dot` rewrite and tuning: batch 64 step 2.634 → 2.426 s, 8.58% → 9.32% MFU

Commit: 8471641 (local, not pushed) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 453565 (A/B), 453564 (microbenchmark), baseline 453384

PR: #9859 (AMD Instinct only; NVIDIA, TPU and megablox unchanged).

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 \
  --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 --compilation-cache-dir $WORK/jax-cache --batch-size 64
```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.426 s (was 2.634) | 108,100 (was 99,500) | 9.32% (was 8.58%) | 184.2 GiB (unchanged) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Loss matches the baseline to 4 decimals (11.7770 vs 11.7769 at step 19).
- Forward and dlhs now launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a device-side tile map, instead of a full row grid per expert. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. drhs uses an explicit flat grid. Rows past the last group are zero-filled.
- Tuned for MI350X: 256×256×64 tiles, 8 warps, 2 stages for forward and dlhs; 256×128×64, 4 warps, 1 stage for drhs; plus chiplet-aware program order. Blackwell, TPU and megablox are unchanged.
- Per call on one GPU at batch 64 (M=131072), before → after TFLOP/s:

  | Layout | w13 | w2 |
  |---|---|---|
  | fwd | 583 → 722 | 555 → 667 |
  | dlhs | 554 → 760 | 538 → 757 |
  | drhs | 410 → 581 | 396 → 573 |

  A dense `jnp.matmul` of the same FLOPs runs at about 925–958; XLA fp16 `ragged_dot` at 24–98. At batch 8 the forward pass goes from 2.27 ms to 0.36 ms. Jobs 453500 and 453564.
- At batch 64 the tile map alone changes nothing. With the old blocks, w13 forward takes 2.95 ms either way. The gain there is block tuning. At batch 8 the tile map is a 4.6× win.
- `plgpu.CompilerParams` exposes only `num_warps` and `num_stages`, so AMD knobs (`waves_per_eu`, `matrix_instr_nonkdim`, `kpack`) can't be set from Pallas.
- drhs, at 573–581 TFLOP/s, is the remaining gap. Both of its operands are contraction-strided.

</details>

The model's async EP all-gathers take 4.1 ms (about 280 GB/s) because they share compute units and HBM with concurrent compute: next to a matmul, an all-gather hides only 42% of it, even with the latency-hiding scheduler on.

Exposed time is 402 ms. It also drops more assignments: 5.4% against ring's 0.9% at capacity factor 1.0.
- Against the old kernel (2.634 s), `save_moe` on the new kernel is 11.3% faster.
- Next, by estimated upside: `save_moe` at batch 64 now (-3.7%, +49 GiB); token-deduplicated EP dispatch (about 58% fewer EP bytes, 100-180 ms); overlap the synchronous reduce-scatters with the shared-expert MLP (50-100 ms); one gradient all-reduce per weight after the layer scan (40-55 ms).

</details>

🤖 Matmul-alone time in the MI350X `--overlap` runs (jobs 453572, 453633, 453651) takes one of two values between runs: about 2.46 ms in `min64`, `ring`, `prio-on` and `lhs-prio-off`, and about 2.88 ms in the other 16. The faster overlap rows of `min64`, `ring` and `prio-on` (all-gather 5.68 ms against 6.05 ms in `base`) match that matmul gap, so they do not show an effect of the RCCL or XLA setting. Details: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9886#issuecomment-6047294744

Because the variance is between processes, re-timing the matmul inside a run does not remove it. To compare settings, run each setting in several processes, interleave them, and compare medians of a per-run ratio such as the hidden fraction `(t_collective + t_matmul − t_both) / min(t_collective, t_matmul)`, using the matmul-alone time of the same run.

### Token-deduplicated EP dispatch (`ring_dedup`): 1.580 s and 14.31% MFU with `save_moe`, -8.7% against ring

Commit: 91286fc (local; `ring_dedup` backend in b31085d, merged onto the gather-combine base 67ca557) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454021 (`ring_dedup`), 454012 (ring baseline)

PR: #9880 (draft, merge after #9860). `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` comes from #9852.

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.580 s | 165,900 | 14.31% | 206.5 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What it does.** `ring` all-gathers every token to all 8 GPUs and reduce-scatters a full-size output, but with top-4 of 256 experts a token reaches only 3.3 GPUs on average. `ring_dedup` (new module `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring_dedup.py`) sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`, plus a small `all_to_all` of per-row combine weights and local expert ids. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule, grouped layout and Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32 and returns one row per token. All hidden-width movement is a gather (ring's `_dispatch_rows`/`_combine_rows`), so there are no scatter-adds in either pass.
- **Sender capacity** is `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing (0.416 × 32,768 per GPU). At 1.1 it sends 537 MB per collective per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring's all-gather or reduce-scatter (46%), and drops no tokens at the sender in these runs.
- **A/B, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile cache per job, `JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`, median of steps 2-19:**

  | Base | Remat | ring | `ring_dedup` | Jobs |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | merged (gather combine + Triton routing top-k) | recompute_all | 1.798 s, 12.57% | 1.688 s, 13.40% (-6.1%) | 454022, 454026 |
  | merged | save_moe | 1.730 s, 13.07% | 1.580 s, 14.31% (-8.7%) | 454012, 454021 |
  | before the gather combine | recompute_all | 1.865 s, 12.13% | 1.735 s, 13.03% (-7.0%) | 453921, 453922 |
  | before the gather combine | save_moe | 1.842 s, 12.28% | 1.637 s, 13.81% (-11.1%) | 453960, 453968 |

  The two changes stack partly. With `save_moe`, the gather combine alone saves 112 ms, `ring_dedup` alone 205 ms, both together 262 ms. Peak memory changes by at most 0.7 GiB. Step-19 loss is within 8e-4 of ring in every pair. The drop rate is 1.00% vs 0.99% (`recompute_all`) and 1.12% vs 0.93% (`save_moe`).
- **Numerics.** f32 CPU unit tests on 8 shards match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in value and in gradients for x, combine weights and both expert weights, including a forced sender-drop case. At full shapes in bf16 on MI350X, one layer differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative in value and gradients. That comes from ring's bf16 summation; `ring_dedup` sums in f32.
- **Profile (steps 10-12, GPU 0, ms per profiled step, ring vs `ring_dedup`, both before the gather combine).** `recompute_all`: large EP collectives take 481 vs 311, exposed collective time is 357 vs 288, and MoE dispatch/combine kernels take 150 vs 42. `save_moe`: 386 vs 211, 402 vs 266, and 147 vs 40. Each large `all_to_all` takes 1.6-2.7 ms, against 3.3-4.2 ms for ring's collectives.
- **What is still exposed:** the forward return and backward dy `all_to_all`s are synchronous (about 60 ms each per step), and the small metadata `all_to_all`s take 0.8-0.9 ms per call under `save_moe`, where they queue behind the large transfers.
- The latency-hiding scheduler gave 1.594 s vs 1.637 s before the merge, but 1.591 s vs 1.580 s after it (job 454027), so leave it off.
- One run (454010) hit the step-5 GPU-7 out-of-memory on a 96.6 GiB allocation, the same failure seen at batch 96 in job 453660, and hung. The retry (454021) ran clean. Since diagnosed as allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer and fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` (#9901).
- **Follow-ups:** packing the metadata into the activation rows and chunking the expert MLP were tried and did not help; see the next comment. Not tested on TPU or NVIDIA.

</details>

### One gradient all-reduce per weight after the layer scan: works, keeps gradients, no speedup on MI350X

Commit: bd8e11a · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Job: 453915 (on 60b253d), 454011 (on 67ca557)

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash --remat-mode <recompute_all|save_moe>
```

| Base | Remat | Variant | Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60b253d | recompute_all | baseline | 1.844 s | 142,200 | 12.26% | 158.4 GiB |
| 60b253d | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.852 s | 141,600 | 12.21% | 158.4 GiB |
| 60b253d | save_moe | baseline | 1.824 s | 143,700 | 12.39% | 205.8 GiB |
| 60b253d | save_moe | deferred reduction | 1.856 s | 141,200 | 12.18% | 205.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | recompute_all | baseline | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | baseline | 1.748 s | 150,000 | 12.94% | 205.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | deferred reduction | 1.741 s | 150,600 | 12.99% | 205.9 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- What the in-scan all-reduces are: on this mesh (`expert=8`, other axes 1), every non-expert block weight is replicated across the batch. Explicit sharding types each layer's weight gradient as replicated, so the backward while body all-reduces it per layer. Per layer that is 5 gradient all-reduces: q/k/v/gate and w_o in the attention `cond` branch, one combined GatedNorm/router/shared w_gate/w_up, shared w_down, and the two RMSNorm weights. The forward body adds one router-stats all-reduce, for 6 × 26 = 156 per step. XLA's combiner can't merge across loop iterations or `cond` branches.
- The change: weights that only feed matmuls are marked `reduced` over the batch axes before the scan (`levanter.grug.sharding.defer_batch_grad_reduction`). Their gradients leave the scan unreduced and are all-reduced once per stacked weight. FSDP-sharded leaves (`data` > 1) are left unchanged. RMSNorm weights keep the per-layer reduction. Stored parameter shardings don't change.
- Gradients match. On CPU (tiny preset, f32, 8 devices) the loss and 26 of 27 leaves are bit-identical. On GPU (medium preset, bf16, job 454079) the loss is identical, and baseline-vs-change errors (at most 0.63% relative L2) equal baseline-vs-baseline. The full-model losses match too.
- The backward loop goes from 5 gradient all-reduces per layer to 1, but the step doesn't get faster. In a profiled A/B (job 453987) the change saves 43 ms per step, but the profiler adds about 0.3 ms to every collective call. Unprofiled, the 130 removed calls cost about 11 ms, and the single 2 GB all-reduce after the scan takes about 16 ms on the main stream. The bytes are the same either way, and the per-layer calls were bandwidth-bound, not latency-bound.
- Not proposing a PR for MI350X. Small collectives should be priced from unprofiled step times, not from trace durations.

</details>

issues.author: asartran
issues.body:
The `github.ci` arm of `scripts/ci/wait_for.py` never fires when the installed `gh` lacks `gh pr checks --json`. It reports `0 checks, none failing, not all done` until the overall timeout, even after every check has finished or one has failed. Two PR monitors in the #9812 work lost their CI signal this way: one waited the full 12 hours, the other sat idle for 2h40m.

Reproduce:
1. Use `gh` 2.45.0 (the Ubuntu 24.04 package): `gh pr checks 9860 --repo marin-community/marin --json name,bucket,state` prints `unknown flag: --json` to stderr and nothing to stdout.
2. Run `uv run scripts/ci/wait_for.py --timeout 1h "github.ci 9860"` on a PR whose checks have all finished.

Expected: the arm fires with the CI result, or the command fails with an error saying `gh` is too old.

Cause: `gh_pr_checks` (`scripts/ci/wait_for.py:171`) treats empty stdout as "no checks registered yet" and ignores the exit status and stderr, so the `--json` error looks like a PR with no checks and `evaluate_ci` keeps waiting.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`github.ci` calls `gh_pr_checks()`, which treats empty stdout as an unregistered check set without inspecting the command exit code. An older `gh` exits nonzero for unsupported `--json`, so the selector repeatedly reports zero checks until timeout.

**Relevant code**
- [`wait_for.py#L170-L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/scripts/ci/wait_for.py#L170-L189) — reads check output
- [`wait_for.py#L534-L557`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/scripts/ci/wait_for.py#L534-L557) — evaluates CI state

# Proposed Fix

`CiSource.check()` passes rows from `gh_pr_checks()` to `evaluate_ci()`; the failed `gh` command currently supplies an empty list. Raise `GhError` when stdout is empty and the exit code is nonzero, retaining empty rows for a successful command with no registered checks. Add a regression using a fake older `gh` executable.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 [PR #9909](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9909) makes `github.ci` report an error when `gh pr checks --json` exits nonzero without output. The regression exits 1 with the old-`gh` diagnostic instead of timing out; all 21 `tests/ci/` tests and the required lint checks pass. CI and review are pending.

issues.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 each layer closes an AttnRes block, so the history at layer *i* is the embedding plus one sum per earlier layer. [¹](#arch-note) ```mermaid flowchart TB tok["token ids
B × 4096, packed documents"] --> emb["token embedding
16384 × 512"] emb --> en["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] en --> S0(["source 0
embedding"]) S0 --> L0 subgraph STACK["6 layers: local KDA ×4, global MLA ×2 (every 4th + last)"] direction TB L0["layer 0 · KDA + MoE"] --> L1["layer 1 · KDA + MoE"] --> L2["layer 2 · KDA + MoE"] L2 --> L3["layer 3 · MLA + Inkling + MoE"] --> L4["layer 4 · KDA + MoE"] --> L5["layer 5 · MLA + Inkling + MoE"] end L0 -. "block sum b0" .-> H L1 -. "b1" .-> H L2 -. "b2" .-> H L3 -. "b3" .-> H L4 -. "b4" .-> H S0 -.-> H H[("AttnRes history, read by every gate

fused CE, vocab tile 8192, z-loss 1e-4"] head --> loss(["next-token loss"]) ``` **2. One layer.** The two sublayers each have an AttnRes gate. The MoE gate also sees the attention output written just before it, as the running partial. ```mermaid flowchart TB Hin[("history
embedding + b0…b(i−1)")] --> GA subgraph GATE["AttnRes gate (one per sublayer, 13 at d512)"] direction TB GA["logit_n = q · rms_norm(source_n)

KDA (local) or MLA + Inkling (global)"}} MIX --> SCA["ShortConv (MLA layers only)"] --> PA(["partial = attn out"]) PA --> GM["AttnRes gate
history + partial"] Hin --> GM GM --> M1["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] --> MOE{{"LatentMoE + 2 shared experts"}} MOE --> SCM["ShortConv"] --> PB(["block b_i = attn out + MoE out"]) PB --> Hout[("appended to history")] ``` **3a. Kimi Delta Attention, the local mixer (layers 0, 1, 2, 4 at d512; D = 512, 4 heads × 128).** ```mermaid flowchart TB kx["x"] --> kq["q = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_q))"] & kk["k = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_k))"] & kv["v = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_v))"] kx --> kg["decay g = −5 · σ(exp(A_log) · (x W_a↓ W_a↑ + dt_bias))
rank-128 gate, per channel; A_log per head"] kx --> kb["write strength β = σ(x W_β), per head"] kq & kk --> kn["L2-norm q, k; q × 1/√128"] kn & kv & kg & kb --> rec["delta rule, chunked Pallas kernels (chunk 16)
S_t = (I − β k kᵀ) Diag(e^g) S_{t−1} + β k vᵀ
o_t = S_tᵀ q_t · state resets at document starts"] rec --> kon["per-head RMSNorm (shared 128-wide scale)"] --> kog["× σ(x W_g), per channel"] --> ko["W_o → sublayer out
no RoPE, no window, no output ShortConv"] ``` **3b. MLA + Inkling, the global mixer (layers 3 and 5 at d512).** ```mermaid flowchart TB mx["x"] --> mq["q = x W_q (full rank, 4 × 128)"] mx --> ml["KV latent = RMSNorm(x W_dkv), 512 wide, learnable gain"] --> mk["k = latent W_uk"] & mv["v = latent W_uv"] mx --> rel["Inkling bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]
R = x W_r (16 per head) · P 16 × 1024, shared across heads"] mq & mk & mv & rel --> fa["FA4 causal attention (fwd + SM90 bwd)
logits × 1/√128 (qk_mult 1) · no RoPE · no QK-norm
Inkling bias added before softmax"] fa --> xsa["XSA: subtract each head's component along its own v"] --> mg["× 2σ(x W_gate), per head, zero-init"] --> mo["W_o → ShortConv → sublayer out"] ``` **3c. LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing (every layer).** ```mermaid flowchart TB ex["x (512)"] --> fused["one fused GEMM:
router · W_latent↓ · shared-expert gate/up"] fused --> rt["router logits (fp32)
top-(8+1) on logit − β_QB; 9th = threshold α"] rt --> qb["QB: β_e = global (1 − 8/384) quantile of logit − α
10k-bin histogram each step; router bias = −β, not trained"] rt --> cw["combine weights = σ(unbiased logits) of the top 8,
renormalized to sum to 2.5"] fused --> lat["latent = RMSNorm(x W_latent↓), 256 wide"] lat & cw --> ep["384 SwiGLU experts, hidden 256
pooled-wave EP all-to-all over 8 GPUs, capacity 1.15"] ep --> up["W_latent↑ 256 → 512"] fused --> sh["2 shared SwiGLU experts, 512 → 256 → 512
down projections fused into one GEMM"] up & sh --> sum["routed + shared → ShortConv → sublayer out"] ``` ¹ AttnRes rolls a new block at layer *i* while `i % max(1, L // 8) == 0` and fewer than 8 blocks exist. At d512 and d768 every layer closes a block. At d1024 (12 layers) and d1280 (14 layers) only layers 0–7 do, so layers 8 and up all accumulate into one running partial instead of their own blocks. **Optimizer routing:** - **MuonH:** every attention and MoE matrix, and every GatedNorm (KDA `W_β` at 2× the MuonH LR). - **AdamH:** lm_head. - **Adam:** embedding, router, attention output gate, norm gains, ShortConv kernels, KDA decay parameters, Inkling weights. - **Adam at 0.1× the Adam LR:** the AttnRes queries. ## Baseline: clean KMA Branch [`fasttrack-moe-kma`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fasttrack-moe-kma) @ `4eba59cafa`. Build from this branch. The recipe below covers every model and optimizer component. Values are for d512 unless noted; the code is `experiments/grug/fast_track/{model,optimizer,heuristic,launch}.py`. **Shape** | Rung | Width D | Layers | Local (KDA) / global (MLA) layers | Heads × head dim | Batch | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | d512 | 512 | 6 | 4 / 2 | 4 × 128 | 128 | | d768 | 768 | 8 | 6 / 2 | 6 × 128 | 128 | | d1024 | 1024 | 12 | 9 / 3 | 8 × 128 | 256 | | d1280 | 1280 | 14 | 10 / 4 | 10 × 128 | 256 | - Every 4th layer and the last layer are global; all other layers are local. - The run uses a 16k vocab and sequence length 4096 with packed documents. Every ShortConv and the KDA state respect document boundaries (the KDA state resets at each document start). - Weights are initialized with std 0.5/√D. Compute is bf16. **Embedding and output** - Token embedding → RMSNorm → GatedNorm. The result is AttnRes source 0. - Output path: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → untied lm_head (`output_proj`). - The fused lm_head + cross-entropy loop uses a vocab tile of 8192. - GatedNorm (every GatedNorm in the model) is `x · sigmoid(W_up · SiLU(W_down · x))`, with a rank-128 bottleneck. **Block (every layer)** - **Attention sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → mixer (KDA or MLA). - **MoE sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → MoE → ShortConv on the MoE output. - Each ShortConv is a 4-tap causal depthwise conv. **Local layers: Kimi Delta Attention** (Kimi K3's layer) - **Projections:** q/k/v are D → N·128 with full heads (no GQA). Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up. Also every GatedNorm `W_down`/`W_up`. | | `kda_beta` | MuonH | 2 × MuonH LR | KDA `W_β` | | `adamh` | AdamH | MuonH LR | lm_head (`output_proj`) | | `adam` | Adam | Adam LR | token embedding; router; attention output gate; router bias slot (overwritten by QB); all 1-D norm gains; ShortConv kernels; KDA `W_a_down`/`W_a_up`, `A_log`, `dt_bias`; Inkling `W_r` and `P` | | `attn_res_query` | Adam | 0.1 × Adam LR | the AttnRes pseudo-queries | - **MuonH:** Nesterov momentum 0.95 → Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (5 quintic steps, bucketed across same-shape matrices) → a step along that direction, then projection back onto the matrix's Frobenius sphere. Each matrix's norm stays fixed at its init value. - **AdamH:** the Adam direction with the same Frobenius-sphere (hyperball) projection. - **Adam:** β1 0.9. Only the router and the attention output gate get decoupled weight decay (0.02). No other parameter gets weight decay, and there's no gradient clipping. - **Schedule:** 1% warmup, then linear decay to 0.05× peak. - **Peak values** from `MoeHeuristic` (they depend on tokens, width and batch): - Adam LR = `0.0876 · tokens^−0.346 · D^−0.345 · √(tokens per batch)`. - MuonH LR = 13/3 × Adam LR. - β2 = `0.999^(tokens per batch / 131072)`. - ε = `9.68e−18 · √(steps)`. - At d512 with 2384 steps: MuonH LR 0.0227, Adam LR 0.0052, β2 0.996, ε 4.7e−16. Submit at **batch** priority (the launcher's default is interactive, so pass it): ``` NO_PROXY="*" uv run python -m experiments.grug.fast_track.launch --submit \ --target-cluster cw-us-east-02a --priority batch \ --run-id --size d512 --recipe kma --num-steps <8-min steps> --version ``` ## Compute - cw-us-east-02a at **batch** priority. - **At most 10 active runs at once**, probes included. - **Limit runs above d768** to keep the experimentation rate high. d1024 and d1280 runs take hours and hold a slot the whole time, so save them for changes that have already passed gate 1 or that need extra scales because of curve-fitting risk. - Don't save checkpoints (the launcher default). ## For humans Comment with a research direction for the agent, for example "try X", or "combine A and B". The agent picks up new comments at its next batch. The main goal of a single experiment should be to learn about the system. This means that if you tweak one knob and the loss goes off the rails, the experiment can still be considered a success! We better understand the system sensitivity! Building knowledge through failed experiments will bring us closer to the long term goal of better models. ## For the agent - Read `experiments/grug/fast_track/README.md` and `agent.md` first. Where they differ from this issue, this issue wins; the main difference is the fixed-time objective. - Run 5–10 experiments per batch, and prioritize human comments when picking the next one. - Ask for clarification in the thread if helpful, but never hold a batch waiting for an answer: state your assumption and correct it in the next batch. - Start at d512. When a change beats the current best by more than 0.005, validate it at d768. - Post **one comment per batch** and edit it as runs finish. Start it with 🤖 and include: - the batch goal, and which human comments it addresses; - a table with one row per run: change | branch@commit | W&B link | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ vs current best; - a 1–3 line takeaway and the planned next batch. - **Branches:** prefix with `ladderclimb_v1_`, and link the exact commit each job ran. - **W&B:** project `marin_moe`, with short prefixed run IDs such as `lc1-b03-…` (names over 128 characters fail at init). - Add the `agent-generated` label to any issue or PR you open. - Keep the **Status** table below updated with a concise chronology of improvements. ## Studies Deep dives and multi-batch studies, newest first. Pages are claude.ai artifacts; batch comments hold the plan, every run and the numbers. | study | what it found | page | batch comments | |---|---|---|---| | **Hyperball decay per matrix** | The MuonH/AdamH hyperball re-projection acts as a per-matrix weight decay that depends on the update's direction (`decay = 1 − |W|/|W+u|` ≈ `lr·cos(W,u) + lr²/2`). Logged every step for every matrix on the ragged base (`lc1-b191-hb2`, 2.9631). Typical matrices decay 0.06–0.10%/step mid-run with cos ≈ 0.07–0.10, so over 90% of the decay comes from updates leaning outward, not from the orthogonal part. Odd ones: KDA `w_beta` (all 4 layers) decays 2–3× anything else (0.17–0.26%/step, 1.3% early) with 4× the rescale and inward swings; the AdamH lm head has the lowest median (0.045%) but the largest spikes (p99 1.27%, cos up to 0.66); layer-5 MLA `w_o` spikes too (p99 1.0%); layer-5 MLA `w_uv` is the only large projection with inward steps; gated-norm matrices hold the highest sustained decay, rising with depth. Code: `--opt-set log_hyperball_decay=true` (`hyperball_metrics`). | [Hyperball Decay Atlas](https://claude.ai/artifact/74PcjNW2PaNkYV5btbq3Ug) | — | | **Learned RMSNorm gains** | What every learned RMSNorm gain learns on candidate 11 (linear gains), per module. No gain goes negative; gains span about 700× across modules (`embed2_norm` 0.01–0.45, `final_norm` up to 7.6) but cluster tightly within one, and the largest (`final_norm`, MoE latent norms) are still rising at the end. Gain functions: `e^w` −0.0026 (within noise; `final_norm` climbs to 15), softplus −0.0008, `2·sigmoid` +0.115 (pins `final_norm` at its cap of 2). Learned output scalars on every sublayer are neutral (linear −0.0003, `2·sigmoid` −0.0015). Code: `norm_gain_fn`, `sublayer_scale_fn`, `norm_gain_lr_mult`, `--weight-diagnostics`. | [Learned RMSNorm Gains](https://claude.ai/artifact/KcoMDyEcULNMFebyS5eTRQ) | [181](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5985074958) | | **lm_head soft-cap shape** | Tanh caps 10–12 are flat on the current recipe (11: +0.0004 on 2 seeds). `A·σ((z+B)/C)` is a tanh cap `A/2` on `A/(4C)·(z+B)`, so its knobs are cap, gain and shift. At cap 11, shift ±4 and gain 0.8 / 1.25 all land within the 0.003 same-function noise; lower gain and either shift lean worse. comments.body:
Some ideas to get started. Treat this as a general pool of ideas, that indicates the spirit of what can be tried.
1. https://blog.tilderesearch.com/blog/online-kl-shampoo. Consider interactions with hyperball and selectively replace matrices.
2. Add a second embedding table with its own random init. Attn residuals queries both embedding tables, treating them as unique inputs.
3. Lets add value embeddings. That is, a second embedding table that gets added to V on the MLA layers. So take KV latent-> project to num_heads of size 128. Then do values = lambda1*values + lambda2*value_embeds[layer_i]. lambda 1 init to 1, lambda2 init to 0. value_embeds has [vocab_size, num_heads*head_dim, num_mla_layers] dimension. Can also try gated value embeds, where instead of lambda2, its conditional on residual stream via sigmoid(linear(x)).
4. Add learnable scalars to each submodule output, that feeds into attention residuals. May be worth tracking and plotting these in wandb, to see if indicates any architecture changes will help.
5. Try different variations of linear attention to replace KDA.
6. It has been shown in many places that the final couple layers of attention dont prefer to attend to outputs from the final MLPs. See if there is any change to attention residuals to help make this more natural.
7. Adding an lm_head auxillary loss to the output of layer 1 for the first X (say 500) steps can help give the routed experts a cleaner role early. Unclear how this interacts with attention residuals.
8. Hash routing on first layer.
9. Instead of Adam/AdamH on embed and lm_head, look into other optimizers here that have shown promise in literature.
10. Do any weights benefit from extremely different beta1/beta2/momentum terms, or swapping their optimizer group.
11. Update the router behavior (sigmoid vs softmax), normalizing over picked experts vs not, sampling over experts instead of top k).
12. Null routing (enable tokens to select null experts which skips their computation, dynamic compute per token).
13. Multi-token-prediction.
14. Sparse attention.

If users give comments with singular specific ideas, give it priority over this laundry list.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 5: @ClassicLarry's three requests: z-loss weight, projection biases, and freezing QB at 50%** (d512, 2817 steps; reference = batch-3 base mean **3.0990**)

**Addresses** the comment asking to vary the logit z-loss, add biases to some weight matrices, and freeze QB updates halfway through training. All runs build on the fp32-embedding base, branch [`ladderclimb_v1_batch05`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ea0592bd02).
- **z-loss:** the current weight is 1e-4 (`--z-loss-weight`). One run turns it off, one raises it 10×.
- **Biases:** zero-initialized and trained with Adam, at three sites:
  - Qwen-style q/k/v: KDA q/k/v before their ShortConvs, and MLA q plus the KV latent before its RMSNorm.
  - The attention sublayer output.
  - The MoE sublayer output.

  If the combined run moves, I'll split the sites next batch.
- **QB freeze:** from step 1408 on, the router bias keeps its last quantile-balanced value (`qb_freeze_step`). Routing can then drift, and load balance is no longer enforced.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ vs 3.0990 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| z-loss weight 0 (vs 1e-4) | [`ea0592bd02`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ea0592bd02) | [lc1-b05-z0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-z0) | 2817 | 751 | 3.3902 | 3.0966 | −0.0024 |
| z-loss weight 1e-3 | [`ea0592bd02`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ea0592bd02) | [lc1-b05-z1e3](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-z1e3) | 2817 | 749 | 3.4029 | 3.1046 | +0.0056 |
| biases: q/k/v + attention out + MoE out | [`ea0592bd02`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ea0592bd02) | [lc1-b05-bias](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-bias) | 2817 | 742 (−1%) | 3.3913 | 3.0993 | +0.0003 |
| freeze QB router biases at step 1408 (50%) | [`ea0592bd02`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ea0592bd02) | [lc1-b05-qbfrz](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-qbfrz) | 2817 | 751 | 3.3924 | 3.1059 | +0.0069 |
| **AttnRes logit bias** per (gate, source), zero-init, Adam at 0.1× (human, 2nd comment) | [`f1734ddcdf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f1734ddcdf) | [lc1-b05-arb](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-arb) | 2817 | 751 | 3.3954 | 3.1001 | +0.0011 |
| AttnRes logit bias + AttnRes z-loss 1e-3 | [`f1734ddcdf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f1734ddcdf) | [lc1-b05-arbz3](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-arbz3) | 2817 | 748 | 3.3996 | 3.1045 | +0.0055 |
| AttnRes logit bias + AttnRes z-loss 1e-1 | [`f1734ddcdf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f1734ddcdf) | [lc1-b05-arbz1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-arbz1) | 2817 | 746 | 3.4570 | 3.1475 | +0.0485 |

**AttnRes logit bias and z-loss** (added for the follow-up comment). Each of the 13 gates gets a zero-init bias per source it reads: one per completed block, plus one for the running partial. It is added to the logit before the softmax and trained with Adam at 0.1× the Adam LR, the same as the queries. The z-loss is the mean over tokens of logsumexp(gate logits)², averaged over gates, and added to the loss. Every run now logs the pseudo-query norms: `train/attn_res/query_norm_{mean,max,gNN}` plus the unweighted `train/attn_res/z`. One caveat: a z-loss can be satisfied by shifting a gate's biases down together, which leaves the mix unchanged. I'll compare the q norms across the three runs.

**Correction:** the AttnRes z-loss runs' eval losses also included the z-loss term (the same bug, found in batch 18). That inflated them by weight × z: about +0.0012 for 1e-3 and +0.001 for 1e-1. Their deltas are about +0.004 and +0.047 instead of +0.0055 and +0.0485, so both are still worse.

**Takeaway (all done).**
- **AttnRes logit bias is neutral (+0.0011).**
- **The AttnRes z-loss hurts:** +0.0055 at 1e-3 and +0.049 at 1e-1.
- **It raises the pseudo-query norms rather than lowering them.** Final values:

  | run | AttnRes z (unweighted) | query norm mean | query norm max |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | bias only | 6.31 | 0.227 | 0.377 |
  | bias + z 1e-3 | 1.23 | 0.286 | 0.583 |
  | bias + z 1e-1 | 0.01 | 0.332 | 0.565 |

  The z-loss is minimized by pushing every logit down. With keys that are RMS-normalized but not mean-centred, the query does this by growing along the direction opposite the common component of the sources, instead of shifting all biases together. That distorts the mix.
- The other results from this batch:
  - Freezing QB at 50%: +0.007.
  - lm_head z-loss 1e-3: +0.006.
  - lm_head z-loss 0: −0.002.
  - Projection biases: neutral.

The base seeds alone span 0.007, and a single seed can mislead: seed 2's gain is only −0.002. Pairing by seed, which shares the data order, is what makes the gain clear.

**β1 0.8 + lm_head z-loss 0 on top of qk 2.5, paired over 4 seeds: −0.0053 / −0.0023 / −0.0060 / −0.0050, mean −0.0047 ± 0.0008 (SE).** Every seed gains and the spread is tight. The mean sits just under the 0.005 bar, but the paired SE makes it a real if small effect. It costs nothing, so I'm including it in the gate-2 bundle, flagged as borderline.

**Takeaway.**
- **1 shared + top-10 routed is worse at fixed time: +0.0148.** The FLOPs are unchanged, but 25% more routed assignments make the EP all-to-all and dispatch 8% slower (691 vs 751 ex/s), so it trains 226 fewer steps. At d512 the step time is bound by communication and dispatch rather than FLOPs, which is a case where d512 may not reflect hero scale. I'm not pursuing it further at this rung.

comments.body: Try a simple version of looped models (w/ and wo/ growing, a la https://github.com/qlabs-eng/slowrun/pull/92 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19107) with untying and see if that improves performance. Make sure to include the input injection as well!

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 9: looped models (@neel04's request): tied looping, with and without growth, with input injection** (d512, paired seed 0 vs qk_mult-2.5 base **3.0858**)

**Addresses** @neel04's comment. It follows [slowrun#92](https://github.com/qlabs-eng/slowrun/pull/92) (1× for 70% of training, then 2×) and [arXiv 2609.19107](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19107) (boundary operator `Norm(h) + α·e`, growth partway through training, backprop through all passes, and FLOPs of every pass counted). Branch [`ladderclimb_v1_batch09`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2803601b0).

**How it maps onto KMA** (`loop_passes`, `loop_grow_step`):
- **The looped core is the whole 6-layer stack**, weights tied. Each pass extends the Block AttnRes history. Pass 2's gates read the embedding, every pass-1 block, and the pass-2 blocks so far. Pass 2 has its own zero-initialized AttnRes pseudo-queries, so its gates start as uniform averages over that longer history.
- **Input injection.** At the start of each extra pass, the running partial is initialized to `α·e`, where e is the normalized embedding source and α is learned (init 1, Adam), and the pass's layers write onto it. The AttnRes gates already see e as source 0. This is the explicit re-injection from both references. The AttnRes softmax already normalizes what each sublayer reads, which plays the part of `Norm(h)`.
- **Growth** uses a step-gated `lax.cond`. Before the growth step only pass 1 executes, at full base speed. After it both passes run, with gradients through both. The router biases are shared per physical layer; their QB statistics are averaged over the passes.
- **Fixed-time steps.** Two passes run at 0.506× the base throughput (80-step probe: 381.8 vs 754.1 ex/s), so every run is given 8 minutes of train-step time:
  - loop2 throughout: 1426 steps.
  - Grow at 70%: N solves `0.7N/751 + 0.3N/380 = 480/128`, so N = 2179 and growth is at step 1525.
  - Grow at 50%: N = 1892, growth at step 946.
- **Not in this batch: untied growth**, where the core is copied at the growth step and the copies train separately. It changes the parameter tree and optimizer state mid-run, so it needs trainer work. It's next if tied growth looks promising.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| loop ×2 throughout (tied, injection) | [`c2803601b0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2803601b0) | [lc1-b09-loop2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-loop2) | 1426 | 381 | 3.5052 | 3.1766 | **+0.0908** |
| grow 1→2 passes at 70% of steps (step 1525) | [`c2803601b0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2803601b0) | [lc1-b09-grow70](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-grow70) | 2179 | | | OOM: 79.8 GiB (lax.cond kept both branches' buffers); fixed, rerun below | |
| grow 1→2 passes at 50% (step 946) | [`c2803601b0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2803601b0) | [lc1-b09-grow50](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-grow50) | 1892 | | | OOM: 79.8 GiB (lax.cond kept both branches' buffers); fixed, rerun below | |
| grow 1→2 at 70% (step 1525), static per-phase programs | [`0d023baad9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/0d023baad9) | [lc1-b09-grow70b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-grow70b) | 2179 | 747 → 380 | 3.5435* | 3.1065 | +0.0207 |
| grow 1→2 at 50% (step 946), static per-phase programs | [`0d023baad9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/0d023baad9) | [lc1-b09-grow50b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-grow50b) | 1892 | 747 → 380 | 3.5647* | 3.1195 | +0.0337 |

The mid-run eval always runs every pass, so for the growth runs the mid loss evaluates a model that has not trained its second pass yet. Only the final loss is comparable.

**Takeaway.**
- **Looping loses at d512 fixed time**, in every variant:

  | variant | Δ |
  |---|---|
  | 2× throughout | +0.091 |
  | grow 1→2 at 50% | +0.034 |
  | grow 1→2 at 70% | +0.021 |

  The less time spent in the 2× slower phase, the smaller the loss. The measured phase throughputs, 747 then 380 ex/s, match the budget, so all three got 8 minutes. \* marks mid losses from evals that ran both passes before the second pass had trained.
- **Why it loses.** The paper's gains are compute multipliers at ≥1e20 FLOPs with 7–8 tokens per parameter for its growth variants. Here the whole run is about 1e17 FLOPs and data-limited: in 8 minutes the model sees only about 1.1B tokens. An extra pass costs tokens, which are the scarce resource at this rung. Untied growth has the same FLOP cost after growth, so I'm not building it for d512. It is a better fit for a hero-scale study.

**Earlier notes.**
- **Fixed 2× looping throughout is much worse at fixed time: +0.091.** It gets only 1426 steps. At d512, one pass of the 6-layer stack is not the bottleneck; tokens seen are.
- **The growth runs first OOMed.** The step-gated `lax.cond` allocated 79.8 GiB, because XLA holds buffers for both branches. I replaced it with two statically compiled train steps, a one-pass program before the growth step and a two-pass one after, chosen per step in Python ([`0d023baad9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/0d023baad9)). Its CPU check matches the plain model exactly.
