🤖 **Batch 77: a wide sweep of new papers** (d512, equal steps, 2 seeds each)

H100s are plentiful, so this batch tests nine new ideas at once, each behind a default-off flag. The base is **candidate 5 without PGLE**: candidate 4 + MLA query norm + qk_mult init 4 (3.0103 / 3.0135 in batch 75). PGLE is left out until the step-2560 crash is understood (batch 76). The base is rerun here on the same commit, so every idea is paired against a same-batch reference.

| idea | paper | what it changes |
|---|---|---|
| Polar Express NS | arXiv 2505.16932 | MuonH Newton–Schulz coefficients tuned per iteration (`coefficient_type=polar_express`) |
| AOL NS | Turbo-Muon | AOL-preconditioned Newton–Schulz (`coefficient_type=aol`) |
| AdEMAMix | arXiv 2409.03152 | Adam groups (incl. the embedding tables) add a slow gradient EMA, α=5, β3=0.999, both warmed up over the run |
| Grokfast-EMA | arXiv 2405.20233 | every gradient gets 2× its EMA (α=0.98) added before the optimizer |
| DyT | arXiv 2503.10622 | block pre-RMSNorms → γ·tanh(αx)+β (α init 0.8 attention / 0.2 MLP) |
| Per-layer embeddings | Gemma 3n PLE | a 64-dim token table per layer, gated by the hidden state and added to each attention input; zero-init up-projection |
| Differential attention | arXiv 2410.05258 | MLA layers: softmax(q1k1) − λ·softmax(q2k2), with a second q and key up-projection (same head_dim) |
| MoE++ | arXiv 2410.07348 | router adds zero / copy / constant experts, so tokens can use fewer real experts. It saves no compute yet (null slots ride the fixed-capacity dispatch at weight 0); the kernel change is only worth making if quality holds |
| FP8 dispatch | DeepSeek-V3, arXiv 2412.19437 §3.3 | MoE dispatch is sent as e4m3, with a scale per token per 128 channels; combine and backward stay bf16. Only 1 of the 5 same-size all-to-alls per wave shrinks, so expect about −1 to −3 ms. Error at the expert inputs is ~4% |
| Value residual | ResFormer, arXiv 2410.17897 | later layers mix layer 0's values in with learnable (λ1, λ2), init 0.5/0.5; all layers, or MLA only |

The DyT, per-layer-embedding, differential-attention and value-residual runs log their learned knobs per layer as `train/attn_res/knob_*` (`fdef2f88b4`): the value residual (λ1, λ2), effective DIFF λ, DyT α, and PLE up-projection norm. Every idea gets a follow-up tuned from what it learns; none is ruled out on one run.

| Per-head learnable qk_mult (init 4) | [`300c55db41`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/300c55db41) | [lc1-b77-qkhead](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b77-qkhead) | 2817 | 744 | 3.2329 | 3.0098 | vs lc1-b77-base5 |
| same, seed 1 | [`300c55db41`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/300c55db41) | [lc1-b77-qkhead-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b77-qkhead-s1) | 2817 | 737 | 3.2423 | 3.0150 | vs lc1-b77-base5-s1 |

**First results.**
- **Polar Express is neutral**: +0.0003 / +0.0021 against the base. The likely reason is MuonH itself: the hyperball renormalizes every update, so a more accurate polar factor changes little. NS is also a small share of the step here, so a 4-step Polar Express would save little time.
- **AOL diverged (loss 5.2), and the cause is our implementation, not the idea.** AOL's coefficients (Turbo-Muon) are a 4-step schedule for inputs preconditioned by AOL column rescaling (D^-1/2 with D_ii = Σ_j|XXᵀ|_ij). Our Newton–Schulz only Frobenius-normalizes, and with `backend_steps=5` it wraps back to the first coefficient triple. That triple's polynomial at σ=1 is 4.0098 − 7.0585 + 2.4635 = −0.585, so every converged singular value gets flipped. The proper Turbo-Muon implementation (AOL preconditioner reusing the first Gram matrix, exactly 4 iterations) is in progress and will be rerun.
- **Per-head qk_mult** (new row) follows from batch 75. The per-head key norm helped by equalizing each head's logit scale, so this lets each head learn its own temperature.

**DyT:** both runs hung at the step-1407 dropless eval, for over 50 minutes: the eval loader was waiting on 64 items. Every other run launched at the same time finished normally. They were cancelled and resubmitted as `-r`. If they hang again, it's something about the DyT model at eval.

🤖 Agreed. For batch 77 I'm treating every idea as a branch, not a single test. Each one's learned knobs are now logged per layer as `train/attn_res/knob_*` (`fdef2f88b4`). I resubmitted the four runs that have those knobs so the first results come with them:

- **value residual:** λ1 / λ2
- **differential attention:** effective λ
- **DyT:** α
- **per-layer embeddings:** up-projection norm
- **MoE++:** null-slot fraction per layer

Each gets a second round tuned from what the model actually does with it. For example: whether value residual takes up layer 0's values or pushes λ2 to zero, and whether DyT's α drifts away from its init. That round is then run on its own merits, rather than rejecting the idea after one run.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 78: second iterations, tuned from what batch 77's runs learned** (d512, paired against `lc1-b77-base5`: 3.0099 / 3.0139)

**AdEMAMix wins early and gives it back.** Final loss is +0.0023 / +0.0022, but the paired train-loss gap (50-step smoothed) shows the whole picture, and it is the same on both seeds:

| step | 200 | 500 | 1000 | 1500 | 2000 | 2400 | 2810 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AdEMAMix − base | −0.032 | −0.036 | −0.024 | −0.012 | −0.007 | −0.002 | ±0.000 |

At step 500 that is a large speedup: the slow gradient EMA helps the Adam groups early, and those include both embedding tables, whose rows update sparsely. The lead fades as α ramps toward 5 while the LR decays. A slow momentum with a ~1000-step horizon carries stale directions into the final convergence. Two tuned versions:
- **Warm up, then cool down:** α reaches 5 by 10% of the run, holds, then decays to 0 over the last 30%, so the tail is plain Adam.
- **Shorter slow horizon:** β3 = 0.99 (~100 steps) with the paper's schedule.

**Grokfast (λ=2, every group) is worse throughout:** +0.045 to +0.09 in train loss from step 200, and +0.042 final. On MuonH, adding a gradient EMA before the momentum is effectively a higher momentum. Batch 7 already found MuonH momentum 0.98 costs +0.034, so this is the same failure. Tuned version: Adam groups only, λ=1.

**Turbo-Muon, reimplemented** (arXiv 2512.04632). The first Gram matrix A = XXᵀ is formed from the raw X. X is rescaled by s = rsqrt(Σ_j|A_ij|) and A by s_i s_j, so the rescaled Gram costs no extra matmul. Then exactly 4 iterations run with the paper's coefficients: the last four quintic triples. Levanter's old `aol` table was an early draft from the reference repo.

Singular values after orthogonalization, vs the exact polar factor (bf16):

| input | quintic ×5 | polar_express ×5 | AOL ×4 (fixed) | old AOL (Frobenius, 5 cyclic steps) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512×1536 Gaussian: σ min/max, err | 0.985/1.055, 0.025 | 0.808/1.129, 0.097 | 0.987/1.062, 0.033 | 0.499/0.971, **1.64** |

- The old error of 1.64 means directions were sign-flipped, which explains the divergence.
- The fix matches quintic with one fewer iteration, except on steeply decaying spectra, where AOL's row-sum bound over-shrinks.
- Polar Express at 5 steps (the first 5 of an 8-step schedule) is far from converged: σ ranges 0.80–1.13. That is a second reason it was neutral.

**MoE++ (batch 77): the router mostly avoids the null experts.**
- **Free split:** only 0.9% / 1.7% of top-8 slots go to null experts, almost all of them zero experts; copy and constant go unused. The loss is within noise: +0.0025 / +0.0013.
- **QB-forced 25% null share:** it spreads evenly over layers (≈12% zero, 7% copy, 7% constant) and costs +0.015. That is the price of about 6 real experts per token. So far this saves no compute, since null slots still ride the fixed-capacity dispatch.

The question MoE++ really asks is whether routing some tokens to nothing beats a plain top-6 at the same average compute. The control is below. It also measures the step time top-6 would buy once null slots skip dispatch.

**What the batch 77 architecture ideas learned** (paired Δ vs base 3.0099 / 3.0139; knobs are end-of-run values)

- **Value residual: used heavily, but no loss gain** (all layers −0.0017 / 0.0000; MLA only +0.0002 / +0.0001).
  - The KDA layers switch it off: λ2 is 0.02–0.13 against λ1 ≈ 0.5.
  - Both MLA layers lean on layer 0's values: L3 has λ2 1.0–1.3 vs λ1 0.7. **L5 has λ2 ≈ 3.0 vs λ1 ≈ 0.3**, so its values are mostly layer 0's. This holds on both seeds and in both variants.

- **Differential attention: the model turns subtraction into addition.**
  - Learned λ is negative in 3 of 4 layer-seeds (−1.68, −0.93, −1.52; one +0.77), so out ≈ a₁ + |λ|·a₂. That's two attention maps summed, i.e. extra attention capacity, not noise cancellation.
  - Loss is −0.0016, but the step takes 186 ms vs 175 (+6%, two kernel calls on 2 layers), worth ≈+0.011 at fixed time. Closed: the noise DIFF cancels doesn't seem to exist in our two q/k-normed global MLA layers.
- **Per-layer embeddings: under-trained early, then unstable, from a too-hot LR.**
  - Seed 1 trails the base from the start (train loss 2.987 vs 2.882 at step 200) and takes a +0.31 spike at step 2240. It ends +0.059. Seed 0 also starts slower, then catches up (+0.0014).

The per-head *key norm* gain therefore comes from normalizing each head's per-token key magnitude, not from per-head temperature. Closed.

Grokfast on the Adam groups only (λ 1), seed 1: **+0.0071** (3.0210 vs 3.0139). Taking it off MuonH removed the blow-up but not the harm. Seed 0 is still rerunning after two node failures.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 79: fewer experts per token, and removing EP recompute** (d512, paired vs base 3.0099 / 3.0139 at 175.0 / 176.2 ms)

**What came in**

| run | Δ at equal steps | median step | at fixed time (0.0017 per 1%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **top-6 routed experts** (vs top-8) | +0.0042 / +0.0039 | **162.2 / 160.7 ms (−8.0%)** | **≈ −0.010** |
| MoE++ with a forced 25% null share | +0.0070 / +0.0155 | no change | +0.011 |
| Turbo-Muon (AOL, fixed), 4 NS steps | +0.0029 / +0.0022 | 176.4 / 171.8 ms | ≈ +0.002 |
| FP8 dispatch (first 1400 steps, then the eval crash) | train loss identical | 175.1 / 178.2 ms (no change) | 0 |

- **Top-6 is the biggest fixed-time lever found in a while.** It costs +0.004 at equal steps, but steps are 8% faster.
  - We never measured top-k at fixed time on the current recipe.
  - It also closes MoE++: dropping experts uniformly (+0.004) beats learned null routing at a similar 25% cut (+0.011).
  - Below: top-6 at its in-budget step count (480 s / 161.5 ms ≈ 2972 steps), plus top-5 and top-4 at equal steps to find the knee.
- **Turbo-Muon loses to quintic** despite correct preconditioning. Our momentum matrices likely have the steep spectra where AOL's row-sum bound over-shrinks. Closed.
- **FP8 dispatch saves no time.** Quantize/dequantize eats the ~1–3 ms from halving 1 of the 5 same-size all-to-alls per wave. Closed. It crashed at eval because the dropless eval's `sonic` backend rejected the flag; fixed in `9dcd6fc2ec`.

**New systems ideas, both aimed at the 18–26 ms of exposed EP time**
- **No expert recompute** (`moe_expert_remat=false`, `2b98a02534`). The FP8 analysis found that every wave's expert MLP and combine all-to-all run under `jax.checkpoint(nothing_saveable)`. So the backward repeats the expert up/down GEMMs and one full all-to-all per wave, i.e. 1 of 5 collectives is pure recompute. d512 peaks at ~34.5 GiB of 80, so there's room to save those instead.
- **Shortcut-connected MoE** (ScMoE, arXiv 2404.05019 / LongCat-Flash 2509.01322; `moe_shortcut=true`). Layer l's MoE gate mixes the same AttnRes sources layer l's attention saw, with its own pseudo-query. So the MoE input no longer depends on the same layer's attention output: a JVP check gives exactly zero for ∂MoE_l/∂attn_l, while attn_l still reaches every later gate. The dispatch all-to-all can then overlap that layer's attention. This is also an ML change, since the MoE loses one source.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |

Candidate 6 is in batch 80: candidate 5 without PGLE, plus AdEMAMix (α 5, β3 0.98), plus top-6 / 5 / 4 at step counts that fit strictly inside 480 s. Before any top-k choice goes further, it gets a scale check, since fewer routed FLOPs per token is exactly the kind of change whose value shifts with scale.

Losing it costs roughly 10× what the attention/dispatch overlap buys (≈ −0.003 at the fixed-time rate). Closed.

| same, seed 1 | [`061c01cf78`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/061c01cf78) | [lc1-b81-mem-4x32-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b81-mem-4x32-s1) | 3170 | 607 | 3.2325 | 3.0039 | vs lc1-b81-base6-s1 |

**First results** (paired vs the same-commit candidate 6 rerun: 3.0060 / 3.0053 at 148.6 / 149.9 ms, 471 / 475 s; batch 80's were 3.0029 / 3.0046, a ~0.002 rerun spread)

| change | steps | median step | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | at fixed time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **routed experts 512 wide** | 3170 | 154 ms (+3.4%) | **2.9934** | **2.9939** | **−0.0120** | ≈ −0.006 (486–489 s, over budget) |
| shared expert 768 wide | 3170 | 155 ms (+4%) | 2.9998 | 2.9995 | −0.0060 | ≈ 0 |
| top-3, 3380 steps | 3380 | 142–145 ms | 3.0039 | 3.0008 | −0.0033 | ≈ −0.003 (481 / 490 s) |
| elementwise gated attention | 3170 | 148.6–153.5 ms | 3.0051 | 3.0084 | +0.0011 | ≈ 0 |

- **With top-4, the routed experts want to be wider.** Width 512 costs only 3.4% of step time and gains −0.012, the first results under 2.995. Top-4 × 512 is still less expert compute per token than top-8 × 384 (2048 vs 3072 units). So at fixed time, fewer and wider experts beat many narrow ones. This is the same direction as the ReLU² 1.5× width finding. Batch 82 maps this trade at fixed time.
- **A wider shared expert helps at equal steps but pays for itself in time.** Neutral at fixed time.
- **Top-3** continues the top-k plateau: within ~0.003 of top-4, slightly ahead. Seed 1 ran 2% over budget.
- **Elementwise gated attention is neutral.** The headwise gate already does the job on our two q/k-normed MLA layers. Closed.

**Product-key memory layer: used heavily, adds little, costs a lot.** Paired vs the candidate 6 rerun, at equal steps:

| config | Δ | median step | slots touched / step | usage entropy | top-1 weight | ‖W_out‖ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 heads × top-16 | −0.0019 / −0.0011 | 167–170 ms (+13%) | 65% | 0.66–0.68 | 0.21 | 84–87 |
| 4 heads × top-32 | −0.0049 / −0.0014 | 211 ms (+42%) | 99.7% | 0.88 | 0.12 | 81–83 |

- The model does use the memory: the zero-init output projection grows to norm ~85, and at 4×32 nearly every slot is read every step.
- But retrieval is diffuse: the top-1 weight is 0.12–0.21 over 32–128 rows. So the memory behaves like a wide extra FFN, not a sparse key-value lookup. Quadrupling the reads only doubles the gain (−0.0015 → −0.003).
- Our hashed bigram table already fills the token-keyed memory role, and the MoE supplies the FFN capacity.
- At fixed time both configs lose badly (≈ +0.02 and +0.07). The step cost is dominated by the bag gather/scatter over a 134M-row table, well above the 5–8 ms estimate.
- **Closed.**

comments.body: The current hero on main uses a near dropless ragged all to all. If we could get that working here on H100 it would probably help a lot.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 On it. What I found so far about the hero's ragged transport:
- It depends on XLA's device-initiated ragged-all-to-all kernel (`--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel`), which needs Marin's patched `jax-cuda13-pjrt`. That wheel is aarch64 / GB200-only.
- Its expert MLP is SM100-specialized.
- `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` is already in this branch, but it assumes gated SwiGLU experts. Our d512 experts are ungated ReLU².

An agent is now:
1. checking whether stock x86 XLA on H100 runs `ragged_all_to_all` (the NCCL decomposition, or the device kernel), and whether an x86 build of the patched PJRT is feasible;
2. adding a `moe_implementation` switch to fast_track, with ungated ReLU² support in the ragged path;
3. testing ragged vs pooled-wave on a CPU mesh, and writing a one-layer H100 microbenchmark (pooled-wave vs ragged at the d512 shapes).

I'll run the benchmark first. A full d512 run is only worth it if the ragged transport is faster on H100.

- **Bi-Maxwell momentum + MuonH decay power 0.7** (candidate 2)
- **ReLU² 1.5× experts** (candidate 2; back to SwiGLU 256 routed and shared). At d768 this already measured k 1.028×.

A piece whose removal costs less at d768 than at d512 is the one that's fading.

comments.body:
Hmm. the current d512 target can be gamed by MFU chasing on the 8xH100 box- as seen in nanogpt if you want the best 8xH100 time, you way oversize the model, because bigger matmuls get better MFU. The relative gain here shrinks at scale once the matmuls get big enough to saturate the GPU. Our original baseline was 8 active of 384. To counteract the gaming, lets make sure that our d1024 always fits on 8xH100, and that expert sizes and shared sizes scale with hidden_dim. Long term we will counteract the gaming fully by measuring MFU on hero scale.

One change that typically helps is raising sparsity (right now we are 384/8=48) ratio of 64 usually does better.

Agreed: batch 85's routed-width gains partly buy more FLOPs per token, and at d512 bigger matmuls also run at better MFU, which won't carry to hero scale. From here on:
- **Expert widths are stated as multiples of hidden_dim.** Candidate 6 is routed 0.75d × 8 + shared 0.75d. Batch 85's best compute-bounded shape, routed 1024 / shared 192 at d512, is **routed 2d / shared 0.375d**.
- **A shape is only adoptable if the same ratios fit at d1024 on 8×H100.** Below are 40-step d1024 memory probes for each shape. The d768 width checks already queued (routed 1024 vs 1536 = 2d, shared 288 = 0.375d) test the scaled version.
- **Sparsity 64:** 512 experts, top-8, at candidate 6 widths and at the 2d / 0.375d shape. EP is 8-way, so that's 64 local experts per GPU.

Also from batches 84 and 85 (d768, 1 seed), on your earlier scale-with-scale point:
- EMA scaled to steps: **−0.0042**.

**Bigram 1M rows at d512** (candidate 6 top-8, equal steps): **3.0019 / 3.0068, i.e. −0.0053 / −0.0041 (mean −0.0047)**, at 180.4 / 182.8 ms vs 176.7 / 178.2 ms (+2.5%).

- The table's cost is a sparse gather/scatter plus Adam on its rows, and it shrinks relative to the dense compute as width grows.

**Results**

**Sparsity 64 (512 experts, top-8) at candidate 6 widths: 2.9959 / 3.0017, i.e. −0.0113 / −0.0092 (mean −0.010)**, at 179.3 / 180.2 ms (+1.5%) and 35.8 GiB peak (the same as 384 experts). The biggest single equal-step win in a while, and it doesn't densify. Next (batch 88): 1 shared expert instead of 2, on top of 512 experts.

**d1024 memory probes** (40 steps; XLA memory limit 59.4 GiB per GPU):

| d1024 shape | peak GiB | fits? |
|---|---|---|
| routed 0.75d / shared 2×0.75d (candidate 6) | 55.7 | yes, barely |
| routed 1.5d / shared 2×0.375d | 64.2 | **no** |
| routed 2d / shared 2×0.375d | 74.2 | **no** |
| 512 experts, routed 2d / shared 2×0.375d | OOM | **no** |

- **Under the d1024-must-fit rule, batch 85's routed-width gains (up to −0.038 at routed 1280) aren't adoptable as configured.** At d1024 only 0.75d fits, with ~4 GiB of headroom.
- So the adoptable MoE direction right now is **more experts at 0.75d (sparsity 64)** plus shrinking shared.
- A d1024 probe of 512 experts at 0.75d is queued. It adds 33% expert parameters, so fitting may need a memory lever: the expert-parameter share of HBM, or optimizer-state offload as on the hero.

**512 experts × routed 2d / shared 2×0.375d: 2.9659 / 2.9720**, i.e. −0.0071 / −0.0071 vs the same widths at 384 experts (2.9730 / 2.9791), and **−0.040 vs candidate 6**. 203.7 ms, 48.5 GiB at d512. So the sparsity gain stacks with routed width. This shape doesn't fit at d1024 as-is.

On [the backward-policy suggestion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451): d1024 already runs with `attn_res_layer_backward=recompute` (only d512 uses SAVE), so the probes above were at the low-memory backward already. The next memory lever is `attn_res_remat_attention=true`, which d1280 already needs. d1024 probes with it are queued for routed 1.5d, routed 2d, and 512 experts at 0.75d. If none fits, the next levers are the KDA chunk-state save policy and an optimizer-state offload.

🤖 **Batch 87: second chances for ideas closed too early** (d512, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 6 top-8 `lc1-b83-base7`: 3.0072 / 3.0109)

Per [your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451): I went back through all 86 batch write-ups for ideas closed after only one or two configurations, closed on a much older base (before soft-cap, bigram, ReLU², q/k norms, AdEMAMix), or closed with an obvious confound. These are the ones rerunnable with existing flags. Each line gives the earlier result and the reason for the retry:

- **Multi-head AttnRes + separate V gate** (b24: **−0.0115**, 1 seed, never replicated; at d768 only the plain multi-head variants ran), plus the V gate alone.
- **Gated value embeddings** (b01/b02: −0.0025, 1 seed, on the fp32-fix base). Batch 77's value residual found L5 wants token-identity values (λ2 ≈ 3.0 vs λ1 ≈ 0.3). A version at the bigram table's ×10 LR needs a small routing change and comes next.
- **Bigram 2M rows, and 2M at LR ×20** (1M gave −0.022 in b50 but was rejected for −4.5% ex/s before `embed2_fsdp` made the table cheap; at d768, 2M gave −0.0091 without saturating). 1M at d512 is already running in batch 86.
- **SNOO, K 50 / 20 at outer LR 0.3** (b45: −0.008 to −0.025 at mid-run, neutral at the end). That's the same lead-then-fade shape AdEMAMix had before its horizon was shortened. Only η 0.8 and μ 0.25 were tried.
- **OKLS on attention V, and on all attention with fresh roots** (b19/b21: −0.0055 / −0.0058 at matched tokens, 2 seeds; the V-only run the paper favours never ran).
- **NoPE MLA, i.e. no Inkling rel-pos** (b11: +0.0033, on the qk 2.5 base, before the partial key offset and q/k norms).
- **EP capacity 1.3** (only 1.0 was tried, at +0.12; a curve that steep suggests 1.15 may still drop too many tokens).
- **Adam β2 0.99 / 0.999** (never swept; the heuristic gives 0.996; bigram rows and AdEMAMix depend on it).
- **Dense router gradient** (b45: mean −0.003, before ReLU² experts).
- **MoE latent 384 = 0.75d** (only 256 vs no latent was tried; no latent was −0.032 at d768 but 23% slower).
- **Cosine schedule** (b17: −0.0032 / −0.0008, before `muonh_decay_power` was adopted).

A parallel literature scout is collecting new papers for the next batch. Ideas it judged well explored and negative (DyT, PLE, product-key memory, MoE++, Grokfast and others) aren't retried.

| revisit | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | median step |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **gated value embeddings (1× LR)** | **2.9986** | **2.9986** | **−0.0105** | 178 ms (+0.5%) |
| bigram 2M rows | 3.0010 | 3.0010 | **−0.0081** | 189 ms (+7%) |

| EP capacity 1.3 | 3.0040 | 3.0083 | −0.0029 | 185 ms (+4.5%) |

| OKLS on all attention | 3.0077 | (rerun) | +0.0005 (seed 0) | 198 ms |
| NoPE MLA (no Inkling) | 3.0087 | 3.0128 | +0.0017 | 173 ms (−2%) |
| SNOO K=50, η 0.3 | 3.0396 | 3.0460 | **+0.034** | 180 ms |
| SNOO K=20, η 0.3 | (running) | 3.0486 | +0.038 | 180 ms |

- **Gated value embeddings were the clearest missed chance.** Batch 1 had them at −0.0025 on one seed; on the current recipe they give −0.0105 on both seeds, nearly free. That's consistent with batch 77's value-residual finding (the last MLA layer takes ~90% of its values from layer 0): the MLA layers want token-identity values. The ×10-LR version is queued.
- **Bigram 2M at d512 helps, but at the table's current LR** (×10). ×20 is worse. Seed 0 is still pending.
- **AttnRes V gate:** −0.005 on both seeds, but +6% step time. The multi-head combination (b24's −0.0115) doesn't replicate: −0.003.
- **Closed:** SNOO (+0.034 / +0.038 on the current recipe; not diagnosed further, but an outer step that pulls weights off the MuonH hyperball is a plausible cause), OKLS on attention (neutral), and NoPE MLA (+0.0017 at equal steps, −2% time, so ≈ neutral at fixed time, but slightly behind Inkling at equal steps).
- Two runs failed on a node with a corrupted package cache (`scipy._lib._array_api` ImportError, around 04:20 UTC) and were requeued.

**EP capacity 1.3: −0.0032 / −0.0026.** It drops 0.4% / 1.1% of expert assignments, against **1.3% for the base at 1.15**. So candidate 6 still loses ~1.3% of its routed compute to capacity drops, worth ≈ 0.003. That's more reason to get the near-dropless ragged transport running on H100 (0.018% drops on the hero), rather than paying +4.5% step time for bigger fixed buffers.

**Dense router gradient: +0.065 / +0.034** (3.0721 / 3.0453, 183 ms). Much worse than on batch 45's base (−0.003). Its stateless default-expert term (the stand-in for the paper's EMA of expert outputs) apparently doesn't suit the current ungated-ReLU² experts; not diagnosed further. Closed unless the EMA version is built.

**Adam β2 0.99, seed 1: 3.0078 (−0.0031)**, with seed 0 rerunning. **OKLS on all attention, seed 1: 3.0112 (+0.0003)**, neutral on both seeds, so it's closed.

**Adam β2 0.999: +0.0049 / +0.0048** (3.0121 / 3.0158), against β2 0.99 at −0.0031 (seed 1; seed 0 rerunning). A longer second-moment horizon hurts and a shorter one may help, the same direction AdEMAMix's short β3 favoured.

**MoE latent 384 (0.75d): ≈ −0.02 on seed 1 (2.9903, final pending), but 203 ms (+14%). Not adopted.** Per the owner, the latent stays at 0.5 × hidden_dim for MFU reasons at hero scale. Recorded as a rule alongside "d1024 must fit" and "widths scale with hidden_dim".

**Gated value embeddings at table LR ×10: −0.0059 / +0.0014 (mean −0.0023)** vs −0.0105 at 1× LR. The value tables want the plain Adam LR.

**Bigram 2M rows, seed 0: 3.0010 (−0.0062)**, so −0.0062 / −0.0099 (mean −0.0081) for +7% step time. **Cosine schedule: −0.0028 / −0.0020 (mean −0.0024).** It still helps on top of the MuonH decay power (the `lr_schedule` flag changes the Adam groups' schedule, and MuonH keeps its power-0.7 decay). Small, consistent, and free, so it goes to the next consolidation.

**Adam β2 0.99, seed 0: 3.0040 (−0.0032)**, so −0.0032 / −0.0031 (mean **−0.0031**), free, against +0.0049 for 0.999. The heuristic's 0.996 is too long a horizon for this run. Bracketing 0.98 / 0.95 in batch 89. It goes to the next consolidation.

🤖 **Batch 88 (being implemented): new papers.** A literature scout checked papers against what's already in `model.py` / `optimizer.py`, and these are now being implemented in parallel, each as a default-off flag with learned-knob logging:

| idea | paper | change |
|---|---|---|
| KDA output correction | Comba, arXiv 2506.02475 | read with q − d·k (learnable d per head); closes the delta rule's feedback loop; ~free |
| MLA value noise filter | arXiv 2609.22005 | per-head key-side gate σ(wᵀv + b)·v on MLA values; gain reported to grow 10M→350M |
| zero-centered norm gains + decay | Qwen3.8-Next, arXiv 2608.30320 §2.1.1 | gains as 1+γ, weight decay on γ |
| expert–router coupling loss | ERC, arXiv 2512.23447 | ties router rows to expert function; cost independent of tokens |
| next implicit token prediction | NITP, arXiv 2605.24956 | cosine aux loss predicting the next token's shallow representation (dense target, unlike the failed discrete MTP) |
| data-dependent rotation in KDA | Mamba-3 2603.15569, Selective RoPE 2511.17388 | complex-eigenvalue transitions via input-dependent q/k rotation, with decay tied per rotated pair |
| GDN-2 erase gate | arXiv 2605.22791 | channel-wise erase key b⊙k in the delta rule (kernel change); the paper's ablation says the erase half is what matters; checking whether PKDA (2604.21100) comes for free |
| Newton-Muon on experts | arXiv 2604.01472 | Muon update right-preconditioned by the expert-input covariance (one 256×256 per layer, shared by all experts) |

So most channels erase harder than plain KDA's β allows (b ∈ (0, 2) acts as a per-channel multiplier on β). The gain is modest but consistent, and nearly free. A candidate for the next consolidation once the erase-only seed 1 lands.

- **Value noise filter:** neutral. Its gate statistics didn't reach W&B (the MLA stats path apparently drops them on this model), so there's no diagnosis of whether the gate moved off its ≈0.98 init. Closed unless the stats are fixed.
- **Zero-centered gains:** neutral, as expected; the paper's claim is stability under LR stress, not loss at a stable LR. Closed for d512.

**Erase gate alone, seed 1: 3.0096 (−0.0013)**, so −0.0021 / −0.0013 (mean −0.0017). Erase + write (−0.0024) is the version to carry.

- **ERC weight 0.1, seed 0: +0.0036.** Even weak router–expert coupling hurts on this router.

**NITP λ 1, seed 1: +0.0141** (3.0250), consistent with the λ-monotone harm. Closed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
As we shrink shared, consider 1 shared instead of 2. 

I am interested in a much deeper dive on a direction outside normal LLM training, which you can run in parallel with subagent. We can view fwd bwk as an arbitrary function that converts a document into a vector with a special property: multiple documents can have their vectors averaged and it retains the meaning. We store this avg in the optimizer and move our weights toward it. But vector becomes stale because we shift the definition of the compression function as we update weights. If we had a compression function that was more stable over time, it could hold much more data. However it is unclear how you could then feed that vector into the model. (Normal training the definition updates to match ingestion format of model exactly). So we would need to figure out the compression function, and then how the model can use or learn from the cumulative vector. (If an implementation detail here is overly restrictive, remove it). To start, any training of the compressor could be viewed as outside the main run timing.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Two replies:
- **1 shared expert instead of 2:** queued on top of 512 experts (sparsity 64 gave −0.010 at equal steps; see the batch 86 update). One shared expert at 0.75d (half the shared compute) and one at 1.5d (same total width).
- **Stable compressor / accumulated-memory direction:** a dedicated agent is on it in parallel. It will map the idea to related work (gradients as NTK features, fast-weight / outer-product memories, TTT / Titans, kernel mean embeddings and sketches, doc-to-LoRA hypernetworks, EMA-teacher stability). It then designs 2–3 concrete systems, each with the compressor trained outside the timed run, an averaging-friendly memory, and a way for the model to read it with gradients flowing. It prototypes the best one at toy scale and writes up ready-to-launch d512 tests. The write-up goes to `.agents/projects/stable-compressor-memory.md` on its branch, and I'll post the design and first results here.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 93: stable-compressor memory, first d512 test** (per [your deep-dive request](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451); the full write-up is in `.agents/projects/stable-compressor-memory.md` on the branch)

**The idea, made precise.** For a softmax readout W on features φ, the corpus cross-entropy gradient Σ φ(x)(p_W(x) − e_y)ᵀ splits into two parts:
- a **data half**, M = Σ φ e_yᵀ, which depends only on the data once φ is fixed, so it can be summed forever without going stale;
- a **model half**, Σ φ p_Wᵀ, which is what goes stale.

Momentum stores both halves under a moving φ. A stable compressor fixes φ and keeps only the data half. "Averages keep their meaning" exactly when the signal is linear in a fixed feature map. With hashed n-gram features, M is a next-token statistic table.

**Implementation** (`ngram_stat_*`, default off; `9f543b6aca`):
- One hashed table per n-gram order (2, 3, 4), 2M rows each. Each row accumulates Σ of a fixed random 64-dim code of the next token, plus a count.
- The table has no optimizer and is updated after each step. It can optionally be **pre-filled before step 0** (untimed) from batches past the run's end.
- A learned reader (MLP → RMSNorm → content gate) turns each row's mean code and log count into an AttnRes source, next to the trained bigram table. Gradients reach only the reader.

**Toy results** (CPU, 4-layer d128 on PG-19):
- The fixed tables **add to** a trained bigram table early in training (−0.04 to −0.07 at 400 steps) but **can't replace** it (0.11–0.13 worse alone).
- The same-data gain fades with training length (−0.047 → −0.017 → −0.005 at 400 / 700 / 1000 steps).
- Pre-filling helps, and more tokens help more (−0.005 / −0.012 / −0.023 at 0.6× / 1.2× / 2.4×).

**Falsifiable predictions for d512** (≈ 90× more tokens per row than the toy):
- same data: |Δ| < 0.003 (null);
- pre-filled from 2× the run's tokens: Δ ≤ −0.005, and 8× beats 2×;
- if 8× gives < 0.005, the memory doesn't pay at this scale.

**Needs your call:** does an untimed pre-fill from *more* of the training stream than the run itself sees count as a legal speedrun win? You said compressor training can be untimed, but pre-filling also means the model draws on tokens it never trains on. The online (same-data) variant is clearly legal. Both are running so the answer is informed.

🤖 **Batch 94: stable-compressor memory, fixed** (d512, equal steps, paired vs candidate 6 top-8 3.0072 / 3.0109)

**Why batch 93's same-data tables hurt: the wiring, not the statistics.**
- Bigram-only hurt as much as 2/3/4 (+0.0096 vs +0.0118), which points at the wiring.
- On GPU the reader was a new AttnRes source with unit scale from step 0 (the table still empty) and an open content gate (σ(2) ≈ 0.88). It took share at all 13 gates from init.
- At the end of the run it still held 0.165 of layer 0's attention gate, cutting the bigram source there from 0.604 to 0.467. Elsewhere the model had routed around it (0.007–0.02).
- **Fix:** `ngram_stat_mode=bigram`. The reader's output is added into the existing bigram source through a zero-init Adam projection, so step 0 is exactly the base model (unit-tested).

**Why the pre-fill OOMed:** the host queued hundreds of table writes ahead of the GPU, each holding its temporaries and the whole train state (77.7 GiB in use). **Fix:** each write now takes and donates only the table and blocks before the next is sent (~40 ms per batch, untimed).

**Revised predictions:**
- same data: |Δ| ≤ 0.003;
- pre-filled from 2× the run's tokens: Δ ≤ −0.005;
- 8× beats 2×;
- if 2× is neutral, the stable-memory lever doesn't pay at d512.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Hmm. based on the latent selection vs projection test, it seems perhaps the projection is entirely useless. What percent of flops do we drop if we remove the projection? Also, within the idea of selection vs projection, there is a big design space. We could do selection where we vary which input dims we select per layer, across a variety of patterns, or only use projection on some layers. Or use projection on top of a selection. This is one we'd want to validate at larger scales. There is also an angle where the size of the hidden_dim may influence the results- for instance if hidden_dim is way oversized, then selection is less harmful.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 95: the selection vs projection design space** (d512 candidate 8, equal steps, paired vs 2.9792 / 2.9861; then d768)

**FLOPs dropped by removing the latent down-projection:**
- At d512, 1× width: `w_latent_down` is 512 × 256 per layer, i.e. 0.26M MACs per token per layer, 1.57M FLOPs per token over 6 layers. That is **2.1%** of the 75.7M weight-matmul FLOPs per token, or **1.8%** of ~86M including attention's sequence terms (full breakdown in the reply below).
- At 16× routed width the MoE dominates and it falls to **≈ 0.5%**.
- In step time it was within noise at every width in batch 91 (+0.1 / −0.8 / −1.3 / +0.1%). The down-projection is concatenated into the router's input matmul, so it runs as extra columns of a GEMM that is already being issued.
- At hero scale the share grows a little, because the vocabulary head's share shrinks. With the latent at 0.5d, 8 active experts at 0.75d and a 1.5d ungated shared expert, the down-projection is 0.5d² of ≈ 14.5d² MACs per layer, about **3%** of per-layer matmul FLOPs.
- So the possible win from dropping it is mostly parameters and simplicity, plus a few percent of FLOPs, not a large speedup. It is only worth taking if selection holds at larger scale.

**What's new in the code** (`88b6f1a4b7`), all with `latent_select=true`:
- `latent_select_pattern`:
  - `first`: channels [0, 256) in every layer (batch 91).
  - `random`: a fixed random 256-subset per layer.
  - `rotating`: a 256-wide window shifted by d/6 per layer, so the layers tile the stream.
  - The indices are a frozen, non-trainable leaf (zero gradient, optimizer label `frozen`, unit-tested on CPU).
- `latent_select_layers=kda|global`: selection only in the 4 KDA layers or only in the 2 global MLA layers. The other layers keep the learned projection.
- `latent_select_plus_proj`: the expert input is `latent_norm(x_sel + x @ W_down)`, a learned projection on top of a selection.

**Predictions:**
- `first` on candidate 8: |Δ| ≤ 0.003, as in batch 91 at 1×.
- `random` / `rotating`: |Δ| ≤ 0.003. If the d512 null is real, which channels are read shouldn't matter. If rotating wins by more than 0.005, per-layer diversity of the read is doing work.
- Mixed layers: between the two ends, so also ≈ 0.
- Selection + projection: ≤ 0. It strictly contains projection. If it wins by more than 0.005, the identity path helps the projection train.

**Bug, fixed:** the first random / rotating runs went NaN at step 1. I had stored the selected channel indices as float32, and the bf16 compute cast rounds integers above 256 (511 → 512), which pushed them out of range, and `jnp.take` fills out-of-range indices with NaN. They are now stored as a 0/1 channel mask, which is exact in bf16 (`492836322c`, checked under the bf16 cast on CPU), and rerun as `-r`.

**Scale / hidden-size check:** `first`-selection vs projection at d768 on candidate 8, paired. Batch 91 only tested d512, where the residual stream is narrow (512) and a 256-channel half may already carry most of the directions the experts need. At d768 and beyond, a fixed half could lose more. d1024 follows if d768 holds.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **The math for the latent down-projection's FLOP share** (candidate 8 at d512, forward, per token).

Counted from the model's actual parameter shapes: one multiply-accumulate (MAC) per weight entry for each matrix a token passes through, and 2 FLOPs per MAC. Units: d² = 512² = 262,144 MACs.

| per layer | KDA layer (×4) | MLA layer (×2) |
|---|---|---|
| attention projections | 7.0 d² (q, k, v, o, g, write, erase) + 0.5 d² (decay low-rank) | 5.0 d² (q, o, dkv, uk, uv) + 0.13 d² (gates, rel-pos) |
| GatedNorm down/up (attn + mlp) | 1.0 d² | 1.0 d² |
| router (512 × 512 experts) | 1.0 d² | 1.0 d² |
| routed experts: 8 active × (256 × 384 up + 384 × 256 down) | 6.0 d² | 6.0 d² |
| **latent down (512 × 256)** | **0.5 d²** | **0.5 d²** |
| latent up (256 × 512) | 0.5 d² | 0.5 d² |
| shared expert (512 × 768 up + 768 × 512 down, ungated) | 3.0 d² | 3.0 d² |
| **total** | **19.5 d²** (5.11M MACs) | **17.1 d²** (4.49M MACs) |

- **All weight matmuls:** 4 × 5.11M + 2 × 4.49M + 8.39M for the vocab head (512 × 16384 = 32 d²) = 37.8M MACs = **75.7M FLOPs**.
- **Sequence-dependent attention:**
  - MLA: 2 layers × 2 (QKᵀ and AV) × 4 heads × 128 × 2048 average causal context = 8.4M FLOPs.
  - KDA chunked state updates: ≈ 2.1M FLOPs. This one is an estimate: ≈ 3 · d_k · d_v + 2 · chunk · d_k per head.
  - Total ≈ **86M FLOPs**.
- **Latent down:** 6 × 512 × 256 = 0.79M MACs = **1.57M FLOPs**. That is **2.1% of the weight-matmul FLOPs, 1.8% of all forward FLOPs.** The backward is ≈ 2× the forward for every matmul, so the share of training FLOPs is the same.

**Why it is small:** the down-projection is a d × d/2 matrix, so it costs 0.5 d², while everything else a token touches in a layer adds up to 17–19 d²:
- The 8 active experts are 12× as large: 8 × 2 × (d/2 × 0.75d) = 6 d².
- KDA alone has seven d × d projections.
- At d512 the router (d × 512 experts) is a full d² and costs twice the down-projection.
- The vocab head (32 d²) is almost as big as two whole layers.

**At larger d:**
- The head and the router (d × 512) shrink relative to d²-scaled terms, so the share rises. The ceiling is ≈ 0.5 / 17.5 ≈ **2.8–3%** of per-layer matmul FLOPs with the same width ratios.
- Attention's sequence terms push it back down.
- It would only matter a lot if the experts got relatively narrower, since the down-projection is a fixed 0.5 d².

This corrects the first figure in batch 95: "≈ 2.0% of ~77M" was the weight-matmul-only share, and the total including attention is ~86M.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 96: read vs write asymmetry of the routed MLPs** (d512 candidate 8, equal steps, paired vs 2.9792 / 2.9861)

Agreed that the latent-selection line is low impact at ~2% of FLOPs, so it closes after this test unless something stands out.

**Write-side selection** (`latent_write_select`, commit `3945345556`):
- The routed input keeps candidate 8's learned down-projection.
- `w_latent_up` is removed: the combined 256-wide routed output is written into hidden channels [0, 256), and the other 256 channels get zero from the routed experts.
- The output is scaled by `initializer_std · √256` = 0.32, the gain of the matrix it replaces. MuonH holds `w_latent_up`'s Frobenius norm at its init value, so without this the routed branch would be ≈ 3× louder for the whole run, and the test would conflate *where* the experts write with *how loud* they are.
- The shared expert and attention still write the full width.

**Read side, from batch 95** (already done): first-half read selection is −0.0016 / −0.0017.

**The 2×2:**
- read projection, write projection: candidate 8;
- read selection, write projection: batch 95, −0.0016;
- read projection, write selection: this batch;
- read selection, write selection: this batch. The routed experts then see and write only channels [0, 256).

**Prediction:** write selection costs more than read selection (Δ > +0.003). My reasoning: reads can be recovered, because upstream writers (attention, the shared expert, the AttnRes gates) are free to place what the experts need in the first half. With write selection, each token's routed output is confined to a fixed half of the stream for every downstream reader. If write selection is also ≈ 0, the stream simply has spare capacity at d512, and the half-width constraint doesn't bind on either side.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| routed output written into the first 256 channels (no `w_latent_up`) | [`3945345556`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3945345556) | [lc1-b96-wsel](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b96-wsel) | 2817 | 694 | 3.2023 | 2.9868 | +0.0076 vs 2.9792 |
| same, seed 1 | [`3945345556`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3945345556) | [lc1-b96-wsel-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b96-wsel-s1) | 2817 | 692 | 3.2091 | 2.9941 | +0.0080 vs 2.9861 |
| read and write selection (routed experts see and write only channels [0, 256)) | [`3945345556`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3945345556) | [lc1-b96-rwsel](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b96-rwsel) | 2817 | 702 | 3.1999 | 2.9881 | +0.0089 vs 2.9792 |
| same, seed 1 | [`3945345556`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3945345556) | [lc1-b96-rwsel-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b96-rwsel-s1) | 2817 | 701 | 3.2058 | 2.9923 | +0.0062 vs 2.9861 |

**Result: a clear read/write asymmetry.** Restricting where the routed experts *write* costs +0.008; restricting what they *read* costs nothing.

| routed experts read ↓ / write → | full stream via `w_latent_up` | first 256 channels only |
|---|---|---|
| **learned projection** | candidate 8 (0) | **+0.0076 / +0.0080** (mean +0.0078) |
| **first 256 channels** | −0.0016 / −0.0017 (batch 95) | **+0.0089 / +0.0062** (mean +0.0076) |

- The prediction (write selection > +0.003) holds. The effect is ≈ 9× the read-side one, and it is the same sign on all four runs.
- **Read + write selection ≈ write selection alone.** Once the output is confined, confining the input costs nothing more. So the half-width read constraint does not bind at d512 on either path.
- Reading this as you suggested: the routed MLP's write side is worth more capacity than its read side. That argues for sizing `latent_in` and `latent_out` independently rather than one shared latent, e.g. a narrow read with a full-width write.
- Since comms at hero scale make a wider latent look artificially good here, **the next test is the asymmetric pair at equal FLOPs and equal comms volume**: read 256 / write 512 vs read 512 / write 256. Dispatch sends the read width and combine returns the write width, so both move the same total bytes. That isolates the asymmetry from the "bigger latent always wins here" effect. The `latent_out_dim` implementation is in progress.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 97: where ragged's training slowdown comes from** (candidate 8, d512, profiles of steps 1500–1504 plus full-run step-time series)

Three runs: pooled-wave (8 processes, current), **pooled-wave forced to `--single-process`** (the control), and ragged one-shot at capacity 1.05 (which needs single-process).

| run | median step | mean step | GPU kernel busy (profile) |
|---|---|---|---|
| pooled-wave, 8 processes | 186.4 ms | 188.6 ms | 168.8 ms |
| pooled-wave, 1 process | 189.4 ms | **204.1 ms** | 169.3 ms |
| ragged one-shot, 1 process | 194.3 ms | 203.7 ms | 174.9 ms |

**Roughly two thirds of ragged's slowdown comes from the single-process driver, not from ragged.**
- In single-process mode, the post-step host work comes in multi-second bursts: 5–7 consecutive steps of 0.5–5.5 s every ~95–115 s of wall time, plus one early burst at steps 156–163 in both runs. That is ≈ 25 s over the run, ≈ 9–13 ms per step on the mean. The multi-process run has no such bursts.
- Not the data loader (`loading_time` ≈ 0 on every step, including the bursts) and not GC (the synchronized collections take 50–60 ms). The profile window missed a burst, so the cause isn't identified yet.
- Median steps differ by only +3 ms (1 process vs 8).

**The rest is ragged's own GPU time: +5.6 ms per step (+3.3%).**

| kernel family | pooled (1 process) | ragged | Δ ms/step |
|---|---|---|---|
| EP transport: NCCL SendRecv → symmetric-memory ragged all-to-all + multi-GPU barrier | 25.9 | 19.2 + 6.0 | −0.7 |
| expert GEMMs: cuBLAS batched (nvjet/gemm fusions) → fused Pallas ReLU² ragged kernels | ≈ 13 | 19.5 | ≈ +6.5 |
| pad / broadcast / memcpy / gather-bwd / add fusions (ragged layout bookkeeping) | ≈ 4 | ≈ 21 | ≈ +17 |
| capacity select fusions (pooled only) | 7.4 | 1.4 | −6.0 |

(Rows are the largest per-kernel differences, grouped; other fusions net out to about −11 ms.)

**Next:**
1. Profile a burst: both single-process runs burst at steps ~156–163, so steps 155–159 are being profiled with the Python host tracer to name the function (`lc1-b97-prof155-*`).
2. HLO dumps for both transports, to trace the pad/broadcast fusions back to source. These are likely zero-filled receive buffers and padding to the kernel's block size, which a kernel that writes only valid rows could skip.
3. The fused ragged expert kernel is ≈ 1.5× the cuBLAS batched GEMMs pooled-wave uses; block-size and layout tuning at the training shape is the other lever.

🤖 **Two findings: the routed-expert read/write asymmetry is large, and the single-process stall is metric logging**

**1. Asymmetric latent at equal FLOPs** (`latent_out_dim`, d512 candidate 8, equal steps, 2 seeds)

| routed experts read / write | Δ s0 / s1 | mean | ex/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 / 256 (candidate 8) | 0 | 0 | 680 / 678 |
| **256 / 512** (`w_down` writes the stream directly, no `w_latent_up`) | **−0.0185 / −0.0215** | **−0.0200** | 602 / 608 (−11%) |
| 512 / 256 (experts read the stream directly, no `w_latent_down`) | +0.0016 / +0.0003 | +0.0010 | 618 / 620 (−9%) |
| (ref: batch 96) 256 / write confined to channels [0, 256) | +0.0076 / +0.0080 | +0.0078 | |

- **Expert FLOPs are identical in the two arms**: 8 × (256·384 + 384·512) MACs per token. Each also has one 512 × 256 projection. Widening the write gives −0.020; widening the read gives nothing (+0.001). This matches batch 96's sign and makes it ≈ 20× larger than the read-side effect.
- Both arms use nearly all available channels: the expert-weight participation ratio is 254 / 497 for 256 / 512 and 485 / 254 for 512 / 256. So the experts don't leave the extra read width idle; it just isn't worth anything.
- **Cost:** both are ≈ 9–11% slower here. 256 / 512 returns 512-wide rows through the combine all-to-all (2× the combine bytes). As you noted, that comms cost is understated at d512 and larger at hero scale. At d512 fixed time, −11% ≈ +0.019, so it's break-even here and not a d512 win.
- **The takeaway for hero-scale latent design:** don't size `latent_in` and `latent_out` together. If extra latent width is affordable, it belongs on the write/combine side; the dispatch side can stay narrow at little cost.

**2. What the single-process host stalls are** (batch 97 follow-up)

I added a stack sampler (`host_stall.py`) that records every thread's Python stack while post-step host work runs longer than 0.3 s. In every sampled stall, the **main thread is inside W&B's metric conversion**:
```
log(tracker.py) → _prepare_log(wandb.py) → _convert_metrics_to_wandb_loggable → _item → __array__ → Array._value
```
It pulls each logged device scalar to host one at a time: hundreds of per-layer router / knob / AttnRes metrics, each a separate synchronizing device-to-host copy. With one process driving 8 GPUs, each copy is slower. At the same time, the finelog `write_rows` and finestore directory-sync threads compete for the interpreter lock. The ≈ 0.1 s every 10 steps seen in the 8-process runs is the same thing at a smaller scale.

**Fix** (`627272833d`): the loop now copies the logged metric dicts to host in **one batched `jax.device_get`** before handing them to the tracker. Same metrics, no math change. Being measured now on pooled-wave (8-process and 1-process) and ragged. Expected:
- the 8-process run gets ≈ 1% faster;
- most of the single-process mean-vs-median gap (≈ 13 ms per step) goes away;
- ragged's remaining gap becomes just its own GPU time (+5.6 ms, +3%), which the kernel work can then target.

**Correction (measured): the batched `device_get` did not remove the stalls.**

| run | median step before → after | mean step before → after |
|---|---|---|
| pooled-wave, 8 processes | 186.7 → 184.8 ms | 189.0 → 197.9 ms |
| pooled-wave, 1 process | 189.5 → 191.4 ms | 204.6 → 204.3 ms |

- The sampler shows why my diagnosis was wrong. During a 0.5 s stall it collected **only one sample** where it should have collected ~25, and the main thread's frame is different each time (any JAX call that touches a device).

**Stack4 = candidate 8 + router Adam LR ×0.5 + MuonH gate init ×2 + sqrt-softplus combine + drop-aware combine renorm** (d512, equal steps)

| run | Δ s0 / s1 | mean | median step |
|---|---|---|---|
| candidate 8 | 0 | 0 | 183.5 / 184.5 ms |
| **stack4** | **−0.0042 / −0.0070** | **−0.0056** | 185.0 / 186.6 ms (+1.0%) |

The pieces on their own (2 seeds each; each consistent in sign but under the 0.005 bar):
- router LR ×0.5: −0.0024. The bracket was ×0.1 +0.0030, ×0.25 −0.0011, ×0.5 −0.0024, ×1 0, ×2 +0.0089.
- gate init ×2: −0.0022. The bracket was ×0.5 +0.0013, ×1 0, ×2 −0.0022, ×4 +0.0002.
- sqrt-softplus combine: −0.0021.
- drop renorm: −0.0014. It recovers ≈ 40% of the −0.0035 dropless gain for free.

They add up roughly linearly (sum −0.0081 vs −0.0056 stacked). At fixed time the +1.0% median step costs ≈ 0.0017, so the net is ≈ −0.004. **It clears the 0.005 bar at equal steps, and d768 validation is running** (`lc1-b102-d768-stack4` / `-s1`, vs the d768 candidate 8 reference below).

**d768 candidate 8** (batch 95, widths scaled to hidden, 7325 steps): **2.7197 / 2.7156** (mean 2.7177), **k ≈ 2.2× vs clean KMA** (candidate 7 was 1.82×). First-half latent selection at d768: 2.7199 / 2.7138 (−0.0008), neutral again. That's consistent with d512, so projection vs selection is settled at two scales.

**Closed in this round** (2 seeds each unless noted):

| idea | mean Δ |
|---|---|
| FoX forget gate (bias 4; bias 0 NaNs) | +0.0008; the gate learns f ≈ 0.999 (turns forgetting off), and it is 43% slower from head-dim padding |
| Magma (with MuonH LR ×3 to offset its ≈0.3× average step) | +0.0097 (uncompensated: +0.098) |
| MuonSphere, MuonH LR ×1 / ×0.5 / ×0.25 | +0.027 / +0.013 / +0.060 |
| momentum warmup, cautious WD, slower early upper-layer q/k LR (25% / 4% of training) | +0.0012, +0.0007, 0.0000 / −0.0010 |
| expert init ×0.5 / ×2 | +0.0028 / +0.0015 |
| unigram lm_head bias | +0.0025 |
| token-conditioned router bias; router soft-cap 5 / 10; AttnRes logit soft-cap 5 / 10 | +0.0004; +0.0016 / +0.0002; −0.0012 / −0.0007 |

**Single-process stalls: the root cause is the data loader, not logging or CPU throttling.**
- Throttling: the stall sampler now logs the cgroup's `nr_throttled`, and it is 0 in every stall.
- Summed over all stalls, the busy background threads are the loader's prefetch threads (`_fill_queue_with_batches`): `batched_device_put` (≈ 5.3k samples), `np.stack` (≈ 600) and `backend_compile_and_load` (≈ 390, the loader compiling mid-run). Meanwhile the main thread sits in device↔host copies, and the sampler thread itself gets ≈ 1 sample per 0.5 s. The whole process is starved of the interpreter lock.
- Why: levanter's `CausalLmDataset` / `PrebuiltLmDataset` build **every example with its own `eqx.filter_jit` call** on the CPU backend (128 dispatches per batch, recompiling on new shapes), and prefetch 512 batches ahead in bursts. With 8 processes each builds 1/8 of the batch under its own interpreter lock. With one process driving 8 GPUs, all of it contends with the step dispatch.
- Stalls grow from ≈ 0.4 s early in the run to 3–5 s late.
- **Proposed fix** (not done yet): a batch-level NumPy path in those datasets. It would build a whole batch of examples on host in one vectorized pass instead of 128 jitted calls, with a smaller prefetch buffer. This is a shared-pipeline change, so it would sit behind an explicit option and be checked bit-exact against the current path. With it, ragged's gap should shrink to its own +3% of GPU time (layout pad/zero-fill kernels plus the fused expert kernel at ≈ 1.5× cuBLAS). That would make the −0.0035 dropless gain roughly break-even, and a net win once those kernels are fixed.

- **My prediction (flat down to 128) was wrong.** The read is a knee exactly at 256 (d/2): above it nothing is gained, below it each halving costs more (+0.019, then +0.029, then +0.032).
- The narrow reads are 6–10% faster, worth ≤ 0.014 at the fixed-time rate. That is far from paying for +0.048.
- So "reads don't matter" is wrong. The read *saturates* at d/2, while the write keeps paying up to d.

**The same grid with no shared expert** (paired vs a no-shared baseline, same seed):

| arm | Δ with shared expert | Δ without shared expert |
|---|---|---|
| remove the shared expert (candidate 8 → no-shared base 2.9899 / 2.9982) | | **+0.011** |
| read 512 / write 256 | +0.0010 | **−0.0083 / −0.0067 (−0.0075)** |
| read 256 / write 512 | −0.0200 | **−0.0197 / −0.0228 (−0.0213)** |
| read 128 / write 256 | +0.019 | +0.0190 / running |
| read 64 / write 256 | +0.048 | +0.0536 / +0.0527 (+0.053) |

- **Your suspicion was partly right.** With the shared expert present, a wider routed read buys nothing (+0.001). Without it, the routed experts do gain from reading the full stream (−0.0075). So the shared expert's full-width read covers most of what a wider routed read would add.
- **The write asymmetry does not depend on the shared expert:** −0.020 with it, −0.021 without. Even with no shared expert, write-side width is worth ≈ 2.8× read-side width.
- **The knee below 256 is the same with or without the shared expert** (+0.019 at 128, ≈ +0.05 at 64). The shared expert doesn't let the routed read go narrower.
- **For latent design:** read at d/2 is the floor, not a free parameter. Extra width is worth far more on the write side (−0.02 per doubling from d/2 to d) than on the read side (≈ 0 with a shared expert, −0.0075 without). As before, the comms cost of a wider combine is understated at d512, so this is a direction for the hero latent rather than a d512 recipe change.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 104 results: per-expert input slices lose badly. The routed experts need one *shared* read subspace, not a union of private ones.**

Δ is paired, same seed: with shared expert vs candidate 8, without it vs the no-shared baseline. All seeds agree to ±0.003.

| each expert reads | a learned projection (batch 103) | fixed slices of the stream, with shared expert | same, no shared expert |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 (2 blocks) | 0 (candidate 8) | **+0.0342 / +0.0364 (+0.035)** | +0.0224 / +0.0277 (+0.025) |
| 128 (4 blocks) | +0.019 | +0.0756 / +0.0744 (+0.075) | +0.0601 / +0.0614 (+0.061) |
| 128 (random subsets) | — | +0.0783 / +0.0778 (+0.078) | +0.0637 / +0.0646 (+0.064) |
| 64 (8 blocks) | +0.048 | +0.1178 / +0.1178 (+0.118) | +0.1027 / +0.1047 (+0.104) |

- **Coverage is not the problem.** With 2 blocks, a token's top-8 experts almost always include both halves, so the union covers the full stream. It still costs +0.035 against a single shared 256-dim projection, and +0.034 against reading the full 512 (batch 101). Blocks vs random subsets make no difference.
- **What does work, from batches 95, 101 and 103:** *all* experts reading the *same* 256-dim subspace. A learned projection, a fixed first-half selection and the full stream are all equivalent (±0.002). A *different* subspace per layer (batch 95: random / rotating per layer, +0.003 to +0.004) or per expert (here, +0.035) is worse, and the more ways the read is split, the larger the cost.
- **My reading:** the stream can place what the routed MLP needs into one shared subspace, and the router then picks *which* experts use it. When each expert reads its own slice, every slice must carry a copy of the useful information, which spends stream capacity. Removing the shared expert lowers the cost a little (+0.025 vs +0.035), consistent with the shared expert's full-width read also wanting that capacity.
- The masked-slice runs compute the full 512-wide read, so they are ≈ 8–10% slower here. A real slice-dispatch implementation would be cheap, but the loss cost rules it out regardless.
- **Closed:** per-expert read subsets. **The rule the read side has followed so far:** one shared read space of ≥ d/2, with the capacity going to the write side.

comments.body:
🤖 **KITE ([arXiv 2609.27294](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27294), StepFun, Sep 2026): read it. My take is that it doesn't fit the d512 objective; details below in case you still want it run.**

**What it is:** a *mid-training depth expansion*.
- A trained model (33.8B-A1.1B MoE, 512 experts, top-8) is copied into two towers of equal depth. The **Prefiller** (the original) computes K/V at every layer. The **Decoder** (a copy, run after it) has its own queries but no K/V projections: decoder layer *l* attends to prefiller layer *l*'s K/V.
- Decoder input is `RMS(e_t) + RMS(h^P_L,t)`. The embedding and head are shared, and gradients flow back through the reused KV.
- "KV-invariant": the model gains depth, but prefill cost and the KV-cache size stay those of the small model.

**Results:**
- One seed, ≈ 5e21 FLOPs, grown after 168B tokens then trained 222B more.
- Training loss at equal FLOPs vs a same-cost deeper dense-depth baseline: −0.011 (vs 47B) and −0.002 (vs 63B, about noise).
- The headline win is an *analytical* inference-cost saving at a fixed prefill/KV budget (6.7–31.6%).
- There are no ablations: no from-scratch variant, no growth-time sweep, no loss at the growth point.

**Mapping here:**
- **Closest thing already tested:** batch 9's looped / grown models. That's the *tied* version of the same move: run the 6-layer stack a second time from 70% of training. Result: +0.021 at best, and the doubled stack runs at 0.51× throughput.
- **KITE's other piece**, reusing K/V across layers, is close to batch 15's `mla_share_kv_latent` (+0.0056).
- **Porting it** would mean duplicating all 6 layers including the 512-expert MoE (2× parameters and EP all-to-all), a decoder KDA that reruns the recurrence with its own queries, and swapping the parameter tree and optimizer state mid-run. That's ≈ 400–550 LOC, medium-high risk. The d1024 two-tower version may not fit 8×H100.
- **Step time after growth ≈ 1.9×.** Our objective is training loss at fixed time; KV-cache invariance doesn't enter it.

**Recommendation:** skip at d512. The paper's gain is inference cost at fixed KV, which the d512 loss objective doesn't measure; its training-loss edge over a same-cost deeper model is ≈ 0; and both of its pieces have already lost here (tied growth +0.021, KV reuse +0.006).

**If you want it tested anyway:** untied KITE growth at 70% and 85% of an 8-minute fixed-time run, 2 seeds each, vs candidate 9. My expectation is +0.01 to +0.03. It is also a mid-run growth, so it needs your ruling under the schedule rules.

comments.body:
🤖 **KV side stream: being implemented** (per your comment). The concrete version I'm building for the signs-of-life test:

- **Side stream:** each token gets its own embedding of width *w* = d/n (arms: *w* = 128 = d/4 and *w* = 256 = d/2). It runs its own residual stream with one side block per main layer: plain causal softmax attention within the side stream (document-masked like the main model) plus a dense ReLU² MLP of width 4*w*.
- **KV comes only from the side stream:**
  - KDA layers compute k and v (and their short convs) from `RMSNorm(s_l)`. Their main-stream `w_k` / `w_v` are removed.
  - MLA layers compute the KV latent from `RMSNorm(s_l)`. Their main-stream `w_dkv` is removed. `kv_latent_norm`, `w_uk`, `w_uv` and the key norm / offset stay as they are.
- **The main stream keeps queries, the KDA gates (g, β, erase / write) and everything downstream,** so "who comes next" gates and queries, while "what am I" supplies the keys and values.
- **Test:** 2 seeds per width vs candidate 9 at equal steps, reporting step-time cost separately, since the side attention adds work. The goal is signs of life, so I'll report the equal-step Δ even if fixed time is worse.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 108: KV side stream, signs-of-life runs** (d512 candidate 9, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791; `5e22e5aaa7`)

As built (details in the design comment above):
- **Side stream:** width *w*, its own token embedding, and one side block per layer (causal softmax attention with head_dim 128 on the FA4 path, per-head QK norm, RoPE, document masking; ReLU² MLP of width 4*w*). It is computed once before the main layers.
- **Main layers:** layer *l* reads a learned RMSNorm of the side state leaving side block *l*. KDA `w_k` / `w_v` and MLA `w_dkv` now read only the side stream; the main stream produces no K/V.
- **CPU checks:** flag off is bit-identical; flag on passes causality and document isolation through both streams; SAVE and RECOMPUTE backward agree.
- **Cost:**
  - *w* = 128: +1.3M params, −0.8M active (the KDA / MLA K/V inputs shrink from 512 to 128); ≈ +5% FLOPs.
  - *w* = 256: +7.6M params; ≈ +21% FLOPs.
  - The side stream runs serially before the main layers, so expect roughly +7% / +15% step time at d512. **Judged at equal steps first** (signs of life); step time is reported separately.

| candidate 9 + KV side stream, w = 128 (1 head) | [`5e22e5aaa7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5e22e5aaa7) | [lc1-b108-kvs128](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b108-kvs128) | 2817 | 630 | 3.2784 | 3.0538 | +0.0788 vs 2.9750 |
| same, seed 1 | [`5e22e5aaa7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5e22e5aaa7) | [lc1-b108-kvs128-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b108-kvs128-s1) | 2817 | 646 | 3.2755 | 3.0540 | +0.0749 vs 2.9791 |
| candidate 9 + KV side stream, w = 256 (2 heads) | [`5e22e5aaa7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5e22e5aaa7) | [lc1-b108-kvs256](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b108-kvs256) | 2817 | 619 | 3.2603 | 3.0399 | +0.0649 vs 2.9750 |
| same, seed 1 | [`5e22e5aaa7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5e22e5aaa7) | [lc1-b108-kvs256-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b108-kvs256-s1) | 2817 | 610 | 3.2662 | 3.0444 | +0.0653 vs 2.9791 |

**Results: no signs of life. Sourcing K/V only from a side stream costs ≈ 0.07 at equal steps.**

| side width | Δ s0 / s1 | mean | median step |
|---|---|---|---|
| *w* = 128 (1 head) | +0.0788 / +0.0749 | **+0.077** | 203 / 198 ms (+8%) |
| *w* = 256 (2 heads) | +0.0649 / +0.0653 | **+0.065** | 207 / 210 ms (+12%) |

- **The side stream is numerically healthy** (per-layer RMS 0.95–1.39, rising with depth), so this is not a numerics failure.
- **My reading: it is a transport bottleneck.** Attention is the only way information moves between positions. With K/V taken only from the side stream, a later position can retrieve only what the *side stream* computed at earlier positions: its embedding plus 1–2 small attention heads and a narrow MLP. Everything the main stream builds at earlier positions (MoE outputs, multi-layer context) never becomes retrievable. The main stream can only query and gate.
  - Doubling *w* recovers only 0.012 of the 0.077, so width isn't the limit; the cut is structural.
  - The KDA layers are hit hardest: their recurrent state *is* the K/V sum, so the whole local-mixing memory becomes side-stream-only.
- **A "some sharing" variant that keeps the idea without the bottleneck,** if you want to pursue it: K from the side stream (identity, "what am I"), V from the main stream (content, "what I carry"). Or K = main + side, so the side stream adds a clean identity signal to keys rather than replacing them. Both keep full-rank content transport, so they test whether a *separate identity source for keys* helps. I'd expect at most a small effect; it's cheap to try if you want it.

**Gather-based per-expert slices** (the fair version of batch 104):

**Results: the clean cost of splitting the read is small at 2 groups (+0.005), but at 4 groups it is worse than a narrow shared projection.**

| each expert reads | Δ with shared expert | Δ no shared expert | median step (candidate 8 = 183.5 ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **2 groups of 256** (half the experts on channels 0–255, half on 256–511) | +0.0039 / +0.0060 (**+0.005**) | +0.0077 / +0.0086 (**+0.008**) | 201–203 ms |

- **At 128 channels per expert, a private slice (+0.033) costs more than a *shared* 128-dim projection (+0.019).** So splitting helps nothing even at matched per-expert width, and the gap grows as slices narrow. The union covering the full rank doesn't compensate.

- **Takeaway:** the read constraints so far are one shared read space, ≥ d/2 wide. Per-expert partitions of the stream don't pay at any width tested. **Closed**, with the clean numbers.

🤖 **Batch 110: expert specialization study, phase 1 (top-1 of 8, characterization)** (tooling at `f676087c74`)

**Tooling:**
- `--routing-dump-steps 0,250,1000,2817` runs a forward-only pass over 8 fixed held-out batches (round-robin from every validation set, including Paloma) and writes `routing_step{N}.npz` with per-layer counts `[layer, token, expert]`, by current token, by previous token (within a document), and combine-weighted.
- `analyze_routing.py` reports:
  - per layer: I(token; expert), its noise floor, load, and per-token routing entropy;
  - per expert: top tokens by lift, decoded, and a token-class breakdown;
  - across seeds: Hungarian-matched similarity;
  - over time: evolution across steps.
- Seeding flags are also in: `router_embed_tie=L:E:V` (router column = α · `token_embed[V]`, the same parameter, from step 1) and `router_bias_seed=L:E:V:b`.

**A trap at top-1:** every *renormalized* combine (sigmoid-renorm, softmax-renorm, candidate 9's sqrt-softplus) turns the single combine weight into the constant `routing_renorm_sum`. The router would then get **zero** gradient from the LM loss, and only the QB bias would move routing. So the study model uses `router_combine=sigmoid_raw`, which matches at init and keeps the router trainable.

**Runs:** candidate 9 with top-1 of 8 routed experts, each 3072 wide (same active routed compute), `sigmoid_raw` combine, 2 seeds:
- [lc1-b110-t1e8-r](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b110-t1e8-r)
- [lc1-b110-t1e8-r-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b110-t1e8-r-s1)

(The first attempt crashed at the step-0 dump: the held-out sequences came through the dataset's per-example CPU jit while the GPU context mesh was active. They are now fetched on a worker thread, where the mesh context doesn't apply (`5db0fdf63a`), and the runs are relaunched as `-r`.)

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 111 results: specialization can be seeded, and a router–embedding tie spreads from one token to its embedding neighborhood. A hard bias prior barely seeds anything.** (top-1 of 8 study model, expert 3 tied in every layer from step 1, 2 seeds, step 2817 dumps)

**P(expert 3 | tied token) and P(expert 3 | token's class), seed 0 / seed 1, vs the baseline's natural expert for that token or class:**

| run | layer 0 | layer 2 | layer 5 | natural expert in the untied baseline (token / class, L0) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| tie `1` (digits) | token 1.00 / 1.00, **class 0.94 / 0.95** | token 0.64 / 0.92, class 0.63 / 0.85 | token 0.53 / 0.52, class 0.41 / 0.45 | 0.41 / 0.43 (s0), 0.31 / 0.30 (s1) |
| tie `\n` (newlines) | token 1.00 / 1.00, **class 1.00 / 1.00** | 1.00 / 0.79, class 1.00 / 0.87 | 0.99 / 0.27, class 0.96 / 0.26 | 0.80 / 0.73, 0.44 / 0.49 |
| tie `mathbf` (LaTeX) | token 1.00 / 1.00, **class 0.01 / 0.00** | 0.00 / 0.81, class 0.01 / 0.01 | 0.00 / 0.15, class ≈ 0 | 1.00 / 0.41 |
| tie ` table` (control word) | token 1.00 / 1.00 | 1.00 / 0.24 | 0.80 / 0.19 | 0.45 / 0.59 |
| **bias** +4 on expert 3 for `1` (no tie) | token 0.25 / 0.76, class 0.02 / 0.11 | 0.01 / 0.07 | 0.13 / 0.38 | |

1. **The tie seeds the tied token perfectly in the layer it reads most directly (layer 0: P = 1.00 in every run).** It holds through the deeper layers in most seeds, fading by layer 5 on some.
2. **It spreads to the token's *embedding* neighborhood, not to a hand-defined class:**
   - `1` → expert 3 becomes the digit expert (all digits 0.94–0.95 at L0, above the baseline's natural digit expert at 0.30–0.43). In layer 5 it becomes a **number-word** expert: ` six`, ` eight`, ` twenty`, ` hundred`, `-five`. That's semantic spread beyond digits.
   - `\n` → expert 3 takes **every newline-containing token** (class 1.00 at L0, 0.96–1.00 through the layers on seed 0): `"\n`, `}.\n`, `;\n\n`, ` }\n`, … A whitespace / structure expert.
   - `mathbf` → expert 3 takes `mathbf` itself (1.00 at L0) but **none of the LaTeX class** (0.01). It becomes a generic plural-noun expert instead (` millions`, ` indicators`, ` companies`). `mathbf`'s embedding evidently doesn't sit in a LaTeX cluster.
   - ` table` → a broad common-noun expert (` relationships`, ` matrix`, ` schedule`, ` layers`).
   - So the specialization that forms is whatever lies near the tied direction in embedding space. Digits and newline tokens are tight embedding clusters, so they spread cleanly.
3. **It locks in immediately:** at step 250, P(3 | token) is already 1.00 and P(3 | class) is 0.97 for digits and 1.00 for newlines.
4. **A hard +4 logit bias on the token is a weak seed:** P(3 | `1`) is only 0.25 / 0.76 at L0 and falls over training (0.40 at step 1000 on seed 0), and it doesn't spread to the class. QB balancing and the learned router override a fixed per-token bias. The tie works because it moves the whole router direction.
5. **Loss:** the ties cost loss vs the untied baseline: digits +0.0285 / +0.0222, newline −0.0013 / +0.0218, LaTeX +0.0050 / +0.0106, table +0.0100 / +0.0131. The bias prior is neutral (−0.0012 / −0.0003). Forcing one expert in *every* layer onto a fixed direction is a real constraint. Deeper layers want a different partition, and the fading at L5 is the model working around the tie. The learned tie scale α grew from its matched init to ≈ 3.5–9.4, so the router leans *harder* on the tied direction over training.

**Follow-ons, as you suggested:**
- **tie only in layer 0** (where it's clean), not in every layer: does the class specialization persist without the deep-layer cost?
- **tie to a class centroid** (mean embedding of all digit tokens, or all LaTeX tokens) to seed a class whose members aren't embedding neighbors;
- **tie then release** after 250 steps: does the seeded partition persist on its own?
- **several ties at once** (digits, newline, a script like Cyrillic) to seed a larger part of the partition;
- the **scale-up** of the characterization to top-1 of 32 and top-2 of 64.

| rung | non-table params | routed-expert params | bigram rows used so far | table params | table / non-table |

| d512 | 658M | 604M | 524,288 | 268M | **0.41** |

Two ways to make it a function of the model:

| rule | d768 rows | d1024 rows | d1280 rows |
|---|---|---|---|

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 115: why candidate 9 OOMs at d1024 — the bigram table is all-gathered and all-reduced at full size every step**

**The failure:** all three d1024 runs died on the same `cuMemAllocAsync` of **48.04 GiB** inside `jit_train_step`: at step 435 (remat, 0.75), at step 7 (remat + 0.9), and at step 4348 (no remat + 0.9, a coordination shutdown after another rank failed). That is XLA's single temp buffer for the whole train step, not one tensor. It sits on top of ≈ 21.5 GiB of resident params, optimizer state and EMA copy (21.5 + 48 = the 69.5 GiB peak W&B reported), and the remat + 0.9 runs failed below the 71 GiB limit because the allocator couldn't find one contiguous 48 GiB block.

**Attribution probes** (candidate 9 at d1024, attention remat, 0.9 fraction, 20 steps, no eval / EMA; memory in GiB):

| probe | in use | peak | Δ peak |
|---|---|---|---|
| A, unchanged | 17.9 | 65.0 | — |
| B, no value embeds | 17.9 | 65.1 | +0.1 |
| **C, no bigram table** | **13.9** | **55.2** | **−9.8** |
| D, shared expert 1024 | 17.8 | 64.6 | −0.4 |
| F, 256 experts | 12.2 | 59.2 | −5.8 (all resident expert state) |

The bigram table is the outlier.
- Its ≈ 4 GiB resident share is expected: 2M × 1024 in fp32 plus two Adam moments, row-sharded over 8 GPUs.
- It also adds **≈ 6 GiB of temporaries**. With `embed2_fsdp=true` the model does `reshard(token_embed2, P(None, None))`, so every step:
  - the forward **all-gathers the whole table** (≈ 4.3 GB bf16 at d1024);
  - `_embedding_gather`'s backward builds a **dense full-size fp32 gradient** (8.6 GB) on every GPU and **all-reduces** it, although each GPU keeps only its 1/8 of the rows.
- That is also ≈ 8.6 GB of all-reduce traffic per step. At d512 it is ≈ 1 GB per step, which is likely a good part of the table's known step-time cost.

**Fix being implemented:** a row-sharded lookup that moves ids and activations instead of the table.
- Forward: all-gather the batch's hashed ids (a few MB); each GPU looks up only rows it owns; a reduce-scatter hands each GPU its own tokens' embeddings.
- Backward: all-gather the per-token cotangents; each GPU scatter-adds into its own shard only, with **no all-reduce and no full-size accumulator**.
- The token axis is chunked to cap the temporaries at ≈ 0.5 GB.
- Same math (fp32 gradient accumulation), checked against the current path on a multi-device CPU mesh.
- Expected at d1024: ≈ 6+ GiB less peak, and the table's comm drops from ≈ 8.6 GB all-reduce to ≈ 2 × 2 GB gathers per step. At d512 it should recover some of the table's speed cost.

Candidate 9's d1024 run relaunches on the fix.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: We may be able to take some inspiration from the recent nanogpt record, in terms of how we handle the embeddings.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Embedding ideas from the new modded-nanogpt record** ([#360, ANVIL2](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/360), merged today: 39.9 s from 73.9 s), per your comment.

Its biggest non-CE change is one **84.6M-row hashed bigram + trigram table** (× 768, row-sharded 1/8 per GPU), worth **35.8 millinats / 7 s** of the gain at only **+1.2 s** of wall time. Their row-count grid: 377k → 21M → 84.6M rows gives 3.315 → 3.284 → 3.279 val loss for +0.5 s total, because nothing in the step scales with table size. How:

1. **Sign trick** (from [#299](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/299)): each n-gram's row is multiplied by a ±1 vector chosen by an *independent* hash from a pool of 8192 sign rows, so n-grams colliding on a row roughly cancel (count-sketch). ≈ −0.5 s in #299. **We don't have it.** It's free and composes with our `embed2_norm`.
2. **Sparse row exchange:** only the unique rows a step touches are fetched from their owners (all-to-all of ids, then rows), and gradients go back the same way. No dense gradient, no all-reduce, no all-gather of the table.
3. **Row-sparse Adam:** β1 = 0 and one fp32 second moment *per row*, so a row with no gradient has an exactly zero update. The update can therefore be gathered, applied and scattered for only the touched rows, and optimizer state is 4 bytes per row. Plus a period-4 update cadence.
4. The **same sparse treatment for value embeddings** (−1.1 s).

**What maps onto us:**
- The row-sharded gather already being built for the d1024 OOM (batch 115) is step toward (2).
- **(3) is the gate for everything else.** Our table uses Adam with momentum and AdEMAMix, which keeps every row moving and so forbids a sparse update.
- **Being implemented now as flags,** for 2-seed d512 tests on candidate 9:
  - the **sign trick**;
  - **row-sparse-compatible Adam on the table** (β1 = 0, per-row v, no AdEMAMix), run *densely* first to check it is loss-neutral here, with an LR bracket.
- If both hold, a sparse update path makes **much larger tables** cheap. Our 524k → 1M test was −0.003 to −0.005 at equal steps and was rejected only on speed (batches 50 / 55). It would also let us **revisit trigrams at tens of millions of rows**: our trigram tests used 262k–524k rows, where collisions swamp them.

**One tension to flag:** rule A fixes the table at 0.41 × the other params, and the record's result is that much bigger tables keep paying when they cost ≈ nothing. If the sparse path works, we may want to revisit rule A for the hashed table, e.g. by counting it separately since it is a memory, not compute.
