comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 148: drop the latent from one layer at half the expert width (parameter-matched), all 6 layers** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5924989546); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`b2a8f69e2e`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b2a8f69e2e))

**Change** (`latent_free_layers`): in the listed layer the routed experts have no latent.
- They read the 512-wide stream directly (no `w_latent_down`) and write it directly (no `w_latent_up`).
- Their hidden width drops from 384 to 192.
- Expert parameters and FLOPs equal the latent layers': up + down is 512×192×2 = 256×384×2 per expert.
- Only the two latent projections are removed: 2 × 512 × 256 parameters per layer.

Like batch 146's full write, the layer lives in a tail stack, and the router and shared expert are unchanged.

| run | latent-free layer |
|---|---|
| `lfree0` … `lfree5` | 0, 1, 2, 3 (MLA), 4, 5 (MLA) |

**How this separates the effects:**
- Batch 146 added about 50M expert parameters per layer.
- This batch keeps expert capacity fixed, and gives the layer both full-width read and write in exchange for narrower experts.
- If the final layers gain here too, the write rank, not capacity, is what matters there.

---

### Results (Paloma macro, equal steps, Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; candidate 9's median step is 184.3 ms)

| latent-free layer | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | batch 146: full write (+50M params) | median step |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (KDA) | −0.0042 | −0.0007 | −0.0025 | −0.0031 | 194 ms |
| 1 (KDA) | −0.0009 | −0.0030 | −0.0019 | −0.0023 | 193 ms |
| 2 (KDA) | +0.0009 | +0.0006 | +0.0008 | −0.0008 | 192 ms |
| 3 (MLA) | +0.0009 | −0.0011 | −0.0001 | −0.0044 | 192 ms |
| 4 (KDA) | +0.0002 | −0.0028 | −0.0013 | −0.0075 | 194 ms |
| 5 (MLA) | −0.0022 | −0.0042 | **−0.0032** | **−0.0113** | 194 ms |

- **At matched expert parameters, removing the latent helps the final layer a little (−0.003) and the others not beyond noise.** The full-rank read and write in exchange for half the expert width is a small, final-layer-leaning gain.
- **Most of batch 145–146's final-layer gain was the extra capacity, not the write rank.**
  - Adding 50M expert parameters is worth −0.002 to −0.003 in early layers, but −0.0075 in layer 4 and −0.011 in layer 5.
  - So the final layers are where extra expert capacity pays most. The bottleneck is how much the last layers' experts can hold, more than the 256-wide write.
  - The clean next test: widen only the final layer's experts while keeping the latent (for example intermediate 384 → 768 in layer 5), with the same +50M parameters but no change to the write.
- **The step-time cost doesn't come from FLOPs.** These layers have the same expert FLOPs as candidate 9 and still take 192–194 ms (+4–5%).
  - The cost comes from moving a layer into its own tail stack, which matches the GPU 0 waiting in batch 149's profiles.
  - Fixing that overhead, so a per-layer variant doesn't cost +4% for structure alone, is now the main implementation task before any of these can be adopted.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 149: is the full-width write's step cost real? Profiles** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5924998100); cw-rno2a, [`b2a8f69e2e`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b2a8f69e2e))

**Measured** (batches 145–146): one full-write layer costs 191.6–194.5 ms per step vs 184.3 ms for candidate 9 (+4–5.5%).

**Expected from the extra math:**
- 8 experts × 384 × 256 extra multiply-adds in that layer's `w_down`, minus the dropped 256 × 512 `w_latent_up`, is about 0.66M MACs per token. Forward plus backward that is about 3.9 MFLOP per token, **+3.7%** of the model's 107 MFLOP per token.
  - The analytic FLOP counter doesn't account for `latent_out_dim` and reports 107 MFLOP for every variant.
- So about 1–2% of the cost is unexplained by compute.

**Candidates for that gap:**
- the combine, which now moves 512-wide rows for that layer;
- the separate one-layer tail stack, which gets its own Newton-Schulz calls and collectives in the optimizer, and splits each main stack into a smaller bucket;
- the expert-sharded `w_down`, now [E, 384, 512].

| run | profiled at steps 500+ (700-step runs) |
|---|---|
| `prof-c9` | candidate 9 |
| `prof-lof5` | full-width write in layer 5 |
| `prof-lfree5` | latent-free layer 5 (same expert FLOPs as candidate 9; only the tail stack and wider combine differ) |

`prof-lfree5` isolates the cost of the tail stack and combine at unchanged expert FLOPs. I'll compare op-level time across the three (expert GEMMs, combine/dispatch, Newton-Schulz and optimizer, collectives) and report what's fixable.


---

### First results (GPU 0's trace, steps 500–505; profiling slows every run's steps to about 270 ms, so compare the differences)

| per step, GPU 0 | candidate 9 | `lof5` (full write, layer 5) | `lfree5` (latent-free, layer 5) |
|---|---|---|---|
| step span | 266.6 ms | 278.9 ms (**+12.3**) | 275.2 ms (+8.6) |
| compute-stream busy | 156.7 ms | 160.1 ms (+3.4) | 160.1 ms (+3.4) |
| compute stream idle (waiting) | 109.9 ms | 118.9 ms (**+9.0**) | 115.1 ms (+5.2) |
| GEMMs | 53.5 ms | 55.0 ms (+1.5) | 53.3 ms (−0.2) |
| expert dispatch/combine all-to-all | 30.3 ms | 31.5 ms (+1.2) | 32.8 ms (+2.5) |
| async all-gathers | 3.6 ms | 11.3 ms (+7.7) | 3.4 ms |

- **The extra math is cheap: about 3.4 ms per step of compute, +2%.** `lof5`'s GEMMs grow by only 1.5 ms per step. `lfree5` has the same GEMM time as candidate 9, as designed, and its 512-wide dispatch adds 2.5 ms of all-to-all.
- **Most of the overhead is GPU 0 waiting: +9 ms per step for `lof5`, +5 ms for `lfree5`.**
  - In `lof5` the waiting shows up in one all-gather: the 604 MB bigram-table gather (`bf16[524288,512]`, `embed2_fsdp`) at the start of the forward, which takes 9.4 ms per step against 2.2 ms in candidate 9.
  - The HLO shows the same all-gathers with identical shapes and bytes in both programs. A collective's kernel time includes waiting for the slowest GPU to arrive, so this is skew between GPUs, not more data.
- **Leading explanation: expert-parallel load imbalance.**
  - Each GPU holds 64 of the 512 experts. In the full-write layer each expert's down-projection is 2× larger, so a GPU hosting busier experts falls further behind, and the others wait at the next collective.
  - `lfree5` keeps expert FLOPs equal and shows less waiting. Its remaining wait plausibly comes from the 2× wider dispatch rows.
  - This is a hypothesis. The trace covers GPU 0 only, so the straggler isn't visible.
- **Next.**
  - Profile all 8 ranks to confirm which GPU is late and in which op.
  - Possible fixes:
    1. keep the full-width layer's experts on the same per-GPU work as the latent layers;
    2. move the bigram-table gather so it overlaps the first layers rather than sitting where the skew lands;
    3. reduce load skew in that layer.
  - The +2% of real compute is the floor. At that cost the final-layer full write (−0.011 at equal steps) would be a clear fixed-time win, about −0.008.

🤖 **Batch 150: more capacity or more compute in the final layers** (follow-up to batches [146](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5924287655) and [148](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5925057549); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`08dcf711d2`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/08dcf711d2))

**What we know so far:**
- Batch 148: at matched expert parameters, removing the latent from layer 5 gains only −0.003.
- Batch 146: adding about 50M expert parameters gains far more in layers 4–5 (−0.0075, −0.011) than early (−0.002 to −0.003).

So the open question is whether the last layers want more expert **parameters** or more **active compute**, with the latent write unchanged. Two new tail modes:
- `wide_expert_layers` / `wide_expert_intermediate_dim`: the listed layers' experts get a wider hidden dim. The latent read and write are unchanged.
- `topk_layers` / `topk_layer_k`: the listed layers activate more experts per token, at the same parameters. This was your suggestion; it is an exception to the top-8 rule in those layers only.

| run | change | extra expert params | extra active expert FLOPs in the layer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wide5` | layer 5 experts 384 → 576 | +50M (same as batch 145 `lof5`) | ×1.5 |
| `wide45` | layers 4 and 5 at 576 | +100M | ×1.5 each |
| `top12` | layer 5 top-12 | 0 | ×1.5 |
| `top16` | layer 5 top-16 | 0 | ×2 |

**How to read it:**
- `wide5` and `top12` add the same compute to layer 5. One adds parameters, the other activates more existing experts.
- `lof5` (batch 145, −0.011) also adds +50M params and ×1.5 expert FLOPs in layer 5. So `lof5`, `wide5` and `top12` all cost the same compute, and `lof5` vs `wide5` differs only in where the extra parameters go: the output (write) width or the hidden width.

**Batch 149, all-rank profiles.** The levanter profiler traced every process, but processes on one node uploaded over each other's file, so earlier runs kept only one GPU's trace. It now uploads one session per process. `prof2-c9` and `prof2-lof5` rerun the profiles to find which GPU the others wait for.

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wide5` | 2.9715 (-0.0053) | — | 190.2 (+3%) |
| `wide45` | 2.9698 (-0.0070) | 2.9733 (-0.0089) | ≈198 (+8%) |

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 151: when should the Bi-Maxwell twin rails start?** (d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`63d02dabdc`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/63d02dabdc))

Candidate 9 runs plain Nesterov momentum until 1/3 of the run (step 939). Then it engages the twin rails (fast EMA rate 0.15, slow 0.02, slow weight 0.5615), both starting from the Nesterov buffer.

**Where that came from:**
- The 1/3 point was set when we ported the rails from modded-nanogpt ([`#339`](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/339)). ANVIL II engages at about 46% of its run.
- Batch 67 tested 1/4 (+0.0002) and 1/2 (−0.0005) on candidate 2, both flat.

**What was never tested:**
1. starting much earlier, including from step 1;
2. ANVIL II's own variant. There the slow rail is a zero-init EMA accumulating **from step 0**, only blended in at the engage step. In our version the slow rail restarts from the Nesterov buffer at the switch, so at that point it has none of the earlier history (new option `bimaxwell_slow_from_start`, tested).

| run | rails engage | slow rail |
|---|---|---|
| `bm0` | step 1 | from the switch |
| `bm10` | 10% (step 282) | from the switch |
| `bm20` | 20% (step 563) | from the switch |
| `slow0` | 1/3 (as candidate 9) | accumulates from step 0 |
| `slow0bm10` | 10% | accumulates from step 0 |

The Muon probe found that early in the run the dense matrices' top gradient directions rotate within tens of steps, which argues against a 50-step slow rail early. These runs measure it directly.

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bm0` | 2.9773 (+0.0005) | 2.9832 (+0.0010) | 183–185 |
| `bm10` | 2.9766 (-0.0002) | 2.9845 (+0.0023) | 184–185 |
| `bm20` | 2.9785 (+0.0017) | 2.9813 (-0.0009) | 184–185 |
| `slow0` | — | 2.9813 (-0.0009) | 184 |
| `slow0bm10` | 2.9776 (+0.0008) | 2.9846 (+0.0024) | 183–185 |

`slow0` seed 0 crashed (cluster churn).

**Takeaway.** Engaging the rails earlier (step 1, 10%, 20%) or accumulating the slow rail from step 0 is within noise to slightly worse (+0.002 at most). Candidate 9's engage-at-1/3 stays.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 153: fewer Newton-Schulz iterations, coefficient schedules, and the truncation study without MuonEq** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927279619); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`8d3363b7e7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/8d3363b7e7))

**1. Fewer iterations.** `ns3` and `ns4` take the first 3 or 4 steps of our quintic schedule. Their exact maps, with x = σ / ‖M‖_F:

| schedule | small-σ gain | output range for x ≥ 0.05 | x where the output reaches 0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| quintic, 5 steps (candidate 9) | 493× | [0.98, 1.03] | 1.1e-3 |
| quintic, 4 steps (`ns4`) | 174× | [0.92, 1.15] | 3.0e-3 |
| quintic, 3 steps (`ns3`) | 60× | [0.38, 1.25] | 8.5e-3 |

Each saved iteration is worth about 0.5 ms per step, about 0.0005 at fixed time; the loss at equal steps is what matters.

**2. Coefficient schedules** (new `coefficient_type`s, 5 steps, the same cost):
- **`tight_top`:** three quintic steps, then two cubic (1.5, −0.5) steps. Large singular values land at exactly 1, and small ones are boosted only 136× (vs 493×). It tightens the high range and leaves the low range small.
- **`boost_low`, the inverse:** the steepest quintic step twice, so small singular values grow about 710×. Large ones land in a looser [0.92, 1.15] band.
- **Correction to my earlier description:** candidate 9's 5-step quintic is already tight, [0.98, 1.03] for x above 1%, not 0.7–1.2.

**3. Truncation without MuonEq.** MuonEq row-normalizes the momentum before Newton-Schulz, and batch 143 ranked singular directions of that normalized matrix. To check whether that interferes:

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 156: a short sliding-window softmax branch in the global MLA layers** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927450868); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`8b67368afc`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/8b67368afc))

KDA replaced every sliding-window layer, so the only softmax attention left is global MLA in layers 3 and 5.

**Change** (`global_local_window`, new `LocalWindowAttention`): each global layer gets a small extra softmax-attention branch, added to its MLA output.
- Its own q/k/v projections of the layer's normed attention input (random init, MuonH).
- Weightless per-head QK RMSNorm and full RoPE.
- The same document boundaries, and the window via FA4's sliding-window bounds.
- A per-head output gate that starts at zero (Adam), so the branch starts as an exact no-op. The output projection can't be zero-initialized: MuonH can't move a zero matrix.
- Tests: no-op at init, present only in the global layers, the gate gets a gradient.

| run | window | heads × head dim |
|---|---|---|
| `lw64` | 64 | 4 × 64 |
| `lw128` | 128 | 4 × 64 |
| `lw256` | 256 | 4 × 64 |
| `lw128h8` | 128 | 8 × 64 |

**Relation to nanogpt's DC.** DC (record [`#315`](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/315)) reuses the base attention's q/k, recomputes softmax over a ≤128 window, and adds a cross-head-composed correction, with a custom Triton kernel; it was worth about −0.005 there. This batch first tests the simpler question, whether local softmax attention helps the global layers at all, with an independent branch. If it does, the DC-style version (shared q/k, dynamic cross-head mixing) is the follow-up. The cost is two FA4 calls over windows ≤ 256, small next to global attention; step time will be reported.

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lw64` | — | 2.9818 (-0.0004) | 174.1 |
| `lw128` | 2.9755 (-0.0013) | 2.9813 (-0.0009) | 173.2 |
| `lw256` | 2.9774 (+0.0006) | 2.9811 (-0.0011) | 174.0 |
| `lw128h8` | 2.9778 (+0.0010) | — | 174.9 |

`lw64` seed 0 and `lw128h8` seed 1 failed (cluster churn).

**Takeaway.** Every window and width is within ±0.0013 at +1–2% step time. Local softmax attention adds nothing next to KDA's local layers, so the DC-style follow-up (shared q/k, cross-head mixing) isn't worth building.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Tokens don't have a clean way for their state to track "I visited experts A, C, G, T". Lets try adding a bias term to each expert, length hidden_dim. x = routed(x)+shared(x)+sum(expert_bias[b] for b in visited_experts).

The intent here is to let the model make conditional decisions like "IF I visited expert B THEN we should visit expert C, or attn can say "Query anyone who visited expert C". This first version is not weighted- another would be, weight bias contribution by weight given to that expert.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 158: a learned residual row for every routed expert a token visits** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927796123); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`17dd004ca0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/17dd004ca0))

**Change** (`expert_visit_bias`, new `ExpertVisitBias` enum): each MoE layer gets an `[E, D]` table (512 × 512 at d512), zero-initialized and trained by Adam. The routed output gains the table's rows for the token's selected experts:

`x = x + routed(x) + shared(x) + Σ_{e ∈ top-8} c_e · bias[e]`

| run | `c_e` | what it tests |
|---|---|---|
| `vb-sum` | 1 | an unweighted record of which experts ran. The router gets no gradient through it |
| `vb-wt` | the expert's combine weight | the same record, weighted by how much the expert was used. The router gets gradient through it |

- **Why:** a token's residual has no direct record of which experts processed it, so later layers can't condition on "I visited expert B" or attention on "tokens that visited C". The table writes that record explicitly.
- **Cost:** about 1.5M parameters across the 6 layers, and a `[T, 512] × [512, 512]` matmul per layer.
- **Implementation:** the per-token visit vector is built as a `[T, E]` one-hot sum. Ids beyond the table (null experts) add nothing. It is applied after the latent up-projection, so it works with every write-width mode.
- **Tests:** no-op at init, the table gets a gradient and then changes the output, the table is in the Adam group.

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

The first launch (`17dd004ca0` / `e0ff6e9475`) crashed near step 515 in every run. That was the pipelined train loop, not these features (batch 160 bisected it), so the `-r` runs repeat it with `--pipeline-depth 0` at [`a1d76fcc23`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a1d76fcc23).

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vb-sum-r` | 2.9835 (+0.0067) | 2.9854 (+0.0032) | 170.4 |
| `vb-wt-r` | 2.9788 (+0.0020) | 2.9806 (-0.0016) | 171.5 |

**Takeaway.** Neither variant helps: weighted is +0.0020 / −0.0016, and sum is +0.0067 / +0.0032, slightly worse. Later layers don't gain from an explicit record of which experts a token visited, at least as a fixed additive vector per expert.

comments.body: KDA has every head run independent. In softmax attn it can be advantageous to let queries from 1 head engage with keys from another- more expressiveness without increasing projection flops. Maybe there is some cross-head interaction in KDA that would be useful. (paired head attn from nanogpt is the main one im thinking of).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: The goal for today is 2.92. I believe you can do it! Keep testing ideas until it is achieved.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 159: paired-head KDA, adjacent heads sharing one delta-rule state** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927919775); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`e0ff6e9475`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/e0ff6e9475))

**Change** (`kda_head_pairing`, every KDA layer). This carries over nanogpt's paired-head attention (record 58, [`#191`](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/191)), which interleaves two heads' q/k/v into one sequence of length 2T. In KDA, heads `2j` and `2j+1` run as one head over the interleaved sequence `A₀ B₀ A₁ B₁ …`.
- **Shared state:** each pair shares one `h × h` state that both heads write to (their own k, v, β, decay and erase gate) and read from (their own q).
- **Visibility:** head A's query at token t sees B's writes up to token t−1; B's query sees A's writes up to token t. That is the same causal arrangement as nanogpt's.
- **Cost:** the projections are unchanged, and the scan covers 2T tokens with half the heads, so the scan FLOPs are unchanged.
- **Trade-off vs softmax:** in softmax attention pairing keeps every key. In KDA the state *is* the memory, so a pair gets one state instead of two, which halves the layer's state.
- **Implementation:** a reshape around the existing kernels, with document ids repeated per sub-position. The output and gate keep the original head layout.
- **Tests:**
  - head A at token t depends on B's value at t−1, but not on B's at t or later;
  - B at t depends on A at t;
  - heads in different pairs stay independent, and unpaired KDA has no cross-head path;
  - the interleave is checked directly.

| run | decay per sub-step |
|---|---|
| `kpair` | half the head's log-decay, so the shared state decays per token at about one head's rate (exact at init) |
| `kpairf` | the head's full log-decay, so the state decays twice per token |

If the halved state turns out to be the limit, the follow-up is a capacity-neutral version: each head keeps its own state and additionally reads its partner's state (one extra readout).

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

The first launch (`17dd004ca0` / `e0ff6e9475`) crashed near step 515 in every run. That was the pipelined train loop, not these features (batch 160 bisected it), so the `-r` runs repeat it with `--pipeline-depth 0` at [`a1d76fcc23`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a1d76fcc23).

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kpair-r (half decay)` | 2.9819 (+0.0051) | 2.9905 (+0.0083) | 173.3 |
| `kpairf-r (full decay)` | 2.9860 (+0.0092) | 2.9935 (+0.0113) | 172.7 |

**Takeaway.** Pairing loses, +0.005 / +0.008 with half decay and +0.009 / +0.011 with full decay. That fits the cost named in the plan: a pair shares one state, so each layer's memory halves. Faster decay (full) makes it worse, also consistent with the state being the bottleneck. The capacity-neutral variant (each head keeps its state and also reads its partner's) is the remaining test of the cross-head idea.

comments.author: ClassicLarry

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batches 152, 157, 160: host dispatch, and pipelining the train loop** (runtime only, no ML change; d512 candidate 9 + PGLE on cw-rno2a)

**Goal:** remove host time from the step. Batch 149's profiles showed every GPU waiting on process 0 to launch each step.

**152, flat-leaves train step** ([`a99a1ef88b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a99a1ef88b) and earlier on `ladderclimb_v1_lc1`)
- **Change:** the step is jitted over the train state's flat list of arrays rather than the equinox tree. That avoids Python flattening the whole module tree on every call (26–40 ms per step at d512, with the GPUs idle).

| run | steps | final Paloma macro | Δ vs candidate 9 | median step (`throughput/duration`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [lc1-b152-flat](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b152-flat) | 2817 | 2.9773 | +0.0005 (same math) | 171.6 ms, vs 184.3 for candidate 9 (**−6.9%**) |
| [lc1-b152-flat-lof5](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b152-flat-lof5), with full write on layer 5 | 2817 | **2.9676** | −0.0092 | 176.1 ms (+2.6% vs flat candidate 9) |

**157 and 160, pipelined loop** (`--pipeline-depth`; [`aa1c82fb35`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/aa1c82fb35), [`17dd004ca0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/17dd004ca0), [`a1d76fcc23`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a1d76fcc23))
- **Change:** step n+1 is dispatched before the host waits on step n, so logging and callbacks overlap the GPUs.
- **Measurement fix:** `throughput/duration` measures dispatch to loss-ready. It leaves out about 20 ms of host time between steps, so wall-clock per step (from wandb timestamps) was **191 ms for the flat step, not 171.6**.
- **First version (157):** a device-side NaN check queued behind the next step, so it saved only 4 ms (187 ms wall-clock). Its full run, [lc1-b157-pipe](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b157-pipe), is 2.9777, so the loop doesn't change the math.
- **Fixed version (`pipe2`), 300-step timing:** lof5 at **171.2 ms wall-clock vs 195.8** without pipelining (−12.6%).
- **But full-length runs crash.** Every one died between steps 512 and 515 (`CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` / `LAUNCH_FAILED`), across features and seeds. Batch 160 bisected it at 700 steps:

| run | pipeline | PGLE | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| lc1-b160-p1 | depth 1 | on | crashed |
| lc1-b160-p1-nopgle | depth 1 | off | crashed |
| lc1-b160-p0 | depth 0 | on | completed |

- **Status:** fully overlapping consecutive steps causes the crash; PGLE doesn't. Root cause not found yet, so `--pipeline-depth` now defaults to 0 ([`f4d76bf53a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f4d76bf53a)).
- **What it's worth under our rule:** `throughput/duration` already excludes the host gap, so pipelining mostly makes wall-clock match the metric (191 → 171 ms). The flat step's −6.9% is the gain that counts, worth ≈ −0.012 at fixed time (1% ≈ 0.0017).

**Toward candidate 10** (flat step + full write on the final layer, or final 2):
- **161:**
  - `c10-s1`, lof5 seed 1 (seed 0 is 2.9676 above);
  - `prof`, a no-PGLE profile with the HLO dump from the same compile, to attribute the 74 ms of elementwise/reduce kernels per step;
  - d768 validation, `d768-c9` vs `d768-lof7` (the last layer, 6929 steps).
- **162:** `lof45` on two seeds (layers 4+5 gained −0.014 at equal steps in batch 145, before the flat step), plus 300-step timing of `lof45` vs candidate 9 on the flat step.

**Results so far**

*Candidate 10 pieces* (equal steps, 2817; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822):

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step (rule metric) |
|---|---|---|---|
| lof5, full write on layer 5 | 2.9676 (−0.0092) | running | 175.7 ms with PGLE (+2.2%) |
| **lof45, full write on layers 4+5** (no PGLE) | **2.9627 (−0.0141)** | **2.9683 (−0.0139)** | 184.0 ms no PGLE, 180.4 with PGLE (+4.9%) |
| d768: candidate 9 / lof7 (6929 steps) | 2.7313 / running | | 425.5 / 436 ms |

lof45's −0.014 on both seeds is the largest equal-step gain since candidate 9. At fixed time its +4.9% step costs about 0.008 (net ≈ −0.006, the same as lof5's net). Its extra cost is mostly host dispatch: 37 ms vs 26 for candidate 9, from the second tail-stack layer's leaves.

*Profile attribution* ([lc1-b161-prof2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b161-prof2): no PGLE, with the HLO of the same compile, 48% of kernel time mapped to ops):
- MoE dispatch/combine/gathers ≈ 32 ms, the EP all-to-all 27 ms, the fused cross-entropy loop ≈ 12 ms, RMSNorm + GatedNorm ≈ 15 ms, KDA ≈ 20 ms, FA4 7 ms.
- The logging-only router metrics (a full softmax and logsumexp over all 512 experts, plus one-hot counts, every layer) are several ms. `router_stats_stride` computes them on every n-th token (training is unaffected; timing pending).

*The crashes* (now flagged automatically: every non-preemption restart is reported with its error signature):
- **Pipelining (`--pipeline-depth 1`) can't fit in memory as it stands.** Each step needs a 35.5 GiB scratch buffer, and dispatching step n+1 before step n finishes asks for a second one. With the BFC allocator ([lc1-b166-p1-bfc](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b166-p1-bfc)) that fails at step 2. Under `cuda_async`, stream-ordered reuse usually covers it, but not always: a run with a 64-batch loader queue hit OOM at step 274 with XLA at 3 GiB in use but only 16.5 of 85 GB free. The ~515 crash moves with the loader queue (512: crash at ~515; 2048: 700 steps clean), consistent with memory pressure. Pipelining also doesn't change the rule's step metric, so it stays off.
- **PGLE crashes plain runs.** Seven PGLE runs crash-looped today (`LAUNCH_FAILED` / `ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` at steps 375–2310, often right after an in-run eval). `train.py`'s runtime env already notes that per-process CUPTI sessions collide with each other and CoreWeave's DCGM; batch 74's first PGLE runs crashed at their mid-run eval the same way. The no-PGLE relaunches (`-np`) have all completed. **ML runs now launch without PGLE** (same math; about +3% step time). PGLE's speedup comes back only for final fixed-time runs, if it can be made stable.
- BFC vs `cuda_async` without pipelining: 173.6 vs ≈174.7 ms, so BFC is the fallback if no-PGLE runs still crash.

comments.author: marin-belay-bot
comments.body:
📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-5928744772)):

> Attention residuals q embedding:
> In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from
>
> exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))
>
> into
>
> exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))
>
> q_e should be initialized as all 0.
>
> Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

<!-- belay-intake:5928744772 -->

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 163: Motif 3's techniques** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934643844); [Motif 3 technical report, arXiv 2608.09119](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09119); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`a4ab5b17c8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a4ab5b17c8))

Every technique in the report, and what this batch does with it:

| Motif 3 technique | what it is | here |
|---|---|---|
| **Grouped differential latent attention (GDLA)** | MLA plus grouped differential attention: `n/(g+1)` noise heads, each shared by `g` signal heads (g = 4), `D = H_S − λ_t ⊙ H_N` with a per-token, per-head `λ_t = σ(x W_λ)`, then an elementwise query-dependent output gate `σ(G) ⊙ D`. Reported to reach MLA's loss with 9.2% fewer tokens. | **testing** (`mla_grouped_diff`) |
| **Expert-specific PolyNorm** | expert activation `Σₙ₌₁³ aₙ zⁿ / RMS(zⁿ) + b`, per-token RMS, coefficients learned per expert | **testing** with fixed equal coefficients (see below) |
| **Multi-token prediction** | DeepSeek-V3 depth-1 MTP, loss weight 0.2 | **testing** (`mtp_mode=deepseek`) |
| Modified manifold-constrained hyper-connections | 4 residual streams with Sinkhorn-projected mixing and a post-scale annealed 2 → 1 | not yet: it replaces the residual path, which Block AttnRes already owns here; a real port is a larger project (next batch if you want it) |
| Decaying Gaussian router noise | cosine-decayed logit noise; the report shows only faster load balancing | skipped: our Gumbel sampling was neutral or worse ([batch 30](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5852213638)), and QB already balances from step 1 |
| FFN magnitude penalty | `ReLU(|y| − 128)²` on layer outputs | skipped: a stability guard for activations far above anything at d512 |
| QK-Clip | caps pre-softmax logits | already covered: QK RMSNorm with a learnable `qk_mult` |
| Sequence-wise aux loss + loss-free bias | load balancing | already covered: QB routing |
| 1 full : 3 sliding-window (128) layers | local attention | already covered: KDA local layers; a local softmax branch was neutral ([batch 156](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927535181)) |
| WSD schedule | warmup-stable-decay | tested: PowerCool lost ([batch 154](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927409237)) |
| MXFP8 experts, parallel Muon, state offload | systems | MXFP8 needs Blackwell; FP8 on H100 stays on the throughput list |

**Grouped differential attention** (`mla_grouped_diff=g`, MLA layers 3 and 5, 4 heads at d512):
- `g` = 4 gives one noise map shared by all 4 heads, and `g` = 2 gives two maps.
- Each noise map has its own query and key up-projection; its columns are repeated for its `g` signal heads, so the q/k transforms apply unchanged. It reads the same values.
- `λ = sigmoid(x W_λ)` per head and token, with `W_λ` zero-init (λ starts at 0.5, Adam). The sigmoid keeps it a subtraction: batch 77's unconstrained DIFF λ went negative and turned the difference into a sum.
- Motif's elementwise output gate is our existing `attn_gate_elementwise`.

**PolyNorm** (`moe_ungated_activation=polynorm`, ungated routed experts): `(1/3) Σₙ₌₁³ uⁿ / RMS(uⁿ)` per token over the expert's hidden units. The expert activation is a static function inside the EP backends, so learned per-expert coefficients need a backend API change. This first tests the function form; the learned version comes next if it helps. The dropless eval's tied-gate backends use the exact rewrite `polynorm(u)/u`.

| run | change | seeds |
|---|---|---|
| `gda4` | grouped diff, g = 4, + elementwise output gate (Motif's GDLA) | 2 |
| `gda2` | g = 2, + elementwise gate | 2 |
| `gda4-hg` | g = 4 with the per-head gate (isolates the gate) | 1 |
| `egate` | elementwise gate alone (control) | 1 |
| `poly` | PolyNorm routed experts | 2 |
| `polysh` | PolyNorm routed + shared | 1 |
| `mtp02` | DeepSeek MTP, weight 0.2 | 2 |
| `mtp02q` | the same, MTP loss on a random 25% of positions (cheaper) | 1 |

Step time will be reported for each: grouped diff doubles the global-layer attention, PolyNorm is a few extra reductions per expert, and MTP adds a block and an lm_head pass.

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gda4 (+ elementwise gate)` | 2.9739 (-0.0029) | 2.9785 (-0.0037) | 183.0 (+6.6%) |
| `gda2 (+ elementwise gate)` | 2.9746 (-0.0022) | 2.9785 (-0.0037) | 183.1 / 185.9† |
| `gda4-hg (per-head gate)` | 2.9760 (-0.0008) | — | 181.3 |
| `egate (elementwise gate alone)†` | 2.9758 (-0.0010) | — | 174.7 |
| `poly (PolyNorm routed)` | 2.9885 (+0.0117) | 2.9942 (+0.0120) | 183.1† / 179.1 |
| `polysh (PolyNorm routed + shared)†` | 2.9908 (+0.0140) | — | 185.0 |
| `mtp02 (MTP, weight 0.2)` | 2.9860 (+0.0092) | 2.9939 (+0.0117) | 188.4 (+10%) |
| `mtp02q (MTP on 25% of positions)†` | 2.9989 (+0.0221) | — | 179.1 |

† launched without PGLE (see below), so its step time is about 3% higher than a PGLE run's; losses are comparable.

**Takeaway.**
- **Grouped differential attention:** −0.003 / −0.004 at equal steps, but it runs the global layers' attention twice (+6–7% step time ≈ +0.011 at fixed time), so it loses. The elementwise gate is most of its gain, and alone it's neutral (−0.001).
- **PolyNorm** experts lose clearly (+0.012 routed, +0.014 routed + shared). ReLU² suits these experts better than an RMS-normalized polynomial, at least with fixed coefficients.
- **MTP** loses at weight 0.2 too (+0.009 / +0.012, +10% step), matching batch 18. Applying it to 25% of positions is cheaper but worse (+0.022).
- None of Motif 3's techniques transfers to this rung.

**Crashes:** several runs here restarted with `CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_FAILED` / `ILLEGAL_ADDRESS`. All of them had PGLE on, and every run relaunched without PGLE completed (details in the [batch 157/160 comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934720837)).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 164: token-embedding AttnRes queries** ([intake suggestion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934727837) from RavnaBergsndot; d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`a4ab5b17c8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a4ab5b17c8))

**Change** (`attn_res_token_query`). Each AttnRes gate's logit for source `n` becomes

`(q_g + q_e[token]) · RMSNorm(source_n)` instead of `q_g · RMSNorm(source_n)`

with `q_e` a zero-initialized `[vocab, d]` table, so the run is exactly candidate 9 at init. This sits between the paper's data-independent query and its input-dependent `d × d` projection, which it ablated as better but more expensive (Table 4, [arXiv 2603.15031](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031)).

| run | table | parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `tqs` | one table shared by all 13 gates | 8.4M |
| `tqg` | one table per gate, as each gate has its own static query | 109M |

**Implementation:**
- The table rows are looked up with the replicated-table gather the value embeddings use (fp32 backward scatter), once per gate.
- Each source's normed key is dotted with the token's row, which adds one read of each source per gate.
- It trains with the AttnRes query group (Adam).

**Tests:** a no-op at init; only the rows of tokens in the batch get a gradient; moving the table changes the output.

**Also, on dropping the NaN check** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934742747)): the device-side check is already gone ([`17dd004ca0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/17dd004ca0)). The loss is copied to the host once per step for logging, and the check runs on that number, so it costs nothing. The pipelining crash ([batch 157/160](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934720837)) started only after the device-side check was removed: that check made each step wait on the next, so the earlier loop never truly overlapped steps.

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tqs (shared table)` | 2.9843 (+0.0075) | — | 175.9 (+2.5%) |
| `tqg (per-gate tables)†` | 2.9983 (+0.0215) | 3.0023 (+0.0201) | 186.3 (+8.6%) |

† without PGLE. `tqs` seed 1 is still running.

**Takeaway.** Token-embedding queries hurt: +0.0075 shared and +0.020 per gate, worse the more parameters. AttnRes routing wants the hidden-state view of the token, not a per-token constant. The table overrides the content-based mixing, and with 109M zero-init parameters at the AttnRes query LR it moves fast. A version at a much lower LR is the only follow-up that might be neutral; I don't plan to run it.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 167: a nonlinearity in the bigram content gate, and a 0.1 logit scale** (your request; d512 candidate 9 without PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`23d846a1be`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/23d846a1be))

Candidate 9's gate is `g = σ((e ⊙ b) A B + c)`:
- `e` and `b` are the RMS-normed token embedding and bigram row.
- `A` is [512, 16], random; `B` is [16, 512], zero-init; `c` = +2.

So each channel's logit is a rank-16 bilinear form in (e, b). Unlike GatedNorm, it has no middle nonlinearity.

| run | gate |
|---|---|
| `gsilu` | `σ(SiLU((e ⊙ b) A) B + c)`, as in GatedNorm |
| `ggelu` | `σ(GELU((e ⊙ b) A) B + c)` |
| `gs01` | `σ(0.1 · (e ⊙ b) A B + c)` |

**Notes:**
- **Same start for every arm:** with `B` zero-init, each one starts at `σ(2) ≈ 0.88` exactly like candidate 9. The 0.1 scale is on the learned logits only, so the bias, and with it the initial gate, is unchanged.
- **What the scale does under Adam:** it makes the gate's logits move about 10× more slowly, and the gate stays smoother. Candidate 9's gate went nearly bimodal per token by step 350 (std 0.34, [batch 69](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5859182603)).
- **Diagnostics:** the gate's mean and std are logged (`train/attn_res/attn_res_bigram_gate_*`), so each arm's learned selectivity can be compared.
- **No PGLE:** launched without it (see the [crash notes](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934720837)); the loss comparison is unaffected.
- **Tests:** every variant starts at `σ(c)`, and the activation and scale enter the logits exactly as written.

**Results**

Several runs were preempted repeatedly on cw-rno2a and moved to cw-us-east-02a (`-ue`). Each is compared against its own cluster's candidate 9: rno2a 2.9768 / 2.9822; 02a 2.9791 / 2.9831 (`lc1-b169-c9-ue`, same code, no PGLE).

| gate | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gsilu`, SiLU | 2.9775 (−0.0016, 02a) | 2.9814 (−0.0017, 02a) | 174.1 ms (0%) |
| `ggelu`, GELU | 2.9768 (−0.0023, 02a) | 2.9830 (+0.0008, rno2a) | 174 ms (0%) |
| `gs01`, 0.1 logit scale | 2.9777 (+0.0009, rno2a) | 2.9814 (−0.0017, 02a) | 173 ms (0%) |

**Takeaway.**
- None clears the noise. SiLU is the most consistent, at −0.0017 on both seeds and no step cost. It could ride along in a bundle, but it isn't a win on its own.
- Slowing the gate's logits 10× changes nothing, so the gate's sharp per-token selection isn't a problem that the scale fixes.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 168: token-embedding AttnRes queries at low LR, with the learned tables dumped for analysis** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5937972246); d512 candidate 9 without PGLE, equal steps, paired vs 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`1629eb97eb`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/1629eb97eb))

[Batch 164](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5935144206) trained the zero-init table with the AttnRes query group (Adam at 0.1 × the Adam LR, 6e-5). That lost +0.0075 (shared) and +0.020 (per gate). The table's rows are dotted with RMS-normed 512-wide sources, so at that LR a row can add logits of several units within a few hundred steps, swamping the static queries. A new `attn_res_token_query_lr_mult` scales the table's LR on top of the query group's.

| run | table | LR | seeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tqs-lr01` | shared | ×0.1 (6e-6) | 2 |
| `tqs-lr001` | shared | ×0.01 (6e-7) | 2 |
| `tqg-lr001` | per gate (13 tables) | ×0.01 | 1 |

**Visualization.** New `--final-param-dump REGEX` writes matching params to `final_params.npz` after training. Each run dumps the token-query table, the 13 static AttnRes queries `q_g` and the token embedding. Planned plots:
1. **Size:** how much the token term moves each gate's query, the distribution over tokens of `‖q_e[v]‖ / ‖q_g‖`.
2. **Direction:** `cos(q_e[v], q_g)` per gate. Does the token term mostly rescale the static query (cos ≈ ±1) or rotate it toward other sources?
3. **What the table encodes:**
   - the table's principal components, with token frequency and token class (punctuation, whitespace, subword pieces, digits);
   - the tokens at each end of the top components.
4. **Relation to the token embedding:**
   - a linear map `q_e ≈ E W` (R² of a ridge fit);
   - nearest-neighbour agreement between the two tables.

   This shows whether the table learns new token structure or re-expresses the embedding.

**Results**

Several runs were preempted repeatedly on cw-rno2a and moved to cw-us-east-02a (`-ue`). Each is compared against its own cluster's candidate 9: rno2a 2.9768 / 2.9822; 02a 2.9791 / 2.9831 (`lc1-b169-c9-ue`, same code, no PGLE).

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| shared, LR ×0.1 | 2.9763 (−0.0028, 02a) | 2.9819 (−0.0012, 02a) | 180.5 ms (+3.6%) |
| shared, LR ×0.01 | 2.9758 (−0.0010, rno2a) | 2.9814 (−0.0017, 02a) | +3% |
| per gate, LR ×0.01 | 2.9763 (−0.0005, rno2a) | — | +6.5% |

**What the tables learned.** Page: [Token-Embedding AttnRes Queries](https://claude.ai/artifact/1dXBT9bmxTFfHNwvk1JGp3).
- **Size:** at ×0.01 the token term stays at 3–4% of each gate's static query, a near no-op. At ×0.1 it reaches about 25%.
- **Direction:** it is nearly orthogonal to the static queries (mean |cos| ≈ 0.1). It rotates each gate's query toward other sources rather than rescaling it.
- **Structure:** weak; the top principal component holds 4–5% of the variance. That component is the same at both LRs:
  - one end is word-continuation fragments and byte pieces (`ud`, `ol`, `qu`, `"><`);
  - the other is whole words with a leading space (` offers`, ` programs`, ` processes`);
  - so tokens shift their AttnRes mixing by whether they start a word.
- **Relation to the token embedding:** a linear map from the embedding explains about 11% of the table. Top-10 nearest neighbours agree 7–12% of the time, against 0.5% for random rows.
- **Per-gate tables:** each gate learns its own small pattern. Mean cross-gate cosine is 0–0.1, up to 0.26 for adjacent early gates.

**Closed.** It is neutral at every LR where it doesn't hurt, and it costs 3–9% step time.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batches 169–173: candidate 10 adopted, its first fixed-time score, and three ideas closed** (cw-us-east-02a, no PGLE, one final eval on the pure EMA weights; [`67e23a4a13`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/67e23a4a13) and earlier)

**Candidate 10 = candidate 9 + full-width routed write in the final two layers** (`latent_out_full_layers=4,5` at d512, `6,7` at d768). Adopted with your go-ahead. Every number below is paired on cw-us-east-02a against same-cluster candidate 9 controls at the current code (batch 169):

| rung | steps | candidate 9 | candidate 10 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512, equal steps | 2817 | 2.9791 / 2.9831 | 2.9616 / 2.9664 | **−0.0175 / −0.0167** |
| d768, equal steps | 6929 | 2.7318 / 2.7268 | 2.7223 / 2.7177 | **−0.0095 / −0.0091** |
| d768, last layer only (`lof7`) | 6929 | 2.7318 | 2.7269 | −0.0049 |
| **d512, fixed time** (each at its own 480 s budget) | 2757 vs 2607 | 2.9795 / 2.9862 | **2.9773 / 2.9797** | **−0.0022 / −0.0065** (mean −0.0044) |

- **Why the final two layers:** they keep about 79% of the d512 gain at d768 in log-k terms, against about 52% for the last layer alone.
- **Fixed-time budgets (batch 171):** each step count is `round(480 s ÷ median step)` from 300-step `--no-eval` probes on this cluster.
  - candidate 9: 174.1 ms → 2757 steps;
  - candidate 10: 184.1 ms → 2607 steps.

  This is the first time both have run at exactly their 480 s budget. The earlier 2817-step numbers, including the Status figures for candidate 9, were 490–525 s of training.

**Closed:**

| idea | Δ vs candidate 10 (seed 0 / seed 1) | step | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| value embeddings on the 4 KDA layers (`kda_value_embeds=gated`) | +0.0037 / +0.0014 | +1% | worse; value embeddings stay on the MLA layers only |
| cautious weight decay inside the MuonH hyperball, λ = 1 (`muonh_cautious_wd`) | +0.0038 / — | 0 | worse |
| the same, λ = 0.25 | +0.0024 / +0.0012 | 0 | slightly worse |

The cautious decay shrinks coordinates whose update agrees in sign with the weight, then re-pins the norm, so it only reshapes the matrix. That doesn't help here.

**Batch 172: momentum vs current-gradient agreement, SNR probe on candidate 9 at steps 300 / 1408 / 2600.**
- **Candidates:** Muon's direction `P = NS(M)` plus `α · P · sym(Pᵀ g)` (rescaled to `α‖P‖`), meant to boost the momentum's singular directions that the current gradient confirms. Scored by held-out loss after a MuonH-sized step, per family (1e-4 nats, vs Muon; negative is better).
- **Result:** clearly worse mid-run at every α. At step 1408, α = 0.25 is +57 (KDA), +240 (MLA), +102 (shared); at step 2600 it is within noise.
- **Why:** the symmetrized term keeps the off-diagonal part of `Uᵀ g V`, so it re-injects a rotated, mis-oriented copy of the gradient. Its first-order payoff is 3–25× Muon's, but it overshoots, as raw momentum does. A correctly diagonal version needs the SVD. That is the SNR-in-momentum-basis candidate already in the probe, and it ties Muon at the real step size.
- **Finding worth keeping:** at step 1408, **Muon's own step raises held-out loss** for KDA (+10), MLA (+36) and the shared expert (+6). It overshoots mid-run, and the eigenbasis SNR direction removes most of that (MLA −32, KDA −9). By step 2600 the effect is gone. This matches ANVIL III's "the gap opens mid-run" and batch 144's −0.003 to −0.004 for eigenbasis SNR. Possible next step: a mid-run-only correction for the dense families, either a lower LR there or the SNR direction applied only there.

**Runtime and operations this round:**
- **Restarts are flagged:** every non-preemption restart is now reported with its error signature.
- **PGLE is off for ML runs:** PGLE runs had repeated `CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_FAILED`; no-PGLE runs have had no GPU crashes since.
- **Startup hangs are now diagnosable:** three runs hung at the first train step's compile until the 80-minute watchdog. The watchdog now dumps Python and native (py-spy) stacks before killing ([`f40fcabaad`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f40fcabaad)).
- **Cluster move:** runs moved from cw-rno2a to cw-us-east-02a after heavy preemption.
- **Literature search:** two rounds. Most candidates were already tried. The new leads are:
  - faster KDA kernels at chunk 64. Our kernel is exact only at chunk 16 with the −5 gate floor (chunk 64 gives 56% relative error), so it needs sub-tiling. A speed benchmark is running.
  - Track 3's newer MuonH momentum and schedule PRs.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batches 174–175: faster KDA kernels, and soft-cap 11 with a cleaner asymmetric sweep** (cw-us-east-02a, no PGLE, candidate 10 base)

**Batch 174: KDA speed options** (`kda_chunk_size=32`, on-chip decay and erase gates, `kda_state_grads=pallas`; [`8983bec6fd`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/8983bec6fd) and earlier)
- **Kernel changes:** chunk-32 kernels stay exact at the −5 decay floor by referencing each tile's decay at its middle token. The gate math and the state-pass cotangents are fused. Kernel error vs the per-document recurrence matches chunk 16's bf16 level (≤ 5.8e-3 relative).
- **Timing** (300-step probes, same cluster): **177.9 ms vs 184.4 ms** for candidate 10 (−3.5%). The kernel benchmark projected −6.2 ms.
- **Equal-steps loss check** (2817 steps, 2 seeds): `lc1-b174-kda`, `lc1-b174-kda-s1`.

**Batch 175: lm_head soft-cap at 11, and the asymmetric form one knob at a time**
- **Background:** cap 11 was last tested on the batch-43 base (+0.0017 vs 10). Cap 12 was +0.0006 on candidate 2 (batch 67). The recipe has changed a lot since, so 11 gets two seeds on candidate 10.
- **The asymmetric form decomposes into three knobs.** `A·σ((z+B)/C)` equals a tanh cap `A/2` applied to `g·(z+B)` with gain `g = A/(4C)`, up to a constant that the softmax ignores. So `(22, 0, 5.5)` is tanh 11 exactly.
- **Why batch 32's speedrun result was hard to read:** the speedrun form `23·σ((z+5)/7.5)` changed all three knobs at once (cap 11.5, gain 0.77, shift 5), so its −0.011 vs tanh 10's −0.024 doesn't say which knob hurt. Here the cap is fixed at 11 and one knob moves per run:

| run | form | cap / gain / shift | seeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cap11` | tanh 11 | 11 / 1 / 0 | 2 |
| `a-eq` | σ(22, 0, 5.5) | 11 / 1 / 0, identical math through the asymmetric kernel path (sanity check) | 1 |
| `a-bm4` | σ(22, −4, 5.5) | shift −4: linear region moves to higher logits | 2 |
| `a-bp4` | σ(22, +4, 5.5) | shift +4: high logits saturate earlier | 2 |
| `a-g08` | σ(22, 0, 6.875) | gain 0.8 | 2 |
| `a-g125` | σ(22, 0, 4.4) | gain 1.25 | 2 |
| `c10` | tanh 10 | fresh control (existing 02a controls: 2.9616 / 2.9664) | 1 |

**Results**

**Batch 174: KDA speed options.** Same loss at equal steps, 3.5% faster.

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| candidate 10 (02a controls) | 2.9616 | 2.9664 | 184.4 ms |
| + KDA options | 2.9621 (+0.0005) | 2.9669 (+0.0005) | **177.9 ms (−3.5%)** |

- **Fixed time** (each run at its own 480 s budget):

| | steps | seed 0 | seed 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| candidate 10 (official) | 2607 | 2.9773 | 2.9797 |
| **candidate 11** = candidate 10 + KDA options | 2698 | **2.9715 (−0.0058)** | **2.9750 (−0.0047)** |

  The mean gain is −0.0053, matching the 1% ≈ 0.0017 rule (−0.006 predicted).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Lets try a radical idea: MLP compression. The intuition is, if we want to fit as many clothes in the closet, it makes sense to spend some effort sorting them. The gradient pushes us to just keep throwing clothes in, but maybe an auxillary loss that encourages sorting will be helpful. Without this, we either run out of space, or have to remove old clothes to fit new ones.

The first thought is that highly sparse routed experts can act as the sponge to absorb new data. However this data wont get absorbed in the most compressed state. Lets combine the 2 shared experts into 1 to simplify. Then we should have some mechanism that takes the knowledge learned by the routed experts and compresses it into the 1 shared expert. One possibility is an aux loss that pulls the shared output towards the routed output. The goal here is that once the shared expert compresses and absorbs what the routed experts are doing, then it frees up space in the routed experts to learn fresh info without worrying about overwriting what they already know.

Think through the design space here carefully, and challenge and rework the initial spec I gave as makes sense. We may need to test in overtrained regime to see benefit here.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 178: MLP compression — move what the shared expert can express out of the routed experts** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`3f0a1199c8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3f0a1199c8))

**Idea** (from the comment above): routed experts absorb new data, but not in a compressed form. If the shared expert takes over what it can express, the routed experts are freer to learn new things without overwriting old ones.

**Changes to the initial spec:**
- **Already one shared expert** (`num_shared_experts=1`, width 768), so no merge is needed.
- **The shared expert is the small side.** Per layer it has ~0.8M parameters against ~100M routed (~150M in the full-write layers 4–5). Only the common, low-rank part of the routed output can move into it, not facts. Growing it would densify d512, so it stays at 768.
- **"Pull shared toward routed" (`‖s − sg(r)‖²`) settles at `s = r`.** Both paths then hold the same function and nothing is freed. This batch tests two forms that do free the routed side (`y = s + r`, `sg` = stop-gradient):
  - **Transfer:** `λ‖s − sg(s + r)‖² / sg(‖y‖²)`. Its gradient moves only the shared expert, along the routed output. The shared expert is evaluated a second time on a stop-gradient input, so no gradient reaches the layers below. The LM loss then sheds the overshoot from the routed side. It stops when the routed output has nothing left the shared expert can express.
  - **Routed penalty:** `λ‖r‖² / sg(‖y‖²)`. Routed output is costly, so the LM gradient moves onto the shared expert whatever it can express. The penalty also reaches the layers below, but only in direction, because the routed input is RMS-normalized.
- **Measured first:** a detached width-768 shadow MLP per layer learns `sg(x) → sg(r)` with no effect on training. Its R² is how much of the routed output a shared-sized expert could absorb.

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `shadow` | shadow probe only (all runs carry it) |
| `xfer01` | transfer, λ = 0.01 per layer |
| `xfer04` | transfer, λ = 0.04 per layer |
| `rpen01` | routed penalty, λ = 0.01 per layer |

**Early read** (`shadow`, step 572):

| layer | shadow R² | routed share ‖r‖²/‖y‖² | cos(s, r) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.69 | 0.49 | +0.33 |
| 1 | 0.52 | 0.74 | +0.27 |
| 2 | 0.44 | 0.71 | +0.22 |
| 3 | 0.55 | 0.60 | +0.27 |
| 4 | 0.35 | 0.71 | +0.23 |
| 5 | 0.43 | 0.67 | +0.20 |

- A shared-sized MLP reproduces 35–69% of the routed output, so there's plenty to compress.
- The routed side carries most of the MLP output.
- The two paths already partly duplicate each other: cos(s, r) is positive in every layer.

**Reads:** Paloma macro vs the candidate 11 equal-steps controls (2.9621 / 2.9669, rerun 2.9625; noise 0.0056); cos(s, r), routed share and shadow R² over training. Anything that clears noise gets seed 1, early-fact retention from the fact probe, and an overtrained check.

**Ops:**
- **Lost gradient fixed:** the AttnRes recompute backward dropped every gradient from per-layer stats, so a loss added there was silently ignored. It now passes the compress term's gradient through.
- **Sharded-autotuning deadlock:** new fusions deadlocked sharded XLA autotuning in the train step, because the per-process autotune caches disagree. Turning sharded autotuning off instead hung the first step, likely from mismatched collective order. `--fresh-autotune-cache` starts every process empty, so all miss alike.


**Results** (Paloma macro, seed 0; control = the two shadow-only runs, 2.9633 / 2.9631, mean 2.9632; candidate 11 controls 2.9621 / 2.9625)

| run | loss | Δ | routed share, late | cos(s, r), late |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `shadow` (control) | 2.9632 | — | 0.52–0.62 | +0.17 to +0.29 |
| transfer λ = 0.01 | 2.9634 | +0.0002 | 0.23–0.32 | +0.18 to +0.29 |
| transfer λ = 0.04 | 2.9700 | +0.0068 | 0.21–0.38 | +0.16 to +0.32 |
| transfer λ = 0.16 | 2.9745 | +0.0113 | 0.39–0.56 | +0.32 to +0.40 |
| gap `‖s − sg(r)‖²` λ = 0.04 | 2.9679 | +0.0047 | 0.47–0.58 | +0.47 to +0.63 |
| gap λ = 0.16 | 2.9711 | +0.0079 | 0.46–0.59 | +0.49 to +0.66 |
| routed penalty λ = 0.01 | 3.0078 | +0.0446 | 0.01–0.31 | 0.00 to +0.14 |
| routed penalty λ = 0.04 | 3.0070 | +0.0438 | 0.03–0.12 | +0.03 to +0.07 |

- **Closed at d512.** Moving routed work onto the shared expert never helps. Every form strong enough to change behavior costs loss.
- **The shadow probe does nothing to training** (2.9632 vs 2.9621 / 2.9625).
- **Transfer works mechanically but buys nothing.**
  - At λ = 0.01 the routed share halves and the shadow's R² drops ~45%, so the routed side keeps mostly what a shared-sized expert can't express. Loss is unchanged.
  - Stronger weights don't move more. They spend the shared expert's fixed-size MuonH updates chasing the routed output, and loss rises with λ.
- **The gap loss duplicates, as predicted.** cos(s, r) roughly doubles while the routed share barely moves, and loss rises.
- **The routed penalty is destructive even at λ = 0.01.** It shrinks the routed path in every layer, almost entirely in layer 4 (share 0.01). The routed bank does work the shared expert can't take over.
- **Reading:** in the 8-minute regime the routed bank isn't short of space, and the shared expert is already fully used. The capacity argument could still hold when overtrained, but nothing here points to a gain to carry over.
- **Ops: the sharded-autotuning deadlock is unsolved.** Programs with new fusions deadlock in compile about half the time on 8 processes. Every rank waits on the key-value exchange for results no rank publishes. Neither an empty per-process cache nor `xla_gpu_autotune_level=0` fixes it; level 0 instead hangs the first step, inside the lazy custom-kernel load. Resubmitting works, since runs that compile train normally.

comments.body:
📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-5968183668)):

> Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):
>
> 1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
> 2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
> 3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
> 4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.
>
> Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:
>
> 1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
> 2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.
>
> These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: marin-belay-bot
comments.body:
📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-5980816116)):

> Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).
>
> Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
> where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".
>
> Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
> where y = s + r
>
> Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.
>
> Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

<!-- belay-intake:5980816116 -->

| `xn2` | transfer λ = 0.04 + counter force `λ₁ (‖s‖² / sg‖y‖²)^{n/2}` (choice 1), λ₁ = 0.01, n = 2 |
| `xn4` | the same with n = 4, a softer cap |

**Comparison:** the shadow-only control from batch 178 (2.9632) and the plain transfer arms (λ = 0.01: 2.9634; λ = 0.04: 2.9700).

**Reads:**
- Paloma.
- Routed share and cos(s, r).
- New: the absolute per-token RMS of `s` and `r`, which separates a growing `s` from a silent `r`.

**New diagnostics** (the other intake suggestion):
- **Weights** (`--weight-diagnostics N`): every N steps, for every projection matrix, the stable rank `‖W‖_F²/‖W‖_2²` (mean and min over stacked or expert matrices) and the max/mean output-channel norm. Also each RMSNorm gain's distance from 1.
- **Layer outputs** (`--model-set layer_output_stats=true`): each layer's attention and MLP output max |x| vs RMS.
- **This batch:** the four runs log the output stats. The weight hook is in an 8-GPU smoke test after two sharding fixes for expert banks. Once it passes, a candidate 11 control with both diagnostics on follows.


**Results** (Paloma macro, seed 0; control: shadow-only runs from batch 178, 2.9632; noise ~0.0056)

| run | loss | Δ | routed share, late | cos(s, r), late | per-token RMS, s / r |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tn01` normalized, λ = 0.01 | 2.9648 | +0.0016 | 0.36–0.52 | +0.32 to +0.49 | 1.9–3.6 / 2.3–4.0 |
| `tn04` normalized, λ = 0.04 | 2.9679 | +0.0047 | 0.43–0.67 | +0.41 to +0.59 | 1.2–2.7 / 2.4–4.5 |
| `xn2` transfer + counter force, n = 2 | 2.9688 | +0.0056 | 0.29–0.43 | +0.32 to +0.47 | 2.7–6.2 / 2.7–6.7 |
| `xn4` transfer + counter force, n = 4 | 2.9697 | +0.0065 | 0.29–0.42 | +0.33 to +0.47 | 2.8–6.3 / 2.9–6.6 |
| plain transfer λ = 0.04 (batch 178) | 2.9700 | +0.0068 | 0.21–0.38 | +0.16 to +0.32 | not logged |

- **Both fixes work mechanically.** `s` no longer runs away: it stays the same size as `r` or smaller.
- **Neither helps the loss.** Both forms land within noise or worse.
- **With a bounded `s`, every form duplicates.** cos(s, r) rises to about +0.4 to +0.6, the same thing the gap loss did. The stretching flaw was real, but it isn't why compression loses at 1×.
- **Closing the direction at d512.** ClassicLarry's read above stands: no signs of life yet. A cleaner place to look for them is a toy task with a known answer.
  - In a side experiment on grokking `(a + b) mod 113` with a ReLU MLP, the generalizing circuit is already present at step 300, right after memorization. Keeping only each neuron's top-2 frequencies and refitting the output layer groks up to 16× sooner (step 800 vs 13,100).
  - Low-rank SVD truncation and norm-based pruning don't help there. Compression that works has to find the solution's own basis.
- **Ops:** 3 of the 4 runs deadlocked in sharded XLA autotuning on their first compile; `tn01` deadlocked twice. Resubmitting fixed all of them.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 181: learned output scalars and RMSNorm gain parameterizations** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`4b2fb2b8d6`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/4b2fb2b8d6))

**Diagnosis first.** Every run logs, every 100 steps, each RMSNorm gain's distance from 1 and each projection matrix's stable rank and max/mean output-channel norm. It also logs each layer's output max |x| vs RMS, and dumps every norm gain and output scalar at the end. The control dump shows what the default gains learn per module, which says which gain function fits.

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `ctrl` | none (diagnostics only) |
| `ss_lin` | learned scalar on every attention and MLP output (`sublayer_scales`), linear, init 1 |
| `ss_sig2` | the same scalar as `2·sigmoid(w)`, init `w = 0`, so it modulates in (0, 2) |
| `g_exp` | every RMSNorm gain as `e^w`, init 0 |
| `g_sp` | `softplus(w)`, init `log(e − 1)`; gain LR ×1.6 |
| `g_sig2` | `2·sigmoid(w)`, init 0; gain LR ×2 |

**Why the functions could matter:**
- **Scale of an output.** AttnRes scores sources on RMS-normed copies but mixes the raw sources, so an output scalar sets that branch's weight in the mix, and the next RMSNorm removes only the overall scale. Batch 01 found learned output scalars neutral (MoE outputs grew to 1.2–2.1×), but that was a much earlier recipe.
- **Positivity and relative steps.** A linear gain moves additively and can cross 0. `e^w` keeps it positive and makes Adam's steps relative (the same fraction at any size), which suits gains spanning orders of magnitude. `softplus` is linear above about 1 and exponential near 0. `2·sigmoid` bounds it in (0, 2), and that bound is the test of whether large gains are needed.
- **Plain `sigmoid`:** I used `2·sigmoid` rather than a plain sigmoid, which can't start at 1 and can only shrink activations. If the control's gains never exceed 1, plain sigmoid becomes worth a run.

**LR.** Gains train with Adam, so a step moves the raw parameter by about lr, and the gain by `f'(w)` times that. At init `f'` is 1 for `exp`, 0.63 for `softplus` and 0.5 for `2·sigmoid`, so the gain LR multipliers (×1.6, ×2) give every arm the same initial step as linear. A ×0.5 / ×2 sweep follows on whichever helps.

**Ops:** the weight-diagnostics hook needed three fixes to run on 8 GPUs (expert-bank sharding twice, then gathering global scalars). Batch 181 waits on a 150-step smoke test that confirms the metrics land in wandb.


**What the default gains learn** (`ctrl`, Paloma 2.9644, within noise of the candidate 11 controls; [per-module plots](https://claude.ai/artifact/KcoMDyEcULNMFebyS5eTRQ))

| module | final gain | trend |
|---|---|---|
| `final_norm` | 1.2–7.6, mean 5.8 | still rising at the end (mean \|g − 1\| 2.1 / 3.5 / 4.5 / 4.8 at steps 500 / 1k / 2k / 2817) |
| MoE `latent_norm` | 1.5–2.1 in most layers (layer 5: 0.16–1.3) | still rising |
| `rms_attn`, `rms_mlp` pre-norms | 0.4–2.8 | mean \|g − 1\| 0.1–0.4, mostly settled |
| `o_norm`, `kv_latent_norm` | 0.44–1.6 | small moves |
| `embed_norm` / `embed2_norm` | 0.16–1.2 (mean 0.62) / 0.01–0.45 (mean 0.30) | shrink |

- **No gain goes negative.** A positive parameterization gives up nothing the model uses.
- **The scale is per module.** Gains span about 700× across modules but cluster tightly inside each one, so each norm acts mostly as one scale plus small per-channel adjustments.
- **The biggest gains were still moving at the end.** Under additive Adam steps a gain climbs about lr per step; `e^w` moves by the same fraction at any size. That makes `g_exp` the best-motivated arm.
- **`2·sigmoid` caps every gain at 2.** It clamps `final_norm` (which reaches about 6) and pins the MoE latent norms, so I expect `g_sig2` to lose. A plain sigmoid (cap 1) would be worse; only the embedding norms stay below 1.
- **`final_norm` likely works as a logit temperature** in front of the `lm_head` (soft cap 10). A learned output scalar there may be the cleaner lever.


**Results** (Paloma macro, seed 0; noise ~0.0056)

| run | loss | Δ vs `ctrl` | `final_norm` gain | MLA L3 latent gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ctrl` (linear gains) | 2.9644 | — | 1.17–7.56 | 1.81–2.11 |
| `ss_lin` (linear output scalars) | 2.9641 | −0.0003 | 1.25–7.64 | 1.49–1.87 |
| `ss_sig2` (`2·sigmoid` output scalars) | 2.9629 | −0.0015 | 1.40–7.65 | 1.53–1.98 |
| `g_exp` (`e^w` gains) | **2.9618** | **−0.0026** | 0.56–**15.0** | 1.87–2.39 |
| `g_sp` (softplus gains, LR ×1.6) | 2.9636 | −0.0008 | 0.86–9.12 | 1.67–2.25 |
| `g_sig2` (`2·sigmoid` gains, LR ×2) | **3.0793** | **+0.1149** | pinned at 1.99 | 1.73–1.92 |

- **The cap prediction holds.** `2·sigmoid` gains pin `final_norm` at the cap and cost 0.115, the largest change in the batch. The output norm needs a gain well above 2.
- **`e^w` gains come out best**, but within noise. The mechanism checks out: with relative steps `final_norm` climbs to 15 rather than about 7.6, and the MoE latent gains grow further.
- **Softplus is in between.** It is linear above about 1, so large gains climb only a little faster.
- **Output scalars are neutral** either way, matching batch 01. MLP outputs scale up (linear: 1.0–1.95×); `2·sigmoid` holds them lower (0.94–1.52×) and lands slightly ahead.
- **Next:**
  - `g_exp` seed 1;
  - the planned gain LR sweep on `g_exp` (×0.5 / ×2);
  - a targeted test of whether the gain is just a faster-growing output temperature: `e^w` on `final_norm` only, or a learned logit-temperature scalar on the head.
- **Ops:** 3 of the 6 runs deadlocked in sharded XLA autotuning on their first compile; resubmitting fixed each.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 182: sigmoid gains on the embedding norms; router on the latent** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`83560499bf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/83560499bf))

| run | change | loss | Δ vs batch 181 `ctrl` (2.9644) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sg_embed` | `sigmoid(w)` gains on `embed_norm` and `embed2_norm` (`sigmoid_gain_norms=embed,embed2`); init `w = 0`, a gain of 0.5 | 2.9634 | −0.0010 |
| `rol` | the router reads the RMS-normed MoE latent (`latent_dim` = 256) instead of the full MLP input (512) (`router_on_latent`); router weight `[256, E]` | 2.9651 | +0.0007 |
| `roe` | every router reads only the RMS-normed token embedding (`router_on_embed`): routing by learned token identity, one router per layer; a token picks the same experts in any context | **3.0063** | **+0.0419** |

- **`sg_embed` is neutral.** Linear `embed_norm` gains rarely pass 1 (1% of channels), so the cap barely binds. The sigmoid gains also moved slowly from their 0.5 start (0.25× step at init): `embed_norm` ended at a mean of about 0.43, below the control's 0.62. A 4× gain LR on these two norms would match linear's initial speed.
- **`rol` barely loses: +0.0007, within noise.** Routing on the 256-wide normed latent costs essentially nothing against the full 512-wide input at d512 (single seed). Step time is unchanged (179.2 vs 178.1 ms).
- **`roe` is the extreme:** context-free routing. Batch 30 found a fixed token-id hash neutral at layer 0 only.
- **Next, sigmoid on the embedding norms plus KDA `o_norm` and `kv_latent_norm`.** KDA layers 0–2 share one module, so a "KDA layer 0 only" version needs per-layer gain functions.

**A finding from the batch 181 control.** Layer 5's MoE latent has one channel acting as a hidden per-token gate.
- **The evidence:** that channel's column in `W_latent_down` grows to 2.37× the mean column norm between steps 400 and 800. Meanwhile its `latent_norm` gain falls from 0.87 to 0.13, while the other 255 rise to about 1.24. Layer 4 shows the same pattern, weaker (1.65×, gain 0.61). The latent-only layers stay at 1.05–1.09×.
- **The reading (inference):** a large `z_j*` inflates the latent's RMS and scales down the other channels for that token. With relu² experts, the MoE output shrinks quadratically. The near-zero gain resizes the outlier back to an ordinary input. Layers 4–5 write full width into the AttnRes history, and the router's renormalized combine can't set per-token output size, so this is the only lever. It is the pattern the GatedNorm paper describes, and what RavnaBergsndot's diagnostics comment asked us to look for.
- **The check:** an explicit per-token MoE output gate (`moe_out_gate`). If the outlier stops forming and loss holds, the reading is right.




**`roe` result:** routing on the token embedding alone costs +0.042, while routing on the 256-wide latent costs +0.0007. The router needs the token's context, not just its identity; given the context, a narrow input is enough.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 183: the routed combine's fixed sum** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`9fd0edb6ae`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9fd0edb6ae))

**Why:** the combine weights are renormalized to a fixed per-token sum (2.5), so the router can't make the MoE output louder or quieter per token. In the batch 181 control, layer 5's MoE latent appears to build that per-token scale another way. One channel's `W_latent_down` column grows to 2.37× the mean, and its `latent_norm` gain falls to 0.16, so it inflates the RMS denominator (see the batch 182 comment).

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `csr` | `router_combine=sqrt_softplus_raw`: the current `sqrt(softplus(logit))` gate with no renorm, scaled so a token's total is 2.5 at init. This changes only the renorm. |
| `srw` | `router_combine=sigmoid_raw`: batch 02's no-renorm variant on today's recipe; it also changes the gate shape |
| `mog` | `moe_out_gate`: keeps the renorm and adds an explicit per-token sigmoid gate on each block's MoE output (13 parameters per block) |
| `lsum` | `routing_sum_learnable`: the 2.5 becomes a learned scalar per MoE layer (init 2.5, Adam), logged as `knob_routing_sum_L*` |

- **History:** batch 02 (Sep 25, a much earlier recipe) found no renorm +0.0013, a sum of 4.0 +0.0033 and softmax +0.011 against its own base. Since then the gate has changed to sqrt-softplus, layers 4–5 write the full width, and `moe_drop_renorm` was added.
- **Drop renorm:** `moe_drop_renorm` stays on. It rescales relative to each token's own pre-drop total, so it still works without a fixed sum.
- **Reads:**
  - Paloma vs batch 181 `ctrl` (2.9644);
  - whether layer 5's outlier channel (2.37× column, gain 0.16) stops forming;
  - where the learned routing sums go, by layer.


**Results** (Paloma macro, seed 0; noise ~0.0056)

| run | loss | Δ vs `ctrl` | L5 lowest latent gain | L5 `W_latent_down` max/mean column |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ctrl` (sqrt-softplus, renorm to 2.5) | 2.9644 | — | 0.163 | 2.37 |
| `csr` (sqrt-softplus, no renorm) | 2.9646 | +0.0002 | **0.984** | **1.11** |
| `srw` (sigmoid, no renorm) | 2.9656 | +0.0012 | **0.94** | **1.13** |
| `mog` (renorm + per-token MoE output gate) | 2.9640 | −0.0004 | 0.234 | 2.07 |
| `lsum` (renorm, learnable per-layer sum) | 2.9644 | 0.0000 | 0.169 | 2.31 |

- **Without the renorm, the layer-5 outlier never forms.** Gains stay near 1 and no `W_latent_down` column stands out. The outlier was a workaround for the fixed per-token sum: the model built its own per-token output scale through the latent norm's denominator. A raw combine gives it that scale directly.
- **Loss doesn't move.** The workaround already delivered the same function, so this explains a mechanism rather than giving a win.
- **The explicit output gate only shrinks the outlier** (2.07×). It reads a fixed 12-channel slice of the input and also scales the shared expert, so it is a coarser stand-in.
- **Learned sums all rise above 2.5,** to 3.3–3.6 in layers 0–3 and 2.95 / 2.69 in layers 4 / 5. The MoE output wants to be louder overall, as the learned output scalars found. One scalar per layer can't provide a per-token scale, so the outlier stays.
- **Next:** with the outlier explained, `csr` is the cleaner design at equal loss. It frees the latent norm and `W_latent_down` from building a gate. A seed-1 pair (`csr` vs `ctrl`) would confirm the loss is the same before adopting it. A raw combine with a learnable scale (`csr` + `lsum`) would test whether a louder MoE output helps once the scale is per token.
