comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 184: two weight sets for the MLA attention (previous step + current)** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`2ebb73734a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/2ebb73734a))

**Idea** (ClassicLarry): keep the previous step's weights for a parameter group, and run half of each batch on them.
- **Implementation** (`dual_attn_prev`): each MLA attention module gets a frozen copy of the previous step's weights, refreshed after every update.
- **Batch split:** in training, odd batch rows run attention at those old weights and even rows at the current ones.
- **Gradient:** the old rows read `sg(θ_old) + (θ − sg(θ))`, so their gradient reaches the current weights. Each update then averages the gradient at both ends of the last step, about its midpoint.
- **Expected effect:** that damps directions that flip sign every step (period-2 bounce) and lags drifting directions by about half a step.
- **Evals** use the current weights only.

| run | loss | Δ vs batch 181 `ctrl` (2.9644) | step time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dual` | 2.9630 | −0.0014 | 193.0 ms (+8% vs 178.1) |

- **Neutral at equal steps** (within ~0.0056 noise).
- **A loss at fixed time.** The extra attention pass in the two MLA layers costs 8% step time, about +0.014.
- **Not pursued further** unless a seed-1 pair shows the equal-steps gain is real and the second pass can be made much cheaper.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Speed track: PR #9708, FP8, and a fresh profile of candidate 11** (d512, 8×H100, steps 300–305; profiled step 233 ms vs 178 ms unprofiled)

**Where the step goes** (GPU 0, ms per profiled step):

| | ms/step | share |
|---|---|---|
| compute stream busy | 152 | 65% |
| compute stream idle | **81** | 35% |
| NCCL, on its own stream (SendRecv 29, AllGather 5, ReduceScatter 3) | 41 | overlapped or exposed |
| GEMMs (excluding FA4) | ~42 | |
| memory-bound XLA fusions (reduce 17, select 9, scatter 5, convert 6, add 7, ...) | ~45 | |
| KDA kernels | ~15 | |
| short conv | ~3 | |

- **Exposed communication is the largest lever.** Net of profiler overhead, roughly 26 ms of a real 178 ms step has no compute running, mostly waiting on the expert-parallel SendRecv all-to-all. At about 0.0017 per 1% of step time, hiding it all is worth up to about −0.02 at fixed time.
- **Memory-bound fusions cost as much as every GEMM together.** Many are probably MoE dispatch/combine; attributing them to source ops comes next.

**PR #9708** (hero MFU 28.2% → 31.1%): most of its gains are in ragged-transport code (transport buffers, token-major scatter, expert-side routing-weight gradient, dispatch overlap). fast_track runs `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all`, so those don't apply.
- **What does apply:** the streaming Triton short convolution. fast_track's KDA calls `short_conv`. I added `sconv_impl=triton_gpu` on a test branch with the PR's kernel ([`5100adbf80`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5100adbf80)).
- **Expected size:** about 3 ms of short-conv kernels, so 1–2 ms at best. A same-code A/B (`lc1-pr-pallas` vs `lc1-pr-triton`, 2817 steps with Paloma) is running.
- **Router top-k:** the PR's Triton top-k (+0.53% on hero) would need wiring into fast_track's own router top-k; it's a later step.

**FP8:** only FP8 dispatch has been tried here (batch 79: no time saved; the quantize/dequantize ate the gain). FP8 GEMMs never have been.
- **The modded-nanogpt scheme:** static scales throughout, so no per-step amax. The input scale comes from the RMSNorm bound `max|x| ≤ sqrt(d)`. e4m3 forward and e5m2 gradients with a static grad scale; weights quantized once per optimizer step into both layouts. It covers the `lm_head`, both MLP GEMMs and the QKV projection.
- **Our GEMMs are about 42 ms per profiled step,** so FP8 on most of them is worth an estimated 10–15 ms, −0.010 to −0.015 at fixed time. The static-scale design matters here because our GEMMs are small (hidden 512).
- **Plan:** attention and shared-expert projections plus the `lm_head` first, then per-expert scales for the routed GEMMs.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batches 188–189: ragged baseline, and an FP8 protocol that holds as width grows** ([`d34ed93f76`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/d34ed93f76), [`274839618f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/274839618f))

**Batch 188: current ragged path on candidate 11** (d512, 2817 equal steps, one-shot ragged transport, drop renorm off)

| run | loss | step ms | Δ loss vs `ctrl` 2.9644 | step time vs pooled wave (176.5 ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `rag105` (capacity 1.05) | 2.9633 | 193.6 | −0.0011 | +9.7% |
| `rag115` (capacity 1.15) | 2.9620 | 203.1 | −0.0024 | +15% |

- Ragged still costs about 10% at d512, which is about +0.017 at fixed time, against −0.001 to −0.002 per step.
- The #9708 ragged commits are being ported onto lc1, keeping ungated ReLU², the fused relu² kernel and FP8 dispatch. Two of three are done. A ported-ragged vs pooled-wave A/B comes next.

**FP8: microbenchmarks on one GB200** (16k tokens, fwd+bwd of one linear `[16k, d] × [d, n]`)

| d (FFN up, n = 4d) | bf16 GEMMs | per-tensor FP8 GEMMs | MXFP8 GEMMs | JAX MXFP8 linear, end to end |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512–1024 | launch-bound | no gain | no gain | 0.4–0.6× bf16 |
| 2048 | 2.1 PF | 4.2 PF | 2.7 PF | 0.78× |
| 4096 | 2.3 PF | 4.5 PF | 3.1 PF | 1.02× |
| 6144 | 2.3 PF | 4.6 PF | 3.0 PF | 1.20× |

- **In the training layouts, block-scaled MXFP8 runs as fast as per-tensor FP8.** In the d=6144 profile, cuBLAS's 1×32 block-scaled kernels (`Avec32UE8M0_Bvec32UE8M0`) take 1.44–1.49 ms per GEMM, against 1.43 ms for per-tensor FP8 and 2.7 ms for bf16. Fine-grained scaling itself costs nothing.
- **The overhead is all in quantization.** `jax.nn.scaled_dot_general` re-quantizes both operands for every GEMM. That is six bf16 reads, separate amax / convert / transpose fusions, about 2.1 ms at d=6144 against 4.4 ms of GEMMs. A fused cast kernel would read x, w and g once and write row- and column-wise e4m3 plus e8m0 scales. By bandwidth that is about 0.4 ms, so about 1.9× bf16 at d=6144.
- **Below d≈2048 FP8 can't pay.** The GEMMs are too small to be tensor-core bound. On the d512 H100 rung, FP8 is a numerics question, not a speed lever.
- **Width dependence of the error:** relative error is 3.8% for MXFP8 (e4m3 everywhere) and 5.9% for per-tensor with e5m2 gradients. It is flat from d=512 to 6144 on Gaussian inputs, and four 100× outlier channels don't change it.

**Protocol chosen: MXFP8, just-in-time scales.** Each 32-element block along each GEMM's contraction axis gets a power-of-two (e8m0) scale from its own amax. e4m3 is used everywhere, gradients included. The router, embeddings, lm head, norms, attention core and optimizer stay high precision.
- **Why not modded-nanogpt-style fixed scales:** they are tuned to one width and one activation distribution. The RMSNorm bound `max|x| ≤ sqrt(d)` grows with d, and the gradient scale drifts with depth, LR and training phase.
- **Why not per-tensor current scaling:** a single outlier channel sets the scale for the whole tensor. Massive activations grow with width and training.
- **With 1×32 blocks, an outlier only coarsens its own block,** and no scale state depends on width, step or calibration. It is also the native Blackwell format (same GEMM speed, as above).

**Batch 189: does MXFP8 hold as width grows?** Simulated MXFP8 (`fp8_recipe=mxfp8_sim`) rounds every operand of every forward, dgrad and wgrad GEMM to exact e4m3 with the recipe's block scales; the GEMMs still run in bf16, so this measures numerics only. It covers the attention/KDA projections, the fused latent/shared projection (router columns excluded), the latent up-projection, the shared expert and the routed experts. Candidate 11 is scaled to each width; steps are the baseline counts.

| run | width | steps | loss | Δ vs bf16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mx512` / `mx512-s1` | d512 | 2817 | ⏳ | vs `ctrl` 2.9644 / 2.9667 |
| `bf768` / `mx768` | d768 | 6929 | ⏳ | ⏳ |
| `bf1024` / `mx1024` | d1024 | 9268 | ⏳ | ⏳ |

- **Pass criterion:** Δ within seed noise (0.0056) at every width, and not growing with d.
- If it passes, next is the real kernel path on GB200: a fused MXFP8 cast plus a `custom_vjp` linear over `jax.nn.scaled_matmul`, starting with the hero-width projections and experts.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batches 190–201: candidate 12 (ragged a2a + 6 MLA heads), ragged and AttnRes speed probes, hyperball decay, and a raised final LR with an EMA sweep** (d512, cw-rno2a; [`0919fe4809`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/0919fe4809) ragged port, [`1c43611fc7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/1c43611fc7) `mla_num_heads`, [`89416d68b9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/89416d68b9) current)

FP8 is dropped (batch 189 stopped).

**Candidate 12** = candidate 11 + ragged all-to-all with the #9708 port (`ragp105`: one-shot transport, single process, capacity 1.05, drop renorm off) + `mla_num_heads=6` on the two MLA layers. Config: `base13`.

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pooled wave, candidate 11 (`ctrl`) | 2.9644 | 2.9667 | 2.9656 | 178.1 |
| ragged, before the port (`rag105`, batch 188) | 2.9633 | — | — | 193.6 |
| **ragged with the port (`ragp105`)** | 2.9610 | 2.9645 | 2.9628 | 182.7 |
| ragged + 6 MLA heads, equal steps (`mla6`) | 2.9538 | 2.9578 | 2.9558 | 190.6 |
| ragged + 6 MLA heads, 2705 steps (`mla6-ft`, equal time to `ragp105`) | 2.9619 | 2.9636 | 2.9628 | 190.3 |
| value-embed gate × learned scalar (`velam`, `value_embeds=gated_lambda`) | 2.9603 | 2.9656 | 2.9630 | 185.4 |

- **The #9708 port takes about 11 ms off ragged's step** (193.6 → 182.7 ms). Against pooled wave, ragged gains 0.003 per step and costs 2.6% step time.
- **6 MLA heads:** −0.0070 at equal steps on both seeds, for +4.2% step time; exactly break-even at equal time to `ragp105`. Kept for the smaller KV cache relative to the head count.
- **`gated_lambda` is neutral** (+0.0002).
- **Candidate 12 at fixed time** (candidate 11's budget, 2526 steps = 2698 × 177.9 / 190 ms): **2.9714 / 2.9750**, exactly candidate 11's 2.9715 / 2.9750. Ragged + 6 heads are a wash at fixed time; the gain is per step only. Candidate 11's numbers were measured on cw-us-east-02a, these on cw-rno2a.

**Ragged speed probes** (candidate 12, 400 steps, median step ms)

| probe | step ms |
|---|---|
| base (`one_shot`, 2 expert chunks, overlap limit 1) | 189.1 |
| collective overlap limit 4 (on `ragp105`) | 184.1 vs 184.9 |
| `device` transport | 200.7 |
| NCCL transport, multi-process | hung while compiling, 3 attempts |
| 1 expert chunk (`moe_ragged_chunks`) | 194.6 |
| 4 expert chunks | 190.8 |

- **Profile (`lc1-prof-ragp105` vs `lc1-prof-c11`):** ragged's step isn't heavier on the GPU (194 vs 195 ms of kernels per profiled step), and inside a step it waits less on the all-to-all (8 vs 15 ms).
  - The extra time is at the step boundary. Ragged needs one process driving all 8 GPUs, which doubles host dispatch (75 vs 38 ms per step).
  - The pad fusions I suspected aren't ragged's; they come from the AttnRes backward.
- **None of the cheap ragged settings help.** Two chunks stays.
- **AttnRes backward pads:** each gate read of a block's precomputed `[G, B, S]` logits, and of its softmax weights, became a pad back to full size in the backward, 290 of them in the HLO.
  - Per-row splits with a one-stack backward are bitwise identical in loss and gradients.
  - Neither step changes speed: 189.4 ms after each, against 189.1 ms. These small kernels are hidden behind other work, so AttnRes is closed as a speed lever. The changes stay, since they're exact.

**Hyperball decay per matrix** ([Hyperball Decay Atlas](https://claude.ai/artifact/74PcjNW2PaNkYV5btbq3Ug); `lc1-b191-hb2`, 2.9631; `--opt-set log_hyperball_decay=true`). The re-projection acts as a per-matrix weight decay, `1 − |W|/|W+u| ≈ lr·cos(W,u) + lr²/2`.
- **Typical matrices:** 0.06–0.10%/step mid-run with cos ≈ 0.07–0.10. Over 90% of the decay comes from updates leaning outward; the orthogonal part contributes almost none.
- **KDA `w_beta`:** decays 2–3× more than any other matrix, with 4× the rescale and swings inward.
- **AdamH lm head:** the largest spikes (p99 1.27%/step, cos up to 0.66).
- **Layer-5 MLA:** `w_o` spikes too, and `w_uv` takes inward steps.
- **Gated-norm matrices:** the highest sustained decay after `w_beta`, rising with depth.

**Batch 199: final LR 0.1 + EMA sweep** (candidate 12, 2817 steps, seed 0; each run also scores the raw final weights and a 50/50 EMA/final blend)

| run | min LR ratio | EMA β / last N | EMA | raw final | 50/50 blend |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ctrl` | 0.05 | 0.995 / 1000 | 2.9535 | 2.9569 | **2.9514** |
| `f10` | 0.1 | 0.995 / 1000 | 2.9543 | 2.9694 | 2.9542 |
| `f10-b99` | 0.1 | 0.99 / 1000 | 2.9561 | 2.9677 | 2.9570 |
| `f10-b998` | 0.1 | 0.998 / 1000 | 2.9584 | 2.9703 | **2.9512** |
| `f10-w500` | 0.1 | 0.995 / 500 | 2.9572 | 2.9720 | 2.9570 |
| `f10-w1500` | 0.1 | 0.995 / 1500 | 2.9556 | 2.9703 | 2.9554 |
| `f10-b998w1500` | 0.1 | 0.998 / 1500 | 2.9605 | 2.9709 | 2.9524 |

- **The 0.1 floor doesn't pay.** Its raw final weights are +0.0125 worse. The best EMA setting on it (β 0.998, 50/50 blend, 2.9512) only ties the 0.05 floor's blend (2.9514).
- **The 50/50 blend helps at the current floor:** −0.0021 against the pure EMA we report now (2.9514 vs 2.9535), on the same trained weights. It needs a second seed before adopting `--ema-blend 0.5` as the reported model.

**Batch 201: `w_beta` sweep** (candidate 12, 2817 steps, seed 0; hyperball logging on every run). Knobs from [`c2317eab2c`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2317eab2c): `init_std_mult_beta`, `kda_beta_scale`, `kda_beta_group`.

| run | Paloma | Δ vs `ctrl` | `w_beta` L0 cos, steps 5–100 / median | L0 decay median |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ctrl` (init ×2, MuonH 2× LR) | 2.9539 | — | 0.25 / 0.084 | 0.15% |
| init ×1 | 2.9529 | −0.0010 | 0.33 / 0.040 | 0.07% |
| init ×4 | 2.9551 | +0.0012 | 0.18 / 0.147 | 0.27% |
| init ×8 | 2.9571 | +0.0032 | 0.19 / 0.190 | 0.36% |
| LR mult 1 | 2.9547 | +0.0008 | — | — |
| LR mult 4 | 2.9534 | −0.0005 | 0.40 / 0.202 | 0.76% |
| learned per-head beta scale | 2.9543 | +0.0004 | 0.25 / 0.164 | 0.29% |
| AdamH | 2.9574 | +0.0035 | 0.02 / −0.020 | ~0 |
| Adam (norm free) | 2.9560 | +0.0021 | — | — |

- **Everything is within noise (0.0056),** but init shows a monotonic trend: ×1 −0.0010, ×2 0, ×4 +0.0012, ×8 +0.0032. `w_beta` doesn't want a bigger sphere.
- **The outward lean is Muon's, not the loss's.**
  - Given a free per-head scale on the logits, the model shrinks it to about 0.8× (median 0.81, 0.90 at the end), while MuonH keeps pushing `w_beta` outward (cos 0.16).
  - Under AdamH the cos is ≈ 0 and the decay vanishes.
  - So the large decay comes from the orthogonalized update of a 512×4 matrix leaning along W, and the projection simply cancels it. It isn't fighting a model that wants larger beta logits.
- **Plain Adam lets the norm drift 4×** (1.98 → 7.85), with no gain.
- Nothing to adopt. If anything, init ×1 is worth a second seed.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batches 203 (GDLA) and df1: differential attention, take two** (candidate 12 = `base14`, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; [`b31b63ac62`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b31b63ac62) GDLA, [`d304c417c7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/d304c417c7) mean noise; branch `ladderclimb_v1_diffattn`)

**Summary so far: candidate 13 proposal.** Candidate 12 + KDA state reshaped to 4 heads × (64 key × 256 value), with the faster state-pass tiling:

`--model-set kda_key_dim=64 --model-set kda_value_dim=256 --model-set kda_state_block_v=64` ([`acec39b84f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/acec39b84f), branch `ladderclimb_v1_diffattn`)

**df21: fixed-time confirmation** (cw-us-east-02a; with `block_v=64` the reshaped model runs at candidate 12's speed, so equal steps is equal time)

| run | steps | seed 0 | seed 1 | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| candidate 12 (`block_v` 64) | 2817 | 2.9532 (2.9543 in df1) | 2.9584 (df4) | 191.3 |
| **4 × (64 × 256)** | 2817 | **2.9482** | **2.9489** | 191.0–191.7 |
| 8 × (64 × 128), fixed time | 2754 | 2.9485 | 2.9512 | 194.4 |

- **4 × (64 × 256): −0.0056 / −0.0095 at fixed time (mean ≈ −0.0075),** with no step-time cost.
  - Earlier two-seed equal-step runs gave −0.0067.
  - d768 gave −0.0064 at equal steps (6929 steps).
  - The state size per head is unchanged: 64 × 256 = 16,384 entries, the same as 128 × 128.
  - The q/k (and erase) projections halve, while v/o and the per-channel output and write gates double. Net, about +0.65M parameters per KDA layer at d512.
- **8 × (64 × 128) at fixed time: −0.0062,** a little behind and +2% step time.
- **16 × (64 × 64)** has the largest per-step gain (−0.0146) but needs a prep kernel that packs several small heads per program (+8.6% step today). That's the next kernel project if you want it.

---

**More, narrower KDA heads; d768; a free KDA kernel speedup** ([`acec39b84f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/acec39b84f))

**Head layout at the same total KDA state** (d512, 2817 equal steps; controls 2.9543 / 2.9584)

| KDA heads × (key × value) | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 × (64 × 256) | 2.9500 | 2.9493 | −0.0067 |
| 8 × (64 × 128) | 2.9439 | 2.9485 | −0.0102 |
| 8 × (64 × 128), chunk 64 | 2.9453 | 2.9476 | −0.0099 |
| 16 × (64 × 64) | 2.9397 | — | **−0.0146** |
| 4 × (64 × 256) + MLA and KDA content gates | 2.9460 | 2.9476 | −0.0096 |

- **At the same total state, more independent narrow states keep helping:** 4 → 8 → 16 heads gives −0.007 → −0.010 → −0.015 per step.
- **The KDA content gate isn't additive** on top of 64 × 256 + the MLA gate.

**d768** (6929 steps, cw-rno2a, MLA heads left at the d768 default in both arms): 4 × (64 × 256) gives **2.7143 vs 2.7207 (−0.0064)**. That's the same per-step gain as at d512 (−0.0067); step time +1.9% before the kernel change below.

**Why many small heads were slow, and the fix.**
- The KDA state pass runs one sequential program per (sequence × head, `d_v` slab), and the slab was fixed at 32.
- With more heads, there are more of these latency-bound programs, each doing less work per step.
- **`kda_state_block_v=64`** (new `state_block_v` argument of `kda_fused`) halves the program count. It's exact, since it only changes the tiling; the kernel tests pass at 32 vs 64 for both state-grad paths.
- Per-layer KDA forward+backward on one H100 (prep + state pass):

| layout | `block_v` 32 | `block_v` 64 |
|---|---|---|
| 4 × 128 × 128 (candidate 12) | 2.21 + 2.14 | 2.21 + 2.07 |
| 4 × 64 × 256 | 1.82 + 2.92 | 1.82 + 2.28 |
| 8 × 64 × 128 | 2.32 + 3.11 | 2.32 + 2.42 |
| 16 × 64 × 64 | 4.08 + 3.21 | 4.08 + 2.53 |

- Full-step timing probes (400 steps, same cluster and session):

| config | step ms |
|---|---|
| candidate 12, `block_v` 32 | 190.9 |
| candidate 12, `block_v` 64 | 190.7 |
| 4 × (64 × 256), `block_v` 64 | **190.1 (no cost)** |
| 8 × (64 × 128), `block_v` 64 | 195.2 (+2.3%) |
| 16 × (64 × 64), `block_v` 64 | 207.4 (+8.6%) |

- **The 4 × (64 × 256) shape is now free.** Its −0.0067 per-step gain should hold at fixed time. Two seeds at 2817 steps with `block_v=64` and a same-run control are running to confirm.
  - 8 heads is now about −0.006 at fixed time and is running at its fixed-time step count (2755).
  - 16 heads is still held back by the intra-chunk prep kernels (4.1 vs 2.2 ms), whose per-program work shrinks with the head width. Packing several heads per prep program is the next kernel lever, worth up to about −0.015 per step if it reached 4-head speed.

---

**df14–df17 results** (cw-us-east-02a; controls 2.9543 / 2.9584 at 2817 steps, about 190 ms)

| run | change | steps | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `hgate` | MLA H-gate, rank 32 | 2817 | 2.9511 | 2.9563 | −0.0027 | 191.5 |
| `kdahg` | the same content gate on the KDA output gate ([`393d68cfa8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/393d68cfa8)) | 2817 | 2.9515 | 2.9551 | −0.0031 | 192.2 |
| `kv-hg` | KDA 64 × 256 + MLA H-gate | 2817 | 2.9466 | 2.9480 | −0.0090 | 195.9 |
| `h8` | **8 KDA heads × (64 × 128)** | 2817 | **2.9439** | **2.9485** | **−0.0102** | 198.0 |
| `h8-ft` | the same at fixed time | 2704 | 2.9527 | 2.9540 | −0.0030 | 198.8 |
| `kv-ft` | 4 KDA heads × (64 × 256) at fixed time | 2766 | 2.9519 | 2.9532 | −0.0038 | 194.4 |

- **Content-conditioned output gates replicate in both mixers.**
  - The gate logits gain a rank-32 term read from what the head retrieved: −0.0027 on MLA and −0.0031 on KDA, both seeds negative.
  - Each costs about 1% step time, so each nets about −0.001 at fixed time.
- **8 KDA heads × (64 × 128) is the best per-step result:** −0.0102 on two seeds.
  - It has the same total state and the same q/k and v/o widths as 4 × (64 × 256). The extra gain comes from more independent states, each with its own β and decays.
  - Its kernel cost (+4.4%) leaves it tied with 4 × (64 × 256) at fixed time (−0.0030 vs −0.0038). If the 8-head kernel ran at the 4-head cost, it would be the better shape.
- **Running:**
  - All three stacked (64 × 256 + MLA and KDA content gates), two seeds.
  - 16 KDA heads × (64 × 64).
  - The d768 pair for 64 × 256.

---

**Why 32 × 512 is slow, and HyGA gates** (cw-us-east-02a)

KDA fused forward+backward on one H100, at the per-GPU d512 shape (B = 16, S = 4096, 4 heads; erase gate, Pallas state grads):

| state | chunk 32 | chunk 16 |
|---|---|---|
| 128 × 128 (candidate 12) | 4.5 ms | — |
| 64 × 256 | 4.7 ms | 5.5 ms |
| 32 × 256 | 6.0 ms | — |
| 64 × 512 | 12.1 ms | 9.5 ms |
| 32 × 512 | 31.9 ms | 7.8 ms |

- **The forward is fine at every shape:** 2.2 ms at 32 × 512 vs 1.6 ms at 64 × 256.
- **The backward degrades** as values widen past 256 (about 2.6×) and as keys narrow to 32 (about 1.3×), and the two compound.
  - The prep backward holds whole `C × d_v` fp32 value tiles per chunk, which very likely spills at `d_v` = 512.
  - Chunk 16 halves those tiles and recovers most of the loss.
- **Even so, 32 × 512 costs about +3 ms per KDA layer over 64 × 256** (+8% step), which outweighs its extra −0.004 per step at fixed time.
  - A fully tuned kernel would at best tie 64 × 256 at fixed time, so I'm not spending kernel work on it.
  - **64 × 256 at chunk 32 is the shape to keep.**

**HyGA gates on MLA** ([arXiv 2608.11805](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11805), [`2629cbe0d4`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/2629cbe0d4); seed 0, control 2.9543)

| run | gate | Paloma | Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `df12-hgate` | H-gate: `SiLU(H_i W_d) W_u` (rank 32) added to the output gate's logits, read from the head's own attention output | 2.9511 | −0.0032 | 191.8 |
| `df12-cgate` | C-gate: per-head `2σ((H W_c)_i)` from all heads' outputs | 2.9540 | −0.0003 | 192.5 |
| `df12-hyga` | both | 2.9534 | −0.0009 | 191.6 |

- Our existing output gates read `x`. HyGA's **H-gate reads the attention output itself** (what the head retrieved), which no earlier gate variant did.
- −0.0032 is within one-seed noise. Seed 1 is running, along with the stack on `k64v256` (two seeds).
- **Also running:** 8 KDA heads × (64 × 128). It has the same total state and the same q/k and v/o widths as 4 × (64 × 256), so it separates head count from per-head value width. The d768 pair (candidate 12 vs `k64v256`, 6929 steps) is on cw-rno2a.

---

**df9 / df10 results: the KDA state shape** (cw-us-east-02a; controls 2.9543 / 2.9584 at 2817 steps, about 190 ms)

| run | state (key × value) | steps | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k64v256`, equal steps | 64 × 256 | 2817 | 2.9500 | 2.9493 | −0.0067 | 193.3 |
| **`k64v256`, fixed time** | 64 × 256 | 2766 | **2.9519** | **2.9532** | **−0.0038** | 194.4 |
| `k32v512`, equal steps | 32 × 512 | 2817 | 2.9446 | 2.9467 | **−0.0107** | 270 (+42%) |
| `k128v256` (2× state, diagnostic) | 128 × 256 | 2817 | 2.9473 | — | −0.0070 | 206.4 (+8.7%) |

- **`k64v256` wins at fixed time on both seeds: −0.0024 / −0.0052.**
  - It changes only the KDA layers' key/value widths (`--model-set kda_key_dim=64 --model-set kda_value_dim=256`).
  - The state size is unchanged. The q/k projections halve and the v/o projections double.
- **Value width is what pays.** Narrowing the keys further to widen the values (32 × 512) gains −0.0107 per step, on both seeds. Doubling the state at 256-wide values (`k128v256`) gains less than 32 × 512 does at the original state size.
- **32 × 512 is held back only by speed.** The fused KDA kernels run +42% slower at that shape. A kernel microbenchmark across shapes is running to find which pass is slow; if it's a tiling problem, 32 × 512 could be worth about −0.008 at fixed time.

**Kalman write strength: parked.**
- Every attempt hit a NaN loss between steps 4 and 31, on both seeds and with either optimizer for the projection.
- A debug run shows why: at step 10 the gradient norm of KDA layer 2's `kalman_b` was **5e18**, with every other gradient below 0.4. Its square overflows fp32 in the global-norm clip, and the loss turns NaN a few steps later.
- The scan itself is not the source. On CPU at 4096 tokens its forward and gradients are finite and O(1) for decays 0.5–0.999 and extreme `ω`/`r`.
- So the blow-up arrives through the kernel's `β` cotangent, on tokens where the Kalman β departs from the sigmoid's narrow range. Finding them needs kernel-level instrumentation; I'm not chasing that further now.

---

**df6–df8 results** (cw-us-east-02a, 2817 steps; controls 2.9543 (seed 0) / 2.9584 (seed 1), about 190 ms)

| run | change | seed 0 | seed 1 | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `df6-fts` | per-token logit temperature `2σ(ĥ·w)` on the lm_head input | 2.9554 (+0.0011) | 2.9577 (−0.0007) | 192.5 |
| `k64v256` (df5 / df7) | KDA state 64 × 256, 4 heads | **2.9500 (−0.0043)** | **2.9493 (−0.0091)** | 193.3 (+1.7%) |
| `df7-k32v512` | KDA state 32 × 512 | 2.9446 (−0.0097) | — | 268.7 (+41%) |
| `df8-h2k128v256` | 2 KDA heads × (128 × 256), same total state | 2.9640 (+0.0097) | — | 187.7 |
| `df8-h2k64v512` | 2 KDA heads × (64 × 512), half the state | 2.9593 (+0.0050) | — | 194.3 |

- **KDA keys 64 × values 256 replicates: −0.0067 mean over two seeds at equal steps.** At +1.7% step time that nets about −0.004 at fixed time.
  - **Wider still (32 × 512) keeps gaining** (−0.0097), but the KDA kernels run far slower at `d_k` = 32. A kernel tile tuned for 32-wide keys might recover this.
  - **The heads matter too:** 2 wider heads at the same total state lose (+0.010 / +0.005).
  - The best shape so far is 4 heads, each with a narrow key address and a wide value.
- **The per-token output temperature is neutral** (mean +0.0002), as the removed final GatedNorm was in batch 10. Closed.
- **df9 (running):**
  - `k64v256` at fixed time: 2766 steps = 2817 × 189.8 / 193.3, two seeds.
  - `k128v256`: values 256 with keys left at 128. This doubles the state; it's a diagnostic of state size vs value width, not a candidate.
  - **Kalman write strength** (`kda_kalman_beta`, [arXiv 2609.07816](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07816), [`9ac96e5826`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9ac96e5826)), two seeds.
    - Each KDA head tracks a scalar memory uncertainty, `b̂ₜ = aₜ bₜ₋₁ + ωₜ` with `bₜ = rₜ b̂ₜ / (rₜ + b̂ₜ)`, and writes with `βₜ = b̂ₜ / (rₜ + b̂ₜ)` in place of `σ(x W_β)`.
    - So a head writes hard while its memory is uncertain and softly once it has absorbed evidence.
    - `ω` and `r` are per-token softplus projections. The recursion is a Möbius map, run as one associative scan of 2 × 2 matrices before the KDA kernel.

---

**df5 results: KDA state shape at fixed size** (cw-us-east-02a, 2817 steps; controls `df1-ctrl` 2.9543 (seed 0, 189.8 ms) and `df4-ctrl-s1` 2.9584 (seed 1, 190.4 ms))

| run | per-head state (key × value) | Paloma | Δ vs seed 0 | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k64v256` | 64 × 256 | **2.9500** | **−0.0043** | 193.1 (+1.7%) |
| `k256v64` | 256 × 64 | 2.9645 | +0.0102 | 227.9 (+20%) |

- **Wider values with narrower keys help, and the reverse hurts.**
  - This matches batch 203's MLA finding, where loss tracked value capacity.
  - The KDA state reads back 256-wide values per head from 64-dim key addresses, with the state size unchanged.
- **Cost:** the v/o projections double (n·256 wide) while q/k halve, so +1.7% step time. That nets about −0.0014 at fixed time, inside noise for one seed.
- **Running (df7):**
  - `k64v256` seed 1.
  - `k32v512`: the same state with even wider values.
  - `k96v192`: a milder reshape (state +12%).

---

**df2 / df3 results** (cw-rno2a, 2817 steps, seed 0; control `df2-ctrl` 2.9542 at 189.7 ms)

| run | change | Paloma | Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `df2-g12n6l01` | GDLA 6 × (1 + 1), λ starts at 0.1 | 2.9543 | +0.0001 | 207.1 |
| `df2-g9n3l01` | GDLA 3 × (2 + 1), λ starts at 0.1 | 2.9539 | −0.0003 | 199.1 |
| `df2-g8n2l01` | GDLA 2 × (3 + 1), λ starts at 0.1 | 2.9603 | +0.0061 | 194.9 |
| `df3-h12x64` | MLA 12 heads × 64 | 2.9557 | +0.0015 | 302.1 |
| `df3-h12x64q` | 12 × 64, `qk_mult` × √2 | 2.9547 | +0.0005 | 302.8 |
| `df3-h8x96` | 8 × 96 | 2.9540 | −0.0002 | 257.6 |

- **The low λ start removes batch 203's small penalty** (`g9n3`: +0.0019 → −0.0003), but there's still no gain. With 2 value heads (`g8n2`) it still loses.
- **Differential attention is closed on this model.** Every variant lands between neutral and worse:
  - Motif's GDLA inside the head budget, plus three larger head counts.
  - DIFF-style pairs.
  - A free mean-value noise map.
  - Two λ starts.
- **Likely reason:** the MLA layers already have the tools DIFF supplies.
  - The ×2-sigmoid output gate can switch a head's read off per token, which is the gated-attention fix for attention sinks.
  - XSA removes the self-value component, and q/k norms with a learned temperature keep maps sharp.
  - λ always collapses early, i.e. at first the model pushes the subtraction out of the way.
- **More, narrower heads at equal FLOPs don't help at equal steps either,** and FA4 runs 64- and 96-dim heads far slower here (+59% / +36% step).
  - So the 4 → 6 head gain was capacity, not head count.
  - Closed.

---

**Follow-ups running** (d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0)

- **df2 (rno2a, own control `df2-ctrl`): GDLA with λ starting at 0.1** (`mla_diff_lambda_init=0.1`, a learned per-head bias) on `g12n6`, `g9n3` and `g8n2`. λ dropped from 0.5 to about 0.1 early in every batch 203 and df1 run.
- **df3 (rno2a): more, narrower MLA heads at equal attention FLOPs** (`mla_head_dim`, [`911452ce68`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/911452ce68)).
  - *Source:* batch 203 shows the global layers' loss tracking their number of value heads, and 4 → 6 heads gave −0.007 (batch 192).
  - The arms trade head width for head count at the same q/k/v/o parameters and attention FLOPs:
    - `h12x64`: 12 × 64 instead of 6 × 128.
    - `h12x64q`: the same with `qk_mult` × √2. Halving the head dim shrinks the normalized q·k/√d logits by √2.
    - `h8x96`: 8 × 96.
  - The KV latent stays at 512.
- **df5 (cw-us-east-02a; controls `df1-ctrl` and `df4-ctrl-s1`): the KDA state's shape at fixed size** (`kda_key_dim` / `kda_value_dim`, [`9abaa83612`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9abaa83612)).
  - Each KDA head's 128 × 128 delta-rule state is reshaped to 64 × 256 (wider values, as Gated DeltaNet's `expand_v`) or 256 × 64 (wider keys).
  - State size per head is unchanged. The q/k vs v/o projections trade width.

---

**Batch df1 results** (cw-us-east-02a, 2817 steps, seed 0; control `df1-ctrl` 2.9543 at 189.8 ms)

| run | noise map | Paloma | Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mu` | uniform prefix mean | 2.9554 | +0.0011 | 194.3 |
| `md16` | decayed mean, half-life 16 at init | 2.9565 | +0.0022 | 195.3 |
| `md64` | half-life 64 | 2.9564 | +0.0021 | 194.7 |
| `md256` | half-life 256 | 2.9554 | +0.0011 | 195.0 |

- **No gain anywhere, and the scan costs about 2.5% of step time.**
- **λ follows the GDLA pattern:** it drops from 0.5 to 0.03–0.16 in the first fifth of training, then settles at about 0.21 (layer 3) and 0.15 (layer 5).
- **The learned decays split by head:**
  - Some heads go to a half-life of about 2.5 tokens, i.e. subtracting the last couple of values.
  - Others go to thousands of tokens, i.e. the uniform mean.
  - The model uses a small common-mode subtraction, but it buys no loss.
- **Closed.** The λ-init question is tested on GDLA in df2.

---

**Batch 203 results** (Paloma macro loss, 2817 steps, seed 0, cw-rno2a. Candidate 12 controls on rno2a: 2.9529 (`b201-binit1`) / 2.9539 (`b202-ctrl`), mean 2.9534, about 194 ms per step with hyperball logging on.)

| run | signal + noise heads | value heads | Paloma | Δ vs 2.9534 | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `g6n1eg` | 5 + 1 | 1 | 2.9697 | **+0.0163** | 190.6 |
| `g6n2eg` | 2 × (2 + 1) | 2 | 2.9625 | +0.0091 | 189.1 |
| `g8n2eg` | 2 × (3 + 1) | 2 | 2.9577 | +0.0043 | 196.9 |
| `g8n2` (per-head gate) | 2 × (3 + 1) | 2 | 2.9590 | +0.0056 | 193.0 |
| `g9n3eg` | 3 × (2 + 1) | 3 | 2.9553 | +0.0019 | 199.3 |
| `g12n6eg` | 6 × (1 + 1) | 6 | 2.9527 | −0.0007 | 207.1 (+7%) |
| `eg` (elementwise gate, no differential) | 6 | 6 | 2.9545 | +0.0011 | 192.0 |

**Reading.**
- **The loss tracks the number of value heads, not the subtraction.** 1 value head: +0.016. 2: +0.004 to +0.009. 3: +0.002. 6: 0.
  - Inside the head budget, GDLA costs the global layers their value capacity. That costs far more than the noise cancellation returns.
  - With values intact (`g12n6eg`, DIFF-style pairs), the subtraction is neutral (−0.0007) and the extra heads cost +7% step time.
- **The elementwise output gate alone is neutral** (+0.0011), as in batch 163.
- **What λ learned** (mean over tokens and heads, at 0 / 20 / 40 / 60 / 80 / 100% of training):

  | run | layer 3 | layer 5 |
  |---|---|---|
  | `g12n6eg` | 0.50 → 0.09 → 0.35 → 0.40 → 0.44 → 0.45 | 0.50 → 0.12 → 0.12 → 0.17 → 0.21 → 0.24 |
  | `g9n3eg` | 0.50 → 0.15 → 0.28 → 0.33 → 0.37 → 0.39 | 0.50 → 0.12 → 0.14 → 0.17 → 0.21 → 0.25 |
  | `g6n1eg` | 0.50 → 0.22 → 0.31 → 0.37 → 0.40 → 0.41 | 0.50 → 0.26 → 0.19 → 0.21 → 0.25 → 0.28 |

  - The noise read is as large as the signal read: RMS ratio 0.93 at layer 3 and 1.00 at layer 5 in `g12n6eg`.
  - So the model does use the subtraction late in training. But it first throws λ down from 0.5 to about 0.1: the start is too strong.
- **Next (df2):** a learned λ bias starting at 0.1 (`mla_diff_lambda_init=0.1`) on `g12n6`, `g9n3` and `g8n2`, against a fresh control.
- To pay at fixed time, `g12n6` needs about −0.012 at equal steps (+7% step time).

---


Note: another agent is also running a batch 203 (`badam*`). My differential-attention batches from here on use the `lc1-df<N>-` prefix.

**Why the batch 163 version lost.**
- Batch 163 got −0.003 / −0.004 at equal steps but cost +6.6% step time.
- It added its noise maps on top of the signal heads, as a second full attention call.
- It also tiled each shared noise map out to all `g` heads of its group, so each map was computed `g` times.
- Motif 3's GDLA ([arXiv 2608.09119](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09119)) does neither:
  - The noise heads come out of the head budget: 80 query heads = 64 signal + 16 noise.
  - Each group's signal and noise heads share one KV head, and only the query differs.
  - Its attention kernel therefore runs no extra heads.

**Batch 203: GDLA inside the head budget** (`mla_gdla_noise_heads=m`, MLA layers 3 and 5)
- The `N` query heads form `m` groups of `g` signal heads plus 1 noise head, and run in one kernel call.
- Each group shares one value head, so `w_uv` and the value embeds have `m` heads. Keys stay per head, since MLA up-projections are cheap.
- The output is `D = H_signal − λ·H_noise(group)`, with `λ = sigmoid(x W_λ)` per signal head and token (zero-init, so 0.5).
- Only the signal heads reach `w_o`.

| run | heads (signal + noise) | value heads | output gate | attention cost vs candidate 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `g6n2eg` | 6 = 2 × (2 + 1) | 2 | elementwise (Motif) | same |
| `g6n1eg` | 6 = 5 + 1 | 1 | elementwise | same |
| `g8n2eg` | 8 = 2 × (3 + 1) | 2 | elementwise | +2 heads |
| `g9n3eg` | 9 = 3 × (2 + 1) | 3 | elementwise | +3 heads |
| `g12n6eg` | 12 = 6 × (1 + 1), i.e. DIFF pairs | 6 (no value loss) | elementwise | ×2 |
| `g8n2` | 8 = 2 × (3 + 1) | 2 | per head (ours) | +2 heads |
| `eg` | 6, no differential | 6 | elementwise | control for the gate |

The `g6` arms test whether the noise subtraction is worth giving up signal heads and value heads at no extra cost. `g12n6eg` tests whether it helps when nothing else is taken away.

**Batch df1: differential attention with a free noise map** (original idea; on cw-us-east-02a with its own control)
- *Source:* DIFF's noise map is meant to cancel common-mode attention, the broad mass a softmax spreads over irrelevant context. The cheapest estimate of that common mode is a fixed average of the values, so no second softmax map is needed.
- *Mechanism:* `D = softmax(qkᵀ)v − λ·mean_{j≤t}(v_j)` per head, within documents, with the same token-dependent sigmoid `λ`. Cost is one segment-reset scan, with no extra kernel call.
- *Variants:*
  - `uniform`: the plain prefix mean.
  - `decay`: an exponentially decayed mean with a learned per-head decay, half-life 16 / 64 / 256 at init. This makes the noise map a local/recent baseline.
- *Logged:* `knob_mean_noise_lambda_mean` and the learned half-lives per layer.

| run | noise map |
|---|---|
| `df1-ctrl` | none (cw-us-east-02a control) |
| `df1-mu` | uniform prefix mean |
| `df1-md16` / `md64` / `md256` | decayed mean, initial half-life 16 / 64 / 256 |

Results will be edited in here.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Partial key offset study: what the shifted half of the MLA heads learns** (d512 current best / candidate 12, EMA weights of `lc1-b234-attn-distance`, 2.9528)

With `mla_key_offset`, each MLA head's first 64 key channels come from the previous token (j−1); channels 64–127 come from the current token. I looked at what that split learns: the query/key directions of each head, then a probe of where the heads attend.

**Method**
- **Directions in the attention input x:** the query direction is the `W_q` column. The key direction is backed out through the latent: `W_dkv · diag(latent norm gain) · W_uk`, with the latent RMSNorm linearized.
- **The 128 per-channel pairs aren't unique:** any rotation of a head's channels gives the same scores. So each head is also analyzed through the SVD of its query–key product `B = W_q W_kᵀ`, which gives canonical (query direction, key direction, strength) pairs. The raw-channel and canonical numbers agree closely.

**1. The shifted half is an induction lookup, built into the weights**

Mean query/key cosine on the shifted half (channels 0–63), per head:

| head | layer 3 | layer 5 |
|---|---|---|
| H0 | 0.61 | 0.90 |
| H1 | 0.87 | 0.70 |
| H2 | 0.41 | 0.85 |
| H3 | 0.80 | 0.85 |
| H4 | 0.85 | 0.45 |
| H5 | 0.89 | 0.88 |

- **Query and key point the same way in all 12 heads.** By pair strength, 92–100% sits on positively matched pairs, and no head has negatively matched pairs. So a query scores keys whose *previous* token resembles its own token: "find where I appeared before and read what came next."
- **The current-token half matches only weakly** (+0.14 to +0.40), except L3 H2 (+0.87), a copy head.
- **The attention probe agrees.** Queries at fixed in-document positions (x = 20…4,000), with each query's full softmax row kept rather than averaged:
  - at x = 4,000, 30–49% of the top long-range keys of the sharp layer-3 heads (H1, H4, H5) are induction targets;
  - half of those heads' long-range mass sits on 6–36 keys;
  - L3 H2 picks earlier copies of the query token (33% of its top keys).
- **Layer-5 heads are induction-shaped in the weights too (0.85–0.93), but diffuse in behavior.** Half their long-range mass needs 93–172 keys. They likely match on broader features, so many keys qualify.

**2. The 64 shifted dims are not redundant in weight space**

| per head, shifted half | range |
|---|---|
| directions for 50% / 90% of B's strength | 11–19 / 40–48 |
| effective rank (of 64) | 41–55 |
| stable rank | 12–28 |
| average \|cos\| between different key channels | 0.04–0.07 |
| top 8 channels' share of strength (uniform = 0.125) | 0.14–0.15 |

The channels are near-orthogonal and none dominates. A dozen or so stronger directions plus a long real tail. This is weight space only: whether the data uses all 64 needs an activation-side rank or an ablation, which isn't run yet.

**3. Tying the query to the key on the shifted half costs nothing**

`mla_tie_prev_qk` (`b759695d8f`): the query's shifted half *is* the token's own un-shifted key half, so those channels score `k_prev(x_i) · k_prev(x_{j−1})`, a symmetric similarity. It needs no query projection for those 64 channels.

| run | Paloma | step ms |
|---|---|---|
| current best (`lc1-b217-ctrl`) | 2.9521 | 190.2 |
| **tied shifted half (`lc1-b236-tie-prev-qk`)** | **2.9517** | 190.3 |

Neutral: the free query directions were re-learning the key. That makes it a free simplification, and it drops 64 query columns per head in both MLA layers.

**4. For sparse attention**

The shifted half is close to a symmetric positive form, a learned similarity between the query token and each key's previous token. A low-rank index over previous-token states (around 16–32 dims) could pre-select long-range candidates for the retrieval heads. The diffuse layer-5 heads look better suited to pooled chunk summaries than to top-k selection.

**Next:**
- an activation-side effective rank of the shifted half;
- shifting 16 or 32 channels instead of 64;
- the Inkling relative-position bias by distance. That probe run (`lc1-b235-relpos-probe`) just finished.

issues.author: mcwitt-agent
issues.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Two ways a profile can break a hero run, both found on one rack while testing the stack (#9830-#9834). A production rollout needs a guard for each.

**1. XLA compile abort (fixed in a candidate plugin, not yet promoted).** With `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading` (#9831), rematerialization may offload values to host when its estimate of the step exceeds its budget. One profiled schedule overshot the budget (124.77 GiB against 114.09 GiB inside the layer loop), and remat picked an f32[] operand of an all-reduce whose start was scheduled before the loop and whose done came after it. `GetCostOfHostOffload` counts users reached through the all-reduce's alias; `OffloadInstruction` places the reload before direct users only, found none unplaced, and failed `CHECK(!place_before_list.empty())` at hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118 on every rank. The bug is unchanged on openxla/xla main and has no upstream report.
- Fix: skip candidates whose buffer `has_indirect_uses` in `GetCostOfHostOffload`, as recomputation already does. Branch `marin/remat-offload-indirect-uses` (0f6dc61dee) on marin-community/xla. A plugin built from it on Iris (`0.11.1+marin.0f6dc61dee6d`, 15 minutes) compiles the case that aborted.
- A second branch, `marin/remat-no-offload-strategy` (ff858b5447), also keeps the flag's host accounting but turns the offload strategy off. Its cost model prices host copies at HBM bandwidth. It is built but untested on the rack.

**2. Out of memory at runtime.** With the fix, the same program compiled and then failed to allocate its 143.75 GiB pool on the first step. Remat estimated the profiled schedule about 26 GiB above the unprofiled one. A near-identical program (the shared expert as two custom VJPs instead of one) trained with its own profile at 119.5 GiB peak, so this depends on the schedule. I have not traced which buffers grow.

What this adds to the done criteria: before a long run, a preflight that compiles the profiled program and runs a few steps, with a fallback to no profile when either fails. Both failures appear within minutes of start.

spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

The expanded GLM-5.3/Pi collection is complete: 1,310 attempts, exactly five for each of 262 tasks, with 1,285 native reward vectors and 25 ungraded attempts. The first SFT baseline will use all available solver traces, including partial-credit, zero-credit, truncated, and interrupted traces, without reward or completion filtering. Native Pi sessions exist for 1,251 attempts; 39 further attempts have raw model-request captures only, and 20 startup failures have no model requests. The initial 30-attempt Pi batch is separate and remains in scope. Collection artifacts are preserved and no owned sandboxes remain. The agreed first run starts from September 21 Datakit SFT, uses biology traces only, peak LR 1e-4, three epochs, 131,072-token sequences, and effective batch 16. Save/export only the final model. Full-parameter SFT uses fresh AdamH, 3% warmup, cosine decay to 1e-5, and frozen router biases. Evaluate BixBench first; broader evaluations are deferred until that result. Preparation is complete: 5,120 reconstructed windows, 73,894,261 assistant target tokens per epoch, and 960 optimizer steps for three epochs. CoreWeave 32 H100s is selected. CPU optimizer/checkpoint tests and full lint/type checks pass. Cache construction is running. The CPU training coordinator is submitted and waits for verified cache completion before requesting the selected 32 H100s; no optimizer updates have run.

## Description

Use the existing [Skill2Env Harbor release](https://hub.harborframework.com/datasets/skill2env/skill2env) to collect GLM-5.3 demonstrations for Snowball. This issue owns task selection, rollout collection, SFT, and the before/after experiment. [#9630](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9630) owns Skill2Env Atlas intake; [#9258](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258) owns biology evaluation coverage and protocols.

Start with biology tasks, prioritizing biological data analysis relevant to BixBench. If the usable pool is too small, consider a separately recorded expansion to general scientific data analysis and statistics. Keep relay methods, where a teacher takes over from student-generated actions, for a later experiment.

### Candidate data

The October 5 metadata inspection covered all 7,496 tasks in release revision 2, version `1.0.1`, with content digest `sha256:bef4f739bde8d865af04c04a2cb1c84ecad83b52dd558f4d582dd46c7933666c`. The 268 candidates are a source-skill and description-based shortlist, not an exhaustive taxonomy or a validated training pool.

| Candidate category | Tasks | Source-skill identifiers |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Genomics and single-cell analysis | 95 | 40 |
| Proteins and structure | 49 | 16 |
| Chemistry and drug discovery | 45 | 22 |
| Biomedical data and lab workflows | 79 | 28 |
| Total | 268 | 106 |

Examples include paired airway RNA-seq analysis with PyDESeq2, sparse CELLxGENE summaries, Scanpy PBMC QC and clustering, DepMap dependency analysis, and pysam BAM/VCF processing. Different skill identifiers can cover related workflows; 106 identifiers do not establish 106 independent task families. Many released tasks repair pipelines against offline fixtures. Their usefulness for BixBench remains a hypothesis.

Skill2Env's [source attribution table](https://github.com/NVlabs/Skill2Env/blob/507eab4d9952968de2be98f8729d3c66d487285a/SkillHub/skillhub_source_licenses.csv) includes K-Dense scientific skills and AlterLab academic skills. Preserve task-specific source and license records when selecting data or sharing traces. The selection rule below preserves this initial shortlist independently of temporary local files.

### Pilot sequence

1. Review candidate instructions, environments, and graders. Six initial tasks passed reference/no-op controls. The user authorized direct collection on the other 262 metadata-selected candidates; those tasks have not passed additional controls. Review grader validity when interpreting scores; it is not a selection gate for the unfiltered baseline. Record any grader defects; the existing Atlas assessment found a grader defect in a separate three-task sample.
2. Freeze the task manifest and evaluation split. Group related tasks and shared-data variants when defining development and held-out sets. BixBench-overlap checking is not a prerequisite for this collection, as decided on October 5; preserve task provenance.
3. Pin the Snowball starting checkpoint, tokenizer, training recipe, agent harness, and evaluation settings. Run a small end-to-end collection and formatting check before expanding collection. Record compute budgets before launching sandbox or training work.
4. Generate GLM-5.3 trajectories. The initial collection finished five attempts per task on the six control-checked tasks, for 30 attempted rollouts. The expanded collection targets five attempts for each of the other 262 tasks, for 1,310 new attempts. Preserve every attempt, raw conversations, tool outputs, exact model settings, task revisions, and the full native reward vector; keep incomplete and ungraded outcomes separate. Inspect component-score distributions, solution diversity, and token volume. The first SFT baseline uses all available solver traces without reward or completion filtering. Preserve interrupted prefixes and record conversion or recovery gaps without manufacturing missing content. Rewards are graded; do not reduce them to binary success or require all components to equal 1 by default. Native executable rewards do not reproduce the paper's additional rubric-scoring layer.
5. Prepare all available solver traces for the first SFT baseline; the earlier 200–500 selected-trace target is superseded. Report attempted, complete, graded, and selected traces; component-score distributions; unique tasks and task families; total tokens; and supervised assistant tokens. Size the first SFT run from those observations; the target is a planning budget, not a proven minimum. Prioritize coverage of distinct tasks when expanding collection. Additional attempts on one task do not increase task diversity.
6. Train with loss on assistant turns, preserving user and tool messages as context. Evaluate the final checkpoint against the unchanged Snowball parent on the fixed BixBench protocol using the same Pi harness and budgets. Decide on broader evaluations after reviewing BixBench. Keep infrastructure failures separate from incorrect answers.

Recent Snowball work motivates a bounded test: a [5,000-conversation GLM continuation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9719) regressed on several benchmarks, while [other agent SFT mixtures](https://gist.github.com/lukedhlee/8669f5b6f97e4e3bae72344a8fd51f4b) improved agent benchmarks. Neither establishes a BixBench benefit from this dataset.

### Agreed SFT settings

| Setting | Selected value |
| --- | --- |
| Parent | `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21`; revision `b8c07f7df1df65525abbfdbcd1572318ba11c42f` and native tokenizer/template pinned |
| Data | All available GLM/Pi biology solver traces; no reward or completion filter; no general SFT or pretraining replay |
| Run count and peak LR | One run at `1e-4` |
| Duration | Three epochs |
| Training sequence length | 131,072 tokens; verify actual lengths with the parent tokenizer |
| Effective global batch | 16 sequences per optimizer update; accumulation as needed |
| Parameter updates | Full-parameter SFT; imported router biases frozen, router weights and other model weights trained |
| Optimizer | Fresh AdamH; beta1 0.9, beta2 0.95, epsilon 1e-8, weight decay 0, gradient clipping 1.0 |
| Schedule | 3% warmup, then cosine decay from 1e-4 to 1e-5 over the run |
| Checkpoints | Final model save/export only; no intermediate or per-epoch checkpoints |
| Initial evaluation | Parent and final model on BixBench with identical Pi harness and budgets; broader evaluations deferred until that result |

The nominal batch is 2,097,152 token positions per update, matching 64 × 32,768 in [the teacher-only reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9582). Masking, padding, and sequence construction determine actual supervised tokens. Three epochs and peak LR 1e-4 follow that precedent; its reported evaluations use final checkpoints, and its intermediate checkpoint cadence is undocumented. The final-only saving decision avoids repeated serialization and storage of this model.

Use reconstructed conversations with each actual assistant output supervised once, carried context masked, and interrupted outputs left without invented termination markers. The finalized dataset has 5,120 windows at length 131,072, 320 steps per epoch, and 960 steps total. Target four CoreWeave nodes with eight H100s each. BixBench comparison uses `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` (205 tasks), Pi, one attempt per task, 32,768 context / 8,192 output, and matched grading. The CPU training coordinator is submitted; GPU training remains gated on cache verification.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Unfiltered GLM-5.3 demonstrations of biological analysis improve Snowball's held-out BixBench accuracy under the same harness and execution budget. Measure paired BixBench changes and uncertainty, task coverage, tool-format failures, and response lengths. Broader evaluation is deferred until the BixBench result. Review trace completeness, native grades, and sequence handling before training; preserve negative results.

## Status

The expanded collection completed all 1,310 original task/repetition slots. The final audit proves exactly five attempts per task, with no missing or duplicate pairs. Native reward vectors exist for 1,285 attempts; 25 are ungraded. There are 946 final assistant `stop` markers, 248 output-limit endings, 49 final tool-use stops, eight final error stops, and 59 without an exported final assistant stop reason. Agent timeouts are an overlapping exception class: 86 attempts record one. No verifier-error diagnostic was recorded. Native Pi sessions and ATIF trajectories are present for 1,251 attempts.

Native score patterns across the graded attempts are 574 vectors with every component equal to 1, 381 with mixed or partial component credit, and 330 with every component equal to 0. These remain graded vectors, not binary success labels. The 946 final `stop` markers cover 238 tasks; nine also record runner exceptions, so this marker alone does not establish a clean run. A historical structural screen requiring native session and trajectory, no exception or recorded verifier error, and matched tool calls/replies retains 933 normal candidates. Of those, 558 have every component equal to 1 and cover 161 tasks. Their provider-counted output usage totals 24,112,468 tokens; this includes reasoning and possible auxiliary compaction output and is not a unique Snowball-supervised token count. Four normal traces have unresolved tool-call diagnostics. These screening counts are diagnostic subsets and do not define the unfiltered training pool.

The original batch retained 875 attempts: 829 verified per-attempt archives and 46 [verified fallback recoveries](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6016912375). The continuation executed only the remaining 435 slots and verified all 435 checkpoints, with no further checkpoint failures. It completed at 14:46:11 UTC; cleanup at 14:46:14 reported zero owned sandboxes. The small final Iris archive and completion audit were copied to private durable storage and retrieved for SHA-256 verification. Final archive SHA-256: `4b06bdb9e491145acaddddb0cd44928191386b22b80b3061a3b1a18c5511e68a` (2,240,445 bytes). Original native grades, checkpoint-failure labels, and interrupted-stream diagnostics are preserved.

Both cohorts used native Pi 0.87.0 with 131,072 total context, 32,768 solver output, thinking enabled, native compaction, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, repetition seeds 0–4, and up to 64 concurrent workers. The continuation repaired capture closure and retried a startup that was preempted before teacher generation; it did not rerun attempted slots. Original expanded protocol SHA-256: `24ebb14feb54c3ec97f4c79732a7d42efb2c8cc7c792c2bc6e714dbeb6833997`; continuation: `36e7a611fb25f8e6625934b123ad00f6b33cdace57945b32d7ac5a7ef9852a58`; 262-task manifest: `87f0276f2fe2a3675eb875079363d20d321a80ca216e265539c39a6524f7cd75`. Source archives, notices, launch snapshots, native results, and raw captures are retained.

The six-task control batch is complete: all reference reward components were 1.0 and all no-op components were 0.0, with verifier diagnostics reviewed. The other candidates remain a metadata shortlist. The [seven-attempt Terminus-2 batch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6004311716) is retained separately as diagnostic evidence; its continuation is superseded.

Pi collection completed all 30 planned attempts and retained 29 native reward vectors. Endings: 17 normal, eight output-limited, four agent timeouts, and one ungraded `DaytonaBadGatewayError`. No verifier errors were recorded. The 17 normal traces have matched tool calls and replies, with full or partial native component credit. They cover DepMap, pysam, CELLxGENE, PyDESeq2, and Scanpy; all five scikit-bio attempts ended at an output limit. They contain 869,472 provider-counted output tokens before reward selection and target-tokenizer accounting. No filtering has been applied; the first baseline retains all available solver traces.

Native Pi sessions and ATIF trajectories were retained for 26/30 attempts. Three timeouts lost native log export because `pi.txt` changed during archiving; the infrastructure failure also lacks native agent logs. Raw API captures are retained for all 30 attempts, including three interrupted response streams. The four timeout traces contain repeated identical tool exchanges. The complete archive, source notices, per-file hashes, configuration, launcher, and audit are privately preserved. Archive SHA-256: `61671f943850c0601a9febb3058bf3e1e2df3689b7ef06594280aa89ce087c9f`. No Daytona sandboxes remain.

The teacher uses native Pi 0.87.0, matching the runtime pin in [evaluation policy #9409](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9409), with the [Skill2Env paper, section 3.4](https://github.com/NVlabs/Skill2Env/blob/main/paper/Skill2Env_arXiv.pdf) teacher budget: 131,072 total context tokens, a 32,768-token solver output cap, high thinking, and native compaction. Pi's high setting maps to GLM chat-template thinking enabled; no provider `reasoning_effort` tier is sent. BixBench policy instead uses 32,768 total context and 8,192 output tokens; collection and evaluation budgets remain separate. Live requests obeyed the configured cap, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, and repetition seeds 0–4. The largest observed prompt was 98,346 tokens; compaction used a 16,384-token output cap. This is not a full context-boundary stress test.

Execution uses upstream Harbor `bf991e490394ef9c3250a6db2bc5cbda903cb4c3` with a configuration-only adapter around Pi. Native tools, prompt, loop, task resources, and component grades are retained. Setup allows the recorded package mirrors; agent execution allows the scoped model endpoint, and verification retains the task's no-network policy. The initial six-task collection used at most three concurrent trials, native 30-minute agent timeouts, a six-hour batch limit, and no whole-trial retries. The expanded batch retains native timeouts and task resources, with the concurrency and batch limit recorded above. Frozen protocol SHA-256: `33a9e03a0a426b9d1ed8c328f2743ec4efa9b0fdf4425907d4f93dce156aa338`. BixBench-overlap checking is not a prerequisite.

Before SFT, recover available recorded content, validate native-format conversion and loss masks, and count supervised tokens. Keep output limits, repeated tool loops, missing exports, and grader diagnostics as annotations. Pin the selected parent weights and tokenizer, validate the chosen training recipe and long-conversation handling, and freeze the BixBench evaluation protocol. No training or BixBench comparison has run.

## Links

- [Completed Pi collection and audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6006473943).
- Logbook: dated updates in this issue; keep this body current as decisions change.
- W&B report: pending the first training run.
- Dataset assessment and known grader issue: [#9630](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9630).
- Biology evaluation protocols and baselines: [#9258](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258).
- Source project: [Skill2Env](https://github.com/NVlabs/Skill2Env).

## Decision Log

- 2026-10-05: Start with released Skill2Env biology tasks and complete GLM-only demonstrations. Use native component rewards to select traces and assistant-only SFT. Defer relay methods.
- 2026-10-05: Treat general scientific data analysis as a possible expansion if the validated biology pool is insufficient.
- 2026-10-05: Track this experiment here and link its evaluation results from #9258. Preserve Atlas intake under #9630.
- 2026-10-05: Completed reference/no-op controls on six pinned tasks. Collection: five attempts per task, 30 total. Treat rewards as graded vectors and choose the SFT selection policy after inspecting pilot distributions; this supersedes earlier binary verified-success wording.

- 2026-10-05: Authorized the 30-rollout collection and removed BixBench-overlap checking as a prerequisite. Preserve source provenance and full component rewards.
- 2026-10-05: Superseded Terminus-2 with Pi to match the intended Snowball harness. Selected the paper's 128k context / 32k output teacher budget if supported. Retain the seven prior attempts separately; do not resume their queue.

- 2026-10-06: Completed the 30-attempt Pi batch with 29 native reward vectors and 17 normal trace candidates. Preserve all native scores and raw captures; keep output-limit endings, timeouts, and the ungraded infrastructure failure separate. SFT selection and training remain pending.

- 2026-10-06: Authorized five attempts for every remaining shortlisted biology task (262 tasks; 1,310 new attempts) while unattended. Selected 64 concurrent rollouts after checking bulk inference guidance and sandbox quota. Preserve every native reward vector and verified private artifacts; defer SFT selection and training.

- 2026-10-06: Recovered the first expanded job's 46 fallback attempts without changing native grades. Continue only the 435 unattempted slots; replace the short capture-close window with a bounded 35-minute wait outside the upload lock. Preserve all prior attempts, including incomplete and ungraded outcomes.

- 2026-10-06: Completed all 1,310 expanded slots without duplicates; all evidence is retained and continuation sandbox cleanup is complete. Keep the issue open for the planned SFT and evaluation stages.

- 2026-10-06: Selected an unfiltered first SFT baseline using all available GLM/Pi solver traces, including truncated and interrupted prefixes; supersedes earlier reward and completeness selection proposals. Preserve scores as annotations and avoid artificial termination targets. GitHub and Discord precedents support a bounded continuation but leave parent, mixture, and hyperparameters open.

- 2026-10-06: Selected September 21 Datakit SFT, biology traces only with no replay, one run at peak LR 1e-4, three epochs, 131,072-token training sequences, and effective global batch 16. Save/export and evaluate the final model only; per-epoch checkpointing was dropped because of model-size overhead.

- 2026-10-06: Confirmed full-parameter SFT with fresh AdamH (betas 0.9/0.95, epsilon 1e-8, weight decay 0, clip 1.0), 3% warmup, cosine decay from 1e-4 to 1e-5, and frozen imported router biases. Start evaluation with BixBench alone; decide on other evaluations after its result.

- 2026-10-06: Selected reconstructed conversations and CoreWeave H100 compute (32 GPUs). Finalized 5,120 windows with 73,894,261 supervised tokens per epoch; batch 16 and three epochs give 960 steps. All 58 preparation artifacts passed full SHA-256 readback. Preserve every available solver output, crop only masked context where necessary, and finish trainer validation before launch.

## Conclusion

Collection is complete: 1,310 expanded attempts plus the initial 30-attempt Pi batch. The first SFT baseline will train on all available solver traces without score or completion filtering. Earlier full-credit and structural screens describe subsets only. Convert recorded reasoning and tool calls to the chosen parent's native format, preserve interrupted prefixes without artificial termination targets, and count unique supervised tokens. The parent, mixture, optimizer, schedule, duration, sequence length, batch size, and final-only saving are selected in the agreed-settings table. Evaluate BixBench first and decide on broader evaluations afterward. Preparation and full SHA-256 readback are complete. Outputs from 1,319 attempts across 264 tasks yield 73,894,261 supervised tokens per epoch; 21 attempts have no solver output. CPU optimizer/checkpoint tests and full lint/type checks pass. The training coordinator is submitted with a gate on verified cache completion before GPU allocation. No optimizer updates or BixBench comparison have run.

🤖
# Research

The 268 biology candidates are a metadata shortlist, and the prepared six-task batch has passed file and hash checks but no reference or no-op trial has run. Task validity, training/evaluation overlap, licenses, and the Snowball before/after baseline remain open. [PR #9632](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9632) covers Atlas intake only; the regressions in [#9719](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9719) and evaluation variability in [#9558](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9558) make a bounded, paired SFT test important.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/sft/launcher.py#L731`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L731) — shared SFT step.
- [`experiments/evaluation/models.py#L28`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/models.py#L28) — Snowball evaluation model setup.

# Proposed Fix

1. Run the prepared 12-trial Harbor batch under the recorded three-hour limit once account billing and the compute cap are confirmed. For each of the six pinned tasks, require a full native reference pass, a non-passing no-op, and clean verifier logs; publish task revisions, component rewards, elapsed time, and grader or infrastructure failures. Exclude ambiguous tasks before collection.
2. Freeze a validated task manifest with task-level source and license records. Group shared fixtures and source-skill families when splitting tasks; exclude BixBench questions, capsules, assets, and close variants. Pin the Snowball parent, tokenizer, harness, generation limits, and scoring policy. Use BixBench-Verified-50 v1.0 with `decimal-precision-v1` for the bounded primary pilot and run the parent on that exact protocol before training; keep the 205-question CLI evaluation as a separately reported follow-up. Coordinate the benchmark record with [#9258](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258).

At the 13:49 UTC collection snapshot, 488 normal-ending traces had every native component at 1. Structural checks leave 482 candidates over 156 tasks, with 20,017,782 provider-counted output tokens. This includes reasoning and possibly auxiliary compaction output; it is not the unique Snowball-supervised token count. The larger normal-ending pool also contains partial-credit trajectories. Preserve their component vectors and decide acceptance after grader review. Repeated rollouts add solution variants without adding independent tasks.

Relevant precedents:

- [Snowball agent SFT #9225](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9225#issuecomment-5753734747): OpenThoughts-Agent plus instruction-following data improved pooled SWE-bench from 14.5% to 24.1%, with weaker Terminal-Bench results. The [recorded recipe](https://gist.github.com/lukedhlee/d152f86a58e8619a988361e1502f9e55) used full-parameter AdamH, LR 1e-4, betas 0.9/0.95, epsilon 1e-8, clip 1, zero weight decay, 3% warmup, 32,768-token sequences, and batch 64. Its second epoch added no SWE-bench gain.
- [Recent Snowball relay continuation](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-acont-step999): 8,982 traces, LR 3e-4, three passes, and batch 16 at 65,536 tokens; reported SWE-bench 45.3%, versus 13.8% for September 21. This starts from an already relay-trained parent, and the author flags possible confounders. It is evidence that thousands of agent traces can matter, not a matched biology recipe.
- [The exact Skill2Env paper, section 5.4](https://github.com/NVlabs/Skill2Env/blob/main/paper/Skill2Env_arXiv.pdf): GLM-5.3 assistant-token SFT at 128k gave weak or negative Qwen results. [Snowball expert negatives #9719](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9719) also include a regressing 5,000-conversation GLM continuation. Data quality, formatting, dose, and parent choice need measurement.

Proposed recipe, pending parent selection and token accounting:

- Parent: recommend the shared September 21 Datakit SFT checkpoint; pin weights, tokenizer, and its own thinking/tool chat template together. The parent is not yet fixed.
- Data: review high-scoring complete traces first; allow partial credit through an explicit component-based policy. Exclude malformed, looping, interrupted, or grader-invalid candidates from the initial training pool. Balance task families and deduplicate near-identical solutions. Hold out 10–15% of task families before sequence construction; all repetitions and segments of a task stay in one split.
- Targets: preserve main-agent reasoning, tool calls, final answers, and end-of-turn tokens; mask system/user/tool observations. Render GLM/Pi messages in Snowball's native format. Count each assistant target once. Keep auxiliary compaction generation outside the initial target set and preserve its resulting summary when it is part of the actual solver context.
- Training: full-parameter fine-tuning with fresh Adam state; betas 0.9/0.95, epsilon 1e-8, clip 1, weight decay 0, BF16 compute, frozen router bias. Start at LR 1e-5 with 5% warmup and cosine decay to 1e-6. These LR and warmup choices are conservative proposals, not a previously successful biology setting. A later 3e-5 arm can test sensitivity.
- Budget: one pass initially, save at approximately quarter/half/full exposure; extend to two passes only if held-out behavior improves. Target 65,536-token examples and effective batch 16, subject to memory validation. Inspect target coverage before finalizing length. Long traces require context-preserving examples at valid turn or compaction boundaries; do not silently truncate them. Use separate examples until the selected implementation proves packed-document isolation. Derive steps from the actual sequence cache, not provider usage totals.

Replay is an ablation. The [September 21 parent card](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21) records 20% long-context pretraining replay, but that does not establish the required fraction for this short continuation. Compare biology-only with 80% biology / 20% audited general SFT replay, at equal biology-token exposure and the same optimizer/schedule. Use token-based allocation and log both processed and loss-bearing tokens. General replay should cover reasoning, instruction following, and compatible tool use. Raw pretraining replay would be a separate arm with full next-token loss; it is most useful to test if broad or long-context retention regresses.

Before training: freeze the parent, audit graders and target formatting, compute unique target and context-token counts with Snowball's tokenizer, then validate one update, checkpoint export, and Pi tool-call parsing. Evaluate parent and selected intermediate checkpoints with identical Pi budgets on biology development tasks and BixBench, plus instruction-following, code/math, and long-context retention checks. Use development results for tuning and reserve the final benchmark comparison. GPU allocation and spend remain to be specified after sequence accounting.

comments.body:
🤖 Heads-up from marin#9920: the HF export in this recipe will fail at the final step unless patched.

`train.py` sets `model_ref` to the regional S3 copy of the parent (`ctx.artifact_path(parent)`), and `train_lm` passes that through as the converter's `reference_checkpoint`. The HF export hook calls `save_pretrained` without `save_reference_code`, which resolves to True for Snowball because `GrugMoeHfConfig` is not a `transformers` class. `_save_code_local` then calls raw `hf_hub_download(repo_id="s3://...")` and raises `HFValidationError` before the config, tokenizer and shard index are written. We hit exactly this on 2026-10-07 at 23:57 UTC in a CruxEval SFT run with the same recipe (marin#9920).

Since this run exports only once (`hf_save_steps=steps + 1`) with native checkpoints disabled (`save_interval=None`, `save_final_checkpoint=False`), a 960-step run would end with nothing saved. Fixes under discussion in #9920: plumb `save_reference_code=False` through `AdaptorExportConfig` → `save_hf_checkpoint_callback` → `save_pretrained` (the parent repo has no code files, so nothing is lost), or make `_save_code_local` URL-aware like the load paths.
